_comment: Every authority the curriculum, the Library and the locale data are allowed to cite. Shape and rules: schemas/source.toml. Cite by `id`; scripts/curriculum-status.js refuses an id that is not here. `licence` and `use` are what make the bundle promise checkable: only `use: verbatim` material may ship inside a release, everything else is either restated in our own words with the body cited, or fetched at runtime and cached on the player's machine.
licence_note: 17 U.S.C. 105 puts works of the US FEDERAL government in the public domain. It does not cover state agencies, county boards, universities, or congressionally chartered nonprofits such as the American Red Cross, none of which waive copyright by being freely readable. Those are `use: facts`: we cite them as the authority and write the fact in our own words, which copyright does not reach (Feist v. Rural Telephone Service, 499 U.S. 340, 1991).

sources.note: Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition (archive.cdc.gov; lesson 1 section 7 last reviewed 18 May 2012; read 2026-10-03): the comparison group as the key feature of analytic epidemiology; experimental and observational studies; association, and the remark that epidemiology by itself can never prove a cause; ratios, proportions and rates; the risk ratio. www.cdc.gov refuses scripted downloads; archive.cdc.gov does not. About Mold (https://www.cdc.gov/mold-health/about/index.html, dated 26 September 2024, read 2026-10-03 through a page summary): a bleach solution of no more than 1 cup of household laundry bleach in 1 gallon of water; "Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners. This will produce a poisonous gas."; rubber boots, gloves and goggles; "Open windows and doors to provide fresh air." About Tetanus (https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/about/index.html, published 15 May 2024, updated 8 September 2026, read 2026-10-03 through a page summary): the bacteria are found in the environment and enter through broken skin; see a healthcare provider about a puncture or deep wound such as stepping on a nail; the 10-year booster. The page does not mention rust. About Mold re-read 2026-10-04: the never-mix-bleach sentence confirmed. Read 2026-10-04 for Chickens and Eggs: Backyard Poultry (https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/about/backyard-poultry.html, published 18 July 2025; fetched with full browser headers, which cdc.gov accepted that day): bird flu, Campylobacter, E. coli, histoplasmosis and Salmonella; young children, older adults and weakened immune systems most at risk; "Remember that poultry can appear healthy and clean, but still spread harmful germs that make people sick."; handwashing after touching birds, eggs or equipment, sanitizer by the coop; no kissing or snuggling; birds and their equipment kept and cleaned outdoors; dedicated shoes kept outside; children under 5 not to handle poultry; bites and scratches washed, a doctor if the bird is sick, the wound serious or inflamed, or the last tetanus shot over 5 years ago; NPIP hatcheries; 30 days apart for new birds; collect eggs often, throw away cracked eggs, clean with fine sandpaper, a brush or a cloth, "Don't wash warm, fresh eggs because colder water can pull bacteria into the egg."; egg dishes to 160 F; local rules for selling eggs; roosters and noise ordinances; a draft-free shelter or a safe heat source in winter; clean before disinfecting, contact time on the label; gloves for droppings; after early deaths tell the hatchery and consider waiting 30 days. Backyard Flock Owners and Bird Flu (https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/risk-factors/backyard-flock-owners.html, 7 March 2025): "Poultry can get very sick from bird flu and usually die from their infection."; no contact with sick or dead birds, droppings or litter without personal protective equipment. Mosquito Control at Home (https://www.cdc.gov/mosquitoes/mosquito-control/mosquito-control-at-home.html, dated 16 April 2024, read 2026-10-04 through a page summary): once a week empty and scrub, turn over, cover or throw out items that hold water; "Tightly cover water storage containers (buckets, cisterns, rain barrels) so mosquitoes cannot get inside to lay eggs." Read 2026-10-04 for Moving Water Without Power: How to Disinfect Wells After an Emergency (https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-disinfect-wells-after-an-emergency.html, dated 29 May 2025, read through a page summary, quoted sentences checked against a January 2025 copy on restoredcdc.org): "Do not enter the well pit. Gases and vapors can build up in well pits, creating a hazardous environment."; "Turn off all electricity to the well area before clearing debris."; "Do not attempt to repair the water system unless you are experienced with this type of work; electrical shock can occur."; "Wells should be disinfected by a well or pump contractor, due to safety concerns."; "Remove the vent cap." Read 2026-10-04 for Stone, Clay and Earth: About Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html, dated 12 January 2026, read through a page summary, checked the same way): "CO is found in fumes produced any time you burn fuel in cars or trucks, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges, or furnaces."; "Never burn charcoal indoors." Read 2026-10-04 for Life in Soil (full browser headers): About Tetanus (https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/about/index.html, 8 September 2026): 1 in 10 United States cases fatal; jaw spasms the first sign; the 10-year booster; first aid for minor wounds; consult a provider for puncture, deep or soiled wounds, and (added after the 2026-10-04 fact check) for wounds that "Contain dead tissue including from burns, fractures, crush injuries, or frostbite". Tetanus: Causes and How It Spreads (https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/causes/index.html, 10 September 2026): "Spores of Clostridium tetani are common in the environment, including soil, dust, and manure."; puncture and contaminated wounds. About Histoplasmosis and Preventing Histoplasmosis (https://www.cdc.gov/histoplasmosis/about/index.html and /prevention/index.html, both 24 April 2024): the fungus in soil and in bird and bat droppings, mainly the central and eastern states; cleaning chicken coops, gardening and demolition as risk activities; large accumulations of droppings cleaned by professionals. About Valley Fever and Preventing Valley Fever (https://www.cdc.gov/valley-fever/about/index.html and /prevention/index.html, both 24 April 2024): Coccidioides in soil in the southwestern US and south-central Washington; avoid dusty areas, a fitted N95 respirator, stay inside in dust storms, avoid activities involving contact with soil such as gardening, use air filtration indoors, and clean skin injuries (a general list, not one limited to people at higher risk). Read 2026-10-04 for How Animals Work, Keeping Animals and Animal Health and Disease (full browser headers): Farm Animals, Healthy Pets, Healthy People (https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/about/farm-animals.html, updated 15 June 2026): "Even healthy animals can carry diseases."; the list of diseases farm animals can spread to people; livestock not to live in the home; handwashing after body fluids, milk and eggs, stalls, feed and equipment, fences and buckets; sanitizer of at least 60 percent alcohol; masks, gloves and boots for body fluids, stalls and births; dedicated shoes and gloves kept outside; not standing behind or approaching from the rear even when restrained; escape routes; children; bites, scratches and kicks (the signs of a serious wound, the 5-year tetanus rule, a kick to the head); animals enclosed at night against rabies; raised feeders, feed off the ground; vaccines for brucellosis, leptospirosis and rabies. About Q Fever (https://www.cdc.gov/q-fever/about/index.html, 15 May 2024): goats, sheep and cows; birth products, urine, dung and milk; dust; no US vaccine; avoid animals giving birth; no raw milk. Q fever Safety at Livestock Birthing Exhibits, fact sheet CS261725, undated (https://www.cdc.gov/q-fever/media/pdfs/QFever-Factsheet.pdf): miscarriage; pregnant women, weakened immune systems and heart problems to avoid birthing work; gloves, sleeves, goggles, boots, N95; respirator training and a doctor first. About Orf Virus (https://www.cdc.gov/orf-virus/about/index.html, 13 May 2024): sheep and goats, gloves. Raw Milk (https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/raw-milk.html, 31 January 2025): the germs, the groups at higher risk, choose pasteurized. About Rabies (https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/about/index.html, 27 January 2026): over 90 percent of animal cases in wildlife. Rabies Prevention (https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/prevention/index.html, 1 July 2025): "Any mammal can get rabies, but some are at higher risk."; never approach injured, sick or dead animals, especially night animals seen by day; wash wounds 15 minutes; urgent care. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check. Farm Animals re-read 2026-10-04: 'If you visit another farm, be sure to scrub your shoes and change your clothes. Do this before interacting with their animals and before coming back to your animals.'; 'Contact your veterinarian if you notice any signs of illness in your animals.' Q fever fact sheet CS261725: 'Be trained and certified to wear a respirator.', footnoted 'Talk to your doctor first about whether it is safe for you to wear a respirator.' About Rabies: 'Rabies is found in many wildlife species, which include: Bats, Raccoons, Skunks, Foxes' (a list, not a ranking). Klumb C, Ireland M, Miller B, et al. Rabies Cluster Among Steers on a Dairy Farm, Minnesota, 2024. MMWR 2025;74(40):622-625, 11 December 2025 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7440a3.htm, read 2026-10-04 through the web reader): five of 35 steers with neurologic signs consistent with rabies in May 2024, likely a point-source exposure to a rabid skunk; drooling, poor coordination, bellowing and head thrashing; postexposure prophylaxis for a veterinarian, two farm owners with extensive contact including possible saliva contact, and two children; 'Preventive vaccination of cattle should be considered in areas where terrestrial rabies is prevalent, the value of the animals is high, and potential for human exposure exists.' Read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning, through a page reader: Handwashing Facts (https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/data-research/facts-stats/index.html, 17 April 2024): "the surfactants in soap lift soil and microbes from skin"; lathering and scrubbing create friction. About Mold re-read the same day for its bleach sentences. Read 2026-10-04 with full browser headers for How Your Body Works: About Heart Attack Symptoms, Risk, and Recovery (https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/heart-attack.html, 24 October 2024): the major symptoms, tiredness and nausea more likely in women, "Call 9-1-1 if you notice symptoms of a heart attack", trained bystanders with CPR or a defibrillator. About Cardiac Arrest (https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/cardiac-arrest.html, 15 May 2024): the signs; call 9-1-1, find an AED, give CPR; more than 356,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year, about 60 to 80 percent dying before the hospital. Signs and Symptoms of Stroke (https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html, 19 May 2026): the five sudden signs; B.E. F.A.S.T.; note the time; best treatments within 3 hours; "Do not drive to the hospital or let someone else drive you."; transient ischemic attack. About High Blood Pressure (https://www.cdc.gov/high-blood-pressure/about/index.html, 28 January 2026): normal less than 120/80 mm Hg, high "consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg", changes through the day, usually no symptoms. Symptoms of Diabetes (https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/signs-symptoms/index.html, 15 May 2024). About Sepsis (https://www.cdc.gov/sepsis/about/index.html, 17 August 2026): "a life-threatening medical emergency"; gut, lung, skin or urinary tract; the six signs. Sepsis patient sheet (https://www.cdc.gov/sepsis/media/pdfs/Simplified-Sepsis-FS-Patient-508.pdf, undated): ask "Could I have sepsis?"; call 911 for severe signs. Heat-Related Illnesses sheet CS280226 (https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/media/pdfs/2026/09/Heat_Related_Illness-NEWLOGO.pdf, undated): heatstroke 103 F or higher, call 911, cool, nothing to drink; heat exhaustion, help if vomiting, worse or longer than 1 hour. Preventing Hypothermia (https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention/index.html, 25 August 2026): a medical emergency; below 95 F get medical attention immediately; possible above 40 F when wet. Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics (https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html, 12 January 2026): "kills without warning"; the common symptoms, "flu-like"; sleeping or intoxicated people can die before symptoms. Read 2026-10-04 for Rats, Flies, Mosquitoes and Ticks: Controlling Wild Rodent Infestations, How to Seal Up, How to Trap Up and How to Clean Up After Rodents (https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/, all 8 April 2024): infestation in and around the home as the main reason rodent diseases reach people; a mouse through a hole the width of a pencil (1/4 inch); steel wool and caulk; food, rubbish, compost bins, woodpiles and brush at 100 feet; snap traps, not glue or live traps; pre-baiting rats; at least 15 days; no sweeping or vacuuming droppings; 1.5 cups of bleach per gallon (1 part to 9), 5 minutes' soak; 30 minutes' airing; double-bagged dead rodents; vehicles aired 20 minutes, battery disconnected; heavy infestations need a respirator; ducts to a professional. About Hantavirus and Hantavirus Prevention (https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/, both 13 May 2024): breathing contaminated air; the deer mouse; symptoms 1 to 8 weeks after contact; 38 percent of those with breathing symptoms may die. About Leptospirosis (https://www.cdc.gov/leptospirosis/about/index.html, 10 February 2026). Preventing Plague (https://www.cdc.gov/plague/prevention/index.html, 5 March 2025). Mosquito Control at Home re-read (16 April 2024). Preventing Mosquito Bites (https://www.cdc.gov/mosquitoes/prevention/index.html, 28 August 2024): the six repellent ingredients; OLE and PMD not under 3; permethrin on clothing, never skin. About West Nile (https://www.cdc.gov/west-nile-virus/about/index.html, 16 June 2026): about 2,000 diagnosed, more than 1,300 severe and more than 130 deaths a year. Preventing Tick Bites (https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/prevention/index.html, 28 August 2024): 0.5 percent permethrin; dryer 10 minutes on high; shower within two hours; the body check; the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station landscaping steps; do not rely on spraying. What to Do After a Tick Bite (https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html, 9 June 2026): fine-tipped tweezers, steady even pressure, no twisting; no petroleum jelly, heat or nail polish; rash or fever within several weeks. About Mold re-read the same day for its never-mix-bleach sentence, cited also in Invasive Species. Added after the fact check (read 2026-10-04): About Sepsis, "A person with sepsis might have one or more of the following signs or symptoms"; the patient sheet, act right away on an infection that is not getting better or is getting worse, and "call 911 immediately" for severe signs (sepsis moved to the call-911 list of How Your Body Works). Symptoms of Diabetes: type 1 symptoms "can appear suddenly, in just a few weeks or months, and can be severe", with nausea, vomiting, stomach pains and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); type 2, "it's important to know the risk factors". Cardiac arrest: the signs include "Don't have a pulse"; not delaying CPR to check for one is labelled general practice. Controlling Wild Rodent Infestations: "The first signs of rodents usually appear before you even see a rat or mouse." How to Clean Up After Rodents, vehicles: "Be sure to wear plastic gloves and a long-sleeved shirt."; "Remove cables from the battery to avoid shock before inspecting the engine compartment."; "Reconnect the battery when the area is dry."; "Consult a qualified mechanic or automotive professional for assistance." Mosquito Control at Home lists screens among several steps ("Install or repair and use window and door screens."). Well Water Safety (https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/safety/index.html, also served at the older private-wells maintenance address; dated 4 June 2024; read 2026-10-04 with browser request headers): private wells not regulated, treated or monitored; setbacks of 50 feet from septic tanks, leach fields and livestock yards, 100 feet from petroleum tanks, liquid-tight manure storage and fertilizer storage, 250 feet from manure stacks; a well checkup and water test every year; retiring an unused well; "People or animals can also get hurt if they fall into a forgotten, crumbling well." Avoid, Spot, Treat: Frostbite and Hypothermia (CS253565-A) re-read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost: hypothermia at cool temperatures above 40 F in a person who is wet from rain, sweat or cold water and becomes chilled.

sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.note: Toxicological profiles. The authority for what a fuel or solvent does to a person. The atsdr.cdc.gov/toxprofiledocs path was retired; the profiles live on wwwn.cdc.gov now. ToxFAQs for Carbon Tetrachloride (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/TSP/ToxFAQs/ToxFAQsDetails.aspx?faqid=195&toxid=35, page last reviewed October 25, 2011, read 2026-10-04; first noted as undated, corrected after the fact check): former uses, including as a pesticide, now banned because of its harmful effects.

sources.name: NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards
sources.publisher: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, CDC
sources.note: Flash points, exposure limits and incompatibilities for common chemicals, in the public domain. Prefer it over any retailer or hobbyist page for fuel properties. Portland cement (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0521.html, page dated 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-03 through a page summary): first aid for the eyes "Irrigate immediately", for the skin soap wash promptly; symptoms include irritation of the eyes, skin and nose, and cough; target organs eyes, skin and respiratory system; first aid for breathing "Fresh air". Calcium hydroxide, synonyms including hydrated lime (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0092.html, page dated 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-03 through a page summary): symptoms include eye and skin burns, cough and bronchitis; prevent skin and eye contact; first aid for the eyes "Irrigate immediately". Phosphoric acid (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0506.html) and oxalic acid (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0474.html), both page dated 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-03 and re-read 2026-10-04 through a page summary: phosphoric acid lists eye and skin burns, oxalic acid irritation of the eyes and skin and eye burns (no skin burns; corrected after the 2026-10-04 fact check); for the eyes "Irrigate immediately"; for the skin "Water flush immediately" (phosphoric) and "Water flush promptly" (oxalic); remove clothing when wet or contaminated; swallowed, "Medical attention immediately" for both. Methyl-2-cyanoacrylate (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0405.html, page last reviewed 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-04 with full browser headers): contact with moisture causes rapid polymerization; irritation of eyes, skin and nose, blurred vision, tearing; first aid for the eyes "Irrigate immediately". Calcium oxide (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0093.html, page last reviewed 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-04 through a page summary): synonyms include burnt lime, quick lime and unslaked lime; incompatible with water "(liberates heat)", reacting to form calcium hydroxide; irritation of the eyes, skin and upper respiratory tract; first aid "Irrigate immediately" for the eyes and "Water flush immediately" for the skin. Calcium oxide also lists the symptoms "irritation eyes, skin, upper resp tract; ulcer, perforation nasal septum; pneumonitis; dermatitis" and the protection "Prevent skin contact" and "Prevent eye contact" (read 2026-10-04 through a page summary). Read 2026-10-04 for Soil Chemistry (full browser headers): Calcium carbonate (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0090.html, last reviewed 30 October 2019): occurs in nature as limestone, chalk, marble, dolomite, aragonite, calcite and oyster shells; irritation of eyes, skin and respiratory system, cough; eyes "Irrigate immediately". Calcium hydroxide (npgd0092, 30 October 2019) re-read: synonyms calcium hydrate, caustic lime, hydrated lime, slaked lime; eye and skin burns; skin "Soap flush immediately". Calcium oxide (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0093.html, 30 October 2019): synonyms burned lime, burnt lime, lime, pebble lime, quick lime, unslaked lime; reacts with water, liberating heat; ulcer and perforation of the nasal septum, dermatitis; skin "Water flush immediately". First Aid Procedures (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/firstaid.html, last reviewed 17 October 2018): what each first-aid code means, including irrigating the eyes with large amounts of water while lifting the lids and getting medical attention immediately. Re-read 2026-10-04 after the Soil Chemistry fact check: the skin codes carry their medical-attention steps, "Water flush immediately" ending "Get medical attention promptly." and "Soap flush immediately" ending "If irritation persists after washing, get medical attention."; calcium hydroxide and calcium oxide both list "Swallow: Medical attention immediately". Zinc oxide (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0675.html, page dated 30 October 2019, read 2026-10-04 through a page summary for Salvage and Reuse): symptoms listed as metal fume fever, with chills, muscle ache, nausea, fever, dry throat, cough, chest tightness and others. Read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning, through a page reader: Sodium hydroxide (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0565.html, page last reviewed 30 October 2019): synonyms "Caustic soda, Lye [Sodium hydroxide], Soda lye, Sodium hydrate"; "Colorless to white, odorless solid (flakes, beads, granular form)."; incompatibilities including water, acids and "metals such as aluminum, tin & zinc"; symptoms "irritation eyes, skin, mucous membrane; pneumonitis; eye, skin burns; temporary loss of hair"; prevent skin and eye contact; provide eyewash and quick drench; first aid irrigate immediately, water flush immediately, medical attention immediately if swallowed. Potassium hydroxide (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0523.html, page last reviewed 30 October 2019): synonyms "Caustic potash, Lye [Potassium hydroxide], Potassium hydrate"; incompatibilities including acids, water and metals when wet; symptoms including eye and skin burns.

sources.name: Occupational Safety and Health Administration
sources.note: 29 CFR 1910.106 defines the flammable-liquid categories by flash point. Federal regulation text, so quotable, unlike the NFPA standard that parallels it. Co-publisher, with NIOSH, of Nail Gun Safety: A Guide for Construction Contractors (September 2011, OSHA 3459-8-11); see niosh. OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 5, Noise (https://www.osha.gov/otm/section-3-health-hazards/chapter-5, updated 6 July 2022, read 2026-10-03): the threshold of pain about 10 million times the threshold of hearing; decibels not summed by arithmetic addition; 6 dB less per doubling of distance in a free field (90, 84, 78 dB at 1, 2, 4 m), less indoors; doubling the sound power adds 3 dB; A-weighting and 500 to 4,000 Hz; near-field readings unreliable; source, path, receiver, hearing protection the last line of defense; any gap through which air can pass lets a significant amount of noise pass; absorption does nothing for the direct sound; damping vibrating panels; a very small leak can destroy an earmuff's effectiveness; people losing hearing often lose quiet high sounds first. Preventing Skin Problems from Working with Portland Cement, OSHA 3351-07, 2008 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA-3351-portland-cement.pdf, read 2026-10-03), which states it is in the public domain: wet portland cement can cause caustic burns, not reliably signalled by pain and able to worsen after contact ends; see a health care professional immediately; butyl or nitrile gloves, sleeves taped to gloves, waterproof boots, kneepads or dry kneeboards, eye protection; wash in clean cool water with pH-neutral or slightly acidic soap; no lanolin or petroleum jelly. Its glove-removal table is credited to CPWR, so restate it. Solutions for Electrical Contractors eTool, Materials Handling: Heavy Lifting (https://www.osha.gov/etools/electrical-contractors/materials-handling/heavy, undated, read 2026-10-03): lifting heavy items one of the leading causes of injury in the workplace; loads heavier than about 50 pounds raise the risk; "Maintain neutral and straight spine alignment whenever possible. Usually, bending at the knees, not the waist, helps maintain proper spine alignment."; use your legs when lifting from a low location; bending lets leverage significantly increase the effective load on the back; keep the load close, bending at the waist only for large, bulky loads to keep them closer (the posture rule added after the 2026-10-04 fact check), turn with the feet, the power zone of mid-thigh to mid-chest, two or more people over 50 pounds, ramps or lift gates rather than lifting, rolling spools hard to stop, cold muscles. Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid (https://www.osha.gov/heat-exposure/illness-first-aid, undated, read 2026-10-03): the signs of heat stroke and heat exhaustion; "When any of these symptoms is present, promptly provide first aid. Do not try to diagnose which illness is occurring."; workers with symptoms allowed to stop working; "When in doubt, call 911!"; move to a cooler area and cool immediately, cold water or an ice bath the best method, ice or cold wet towels on the head, neck, trunk, armpits and groin, outer clothing off, fans; never leave the person alone. Read 2026-10-04 for Organising Shared Work and Teaching What You Know: Job Hazard Analysis, OSHA 3071, 2002 (Revised) (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha3071.pdf): break a job into steps; what can go wrong, the consequences, how it could arise, contributing factors and likelihood; priority to jobs with severe potential, "Jobs in which one simple human error could lead to a severe accident or injury", and new jobs; act at once on an immediate danger; engineering controls first, then administrative controls, then personal protective equipment; photograph or videotape the job for reference. Materials Handling and Storage, OSHA 2236, 2002 (Revised): seek help when a load is too bulky to grasp, cannot be seen over, or cannot be safely handled. Heat pages, undated: Protecting New Workers ("Almost half of heat-related deaths occur on a worker's first day on the job or a worker's first day back after an extended absence"; shorter work, more breaks, monitoring, "Use a buddy system and don't allow new workers to work alone."; the Rule of 20 percent); Water. Rest. Shade. (drink frequently, "not just if they are thirsty"; electrolytes for jobs over two hours; breaks in a cool place; "skipping breaks is not safe"); Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid ("When in doubt, cool the worker and call 911."). Heat pages re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check. Protecting New Workers: the Rule of 20 percent example, "if the normal workday lasts 8 hours, then new workers should work no more than 1 hour and 40 minutes (20 percent of 8 hours) on their first day in the heat. They can spend the rest of the work day without heat stress."; existing workers lose heat tolerance during an absence or over the winter and are at increased risk after an absence of one week or more, when temperatures first rise, and "Whenever the weather is significantly warmer than on previous days". Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid: the listed signs of heat stroke and of heat exhaustion; "any unusual symptom can be a sign of overheating"; "Do not try to diagnose which illness is occurring."; cold-water or ice-bath immersion "is the best method to cool workers rapidly in an emergency"; removing outer layers, ice or cold wet towels on the head, neck, trunk, armpits and groin, fans; "Confusion, slurred speech, or unconsciousness are signs of heat stroke."; "Never leave a worker with heat-related illness alone." Resource for Development and Delivery of Training to Workers, OSHA 3824-05R 2021 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha3824.pdf), which states its material is in the public domain: activity-based learning at least two-thirds of training hours; training in a language and vocabulary workers understand; the principles of adult education, including "Adults learn best by doing". Read 2026-10-04 for Stone, Clay and Earth: Trench collapses can be deadly, OSHA 3971-06, 2022 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3971.pdf): cave-ins more likely than other excavation incidents to kill; "It only takes seconds to become buried in thousands of pounds of soil." Silica, Crystalline topic page (https://www.osha.gov/silica-crystalline, undated): silica in sand, stone, concrete and mortar; respirable particles created when cutting, sawing, grinding, drilling and crushing stone, rock, concrete, brick, block and mortar; silicosis "an incurable lung disease that can lead to disability and death", lung cancer, COPD and kidney disease. The heavy lifting eTool ("Avoid twisting... Turn by moving the feet rather than twisting the torso.") and OSHA 3351 re-read the same day. Silica, Crystalline overview page (https://www.osha.gov/silica-crystalline, undated, read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You): crystalline silica in sand, stone, concrete and mortar; respirable dust from cutting, sawing, grinding, drilling and crushing; silicosis "an incurable lung disease that can lead to disability and death". Hazard Alert: Falls and Other Hazards to Workers Removing Snow from Rooftops and Other Elevated Surfaces, HA-3513, December 2017 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA-3513ROOF-SNOW-HAZARD.pdf, read 2026-10-04 for How a Building Stands Up; osha.gov refuses curl, so the PDF was fetched through the web reader and its text extracted with pdftotext): shock and electrocution from contacting power lines among the hazards; "Always treat power lines, wires and other conductors as energized, even if they are down or appear to be insulated."; "Maintain a distance of at least 10 feet from any power line"; snow rakes and drag lines from the ground. Read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out, Repairing a Building and Salvage and Reuse: Fall Prevention Campaign (https://www.osha.gov/stop-falls, undated): falls the leading cause of death in construction; "In 2024, there were 389 fatal falls to a lower level out of 1,034 construction fatalities (BLS data)." Protecting Roofing Workers, OSHA 3755-05 2015 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3755.pdf), which states its material is in the public domain: falls from roofs nearly 1,200, or 34 percent, of construction fall deaths 2003 to 2013; three points of contact as good practice; tools hauled up in a bucket on a rope; most roofer electrocutions from overhead power lines, service drops the most common; inspect an older roof from inside for integrity; high winds, wet weather and ice especially hazardous, slate, tile, metal and some single-ply membranes slippery when wet; heat illness signs and "WATER, REST, SHADE". Agricultural Operations, Hazards and Controls (https://www.osha.gov/agricultural-operations/hazards, undated, read 2026-10-04): zoonoses and how people catch them (direct contact with animals or products such as manure or placenta, raw meat or raw milk, bites, contaminated soil, food or water); needlesticks in veterinary work (an approved sharps container, never removing a cap by mouth, avoiding recapping, gloves); respiratory hazards in barns and manure pits from organic dust and the breakdown of grain and animal waste. Read 2026-10-04 for Pottery and Firing: Silica, Crystalline (https://www.osha.gov/silica-crystalline, undated): crystalline silica used to make glass, pottery, ceramics and bricks; manufacturing ceramic products among exposures; silicosis an incurable lung disease. Read 2026-10-04 for Making a Tool: Hand and Power Tools, OSHA 3080, 2002 (Revised) (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha3080.pdf): "The greatest hazards posed by hand tools result from misuse and improper maintenance."; the chisel used as a screwdriver, the loose handle, the sprung wrench and mushroomed heads; portable abrasive wheels inspected and ring-tested, "Take care to ensure that the spindle speed of the machine will not exceed the maximum operating speed marked on the wheel.", never standing in the plane of rotation at start-up, "Portable grinding tools need to be equipped with safety guards", eye or face protection, never clamping a hand-held grinder in a vice (speed rating and guards added after the 2026-10-04 fact check). For Wells and Groundwater, Water and Wind Power and Cold Storage Without a Fridge (read 2026-10-04): 29 CFR 1926.651(g), 1926.652(a)(1) and 1926.501(b)(1); see ecfr. Read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows, Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops and Power Tools: Controlling Electrical Hazards, OSHA 3075, 2002 (Revised) (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha3075.pdf), which states it is in the public domain: conductors and insulators, the earth, air in an arc or lightning; pure water a poor conductor, impurities and wet skin; the four ways the body completes a circuit; amount, path, time and frequency; the effects table for hand to foot for one second, which OSHA credits to W. B. Kouwenhoven, Human Safety and Electric Shock, Instrument Society of America, November 1968, so restate it; burns the most common shock-related injury, electrical, arc and thermal; freezing, blisters, "Low voltage does not imply low hazard."; hidden internal injuries and emergency medical help; static electricity; insulation colours; system and equipment grounding, a secondary measure; fuses and breakers protect conductors and equipment; GFCIs at 5 milliamperes within 1/40 of a second; arc-fault devices; 10 feet from overhead lines. Hand and Power Tools, OSHA 3080, 2002 (Revised), re-read in full the same day: the five basic rules; power tools fitted with guards and safety switches; the general precautions; guards never removed in use; circular saw guards; switches; electric tools (burns and shocks, fibrillation, falls from ladders, three-wire grounding, double insulation, isolation transformers, the third prong, gloves and footwear, damp or wet locations); abrasive wheels (ring test, spindle speed, disintegration at start-up, the plane of rotation, eye or face protection, never clamped in a vise); pneumatic, liquid fuel, powder-actuated and hydraulic tools. The text layer splits some words with stray spaces (manuf acturers); quotations close them up. Woodworking eTool, undated: Kickbacks (https://www.osha.gov/etools/woodworking/machine-hazards/kickbacks: a saw seizing the stock and hurling it back; causes; spreaders and anti-kickback fingers; sharpening prevents kickback; avoid deep cuts; stand back or to the side) and Handheld Circular Saws (https://www.osha.gov/etools/woodworking/production/machines-tools/handheld-circular-saws: kickback as the blade catching the stock and throwing it back toward the operator; the proper blade, sharpening, the maker's speed, clearance, supporting all pieces of stock; hands out of the line of the cut). Green Job Hazards, Solar Energy: Lockout/Tagout (https://www.osha.gov/green-jobs/solar/lockout-tagout, undated): solar energy equipment can generate electrical energy, and employers should assure that workers cover the panels while installing or servicing them. Silica, Crystalline (undated) and HA-3513 (DTSEM 12/2017) re-read the same day. Working Safely Around Downed Electrical Wires, Fact Sheet DOC FS-3941, February 2018 (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/downed_electrical_wires.pdf, read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows and Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops): "Never go near a downed or fallen electric power line."; fallen lines can electrocute you if you touch them or the ground nearby; contact the utility; treat everything electrical as energized until tested and proven de-energized. Written for workers in storm cleanup; applying it to rescuing a person touching a line is the guides' own reading, labelled as such.

sources.name: National Fire Protection Association
sources.note: NFPA 30 and friends are copyrighted standards, free to read online and not free to copy. Where a definition exists in both NFPA and OSHA, cite OSHA.

sources.name: IAEI Magazine
sources.note: The electrical inspectors' association's magazine: explanatory articles on the National Electrical Code, a SECONDARY source for what the code says, since NFPA 70 is copyrighted and its free online view needs an account. Read 2026-10-04 for Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops: Lofland, Keith, Are there any other such receptacle replacement requirements?, Focus on the Code, 16 May 2012 (https://iaeimagazine.org/columns/focus-on-the-code/are-there-any-other-such-receptacle-replacement-requirements/): under the 2011 NEC, 406.4(D)(3) to (6), a replacement receptacle must have GFCI protection, AFCI protection (enforced from 1 January 2014), tamper resistance or weather resistance where the current code requires it at that outlet. Hunter, Randy, Article 406: Receptacles, Cord Connectors, and Attachment Plugs, November/December 2014 issue, posted 2 December 2014 (https://iaeimagazine.org/2014/novemberdecember-2014/article-406-receptacles-cord-connectors-and-attachment-plugs/), which says it is based on the 2011 NEC: 406.4(D)(1) a grounding-type replacement where a grounding means exists; (D)(2) without one, a non-grounding receptacle, a GFCI receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground", or a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI and marked "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground"; (D)(3) to (6) the GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant and weather-resistant replacement requirements, described as retroactive when replacements are made. Neither describes the 2023 edition Washington enforces; say so whenever citing them, and never quote them.

sources.name: Environmental Protection Agency
sources.note: Household waste and mixing pages read 2026-10-03: Composting at Home (last updated 8 December 2025: what to avoid in a backyard pile and its two footnotes; at least two to three times the volume of browns to greens; a bin lid and no gaps over a quarter inch; three to five months); Household Hazardous Waste (1 June 2026: never mix, original containers, corroding containers to the fire department; read labels for disposal directions to reduce the risk of products exploding, igniting, leaking or mixing on the way to a disposal facility; the glass cleaner of one tablespoon of vinegar in a quart of water); Used Household Batteries (21 July 2026) and Used Lithium-Ion Batteries (20 March 2026); Managing, Reusing, and Recycling Used Oil (25 June 2026: one oil change can contaminate one million gallons of fresh water); Cleaning Up a Broken CFL (28 September 2026); What to Do if a Mercury Thermometer Breaks (14 November 2025: open windows and doors to the outside before cleanup, cut out only the affected part of a carpet, keep the area ventilated to the outside for at least 24 hours after); Chromated Arsenicals (CCA) (22 December 2025: do not burn treated wood, not reused as mulch); Burn Wise, What You Can Do (3 November 2025; programme ended 2025, kept as a historic record: never burn garbage, plastic or pressure treated wood); the archived Backyard Burning pages at archive.epa.gov (undated, no longer updated; use their pollutant and ash findings, not their old dioxin-source rankings); Protect Your Family from Exposures to Asbestos (25 June 2026); Protect Your Family from Sources of Lead (19 August 2026); Safe Disposal of Pesticides (25 June 2026); Read the Label First brochure EPA 740-F-15-006 (undated: use the right amount, original containers, never in food or drink containers); Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (24 February 2026: the 6 and 8.25 percent bleach table; the calcium hypochlorite stock of about 500 mg/L used at 1 part to 100). Read 2026-10-03: Sources of Combustion Products (https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/sources-combustion-products, last updated 17 December 2025): never use a gas stove to heat your home. Lead-Safe Renovations for DIYers (https://www.epa.gov/lead/renovation-repair-and-painting-program-do-it-yourselfers, last updated 20 August 2026): a home built before 1978 may have lead-based paint; assume it if the age is unknown; EPA recommends hiring a lead-safe certified contractor; the do-it-yourself setup, N-100 respirator, misting, HEPA vacuum and cleanup, with a low-temperature heat gun under 1,100 F among the tools. Chromated Arsenicals (CCA) re-read 2026-10-04: used in residential decks and playsets before 2004; do not burn; goggles and a dust mask when sawing, and wash hands after handling. Volatile Organic Compounds' Impact on Indoor Air Quality (https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/volatile-organic-compounds-impact-indoor-air-quality, last updated 23 June 2026, read 2026-10-04): glues and adhesives among VOC sources; very high levels during use that persist; "if a label says to use the product in a well-ventilated area, go outdoors or in areas equipped with an exhaust fan to use it. Otherwise, open up windows to provide the maximum amount of outdoor air possible."; keep out of reach of children and pets; buy only what you will use soon; household hazardous waste collection; methylene chloride in adhesive removers converted to carbon monoxide in the body, used outdoors when possible. Cross-Connection Control Manual, EPA 816-R-03-002, February 2003 (first printed 1973, revised 1989, technical corrections 2003; read 2026-10-04 from the copy at https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/sites/static/files/2015-09/documents/epa816r03002_0.pdf): 62.4 pounds for a cubic foot of water; "The rate of increase for water is 0.433 psi per foot of depth."; 100 feet of head equal to 43.3 psig; 14.7 psia at sea level and the 33.9 foot column; the siphon, and its crest no higher than 33.9 feet above the upper liquid level; the air gap "twice the supply pipe diameter but never less than one inch"; hose bibb vacuum breakers; the 1979 chlordane backsiphonage case (a garden hose left in a barrel of diluted pesticide); testing of backflow preventers, and certified backflow device testers in the sample ordinance. Read 2026-10-04 for Soil Chemistry and The Ground Under You: Read the Label First: Protect Your Household (brochure 740-F-15-006, undated, https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-02/documents/household.pdf; its web page last updated 5 November 2025): labels give safe use, storage, first aid and help numbers; "It is very dangerous to put products in food and beverage containers"; the right amount; keep products out of water and never pour lawn and garden products down the drain; poison control and the label. National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/national-primary-drinking-water-regulations, last updated 31 August 2026): nitrate measured as nitrogen 10 mg/L and the risk to infants below six months. A Citizen's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-12/002, listed by EPA as December 2016; the current file at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-12/documents/2016_a_citizens_guide_to_radon.pdf carries corrected links and contact details): "Radon is a cancer-causing, radioactive gas."; about 21,000 deaths a year from EPA's 2003 assessment; the Surgeon General's warning; nearly 1 in 15 US homes estimated to have elevated radon; "Any home may have a radon problem."; test all homes below the third floor; kit placement; fix at 4 pCi/L; follow-up testing; average indoor 1.3 and outdoor 0.4 pCi/L; soil suction systems by trained contractors; retest every two years; radon in well water. Publications about Radon (https://www.epa.gov/radon/publications-about-radon, last updated 9 July 2026): no known safe level; consider fixing between 2 and 4 pCi/L. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check of Soil Chemistry and The Ground Under You: Will boiling my water help? (https://www.epa.gov/mn/will-boiling-my-water-help, EPA in Minnesota, one of its frequently asked questions on nitrate in southeast Minnesota ground water, last updated 11 June 2026, downloaded and read in full): "Boiling water will NOT reduce nitrate levels. In fact, it will make the level of nitrate worse because some of the water will evaporate but the nitrate will not." The Read the Label First brochure (740-F-15-006) re-read: it is written for "household products such as cleaners and pesticides", so applying it to plain fertilizer is our application; it also says "Keep pets and children away from treated areas as directed on the label." A Citizen's Guide to Radon re-read for its dates: the front cover prints "EPA402/K-12/002 | 2025", the back cover "May 2012", and the file's properties give created 16 December 2016 and last modified in 2025. Moisture Control Guidance for Building Design, Construction and Maintenance, EPA 402-F-13053, December 2013 (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2014-08/documents/moisture-control.pdf, read 2026-10-04): why foundations get wet ("Crawl spaces and basements are holes in the ground and have more extensive contact with soil than slab-on-grade foundations."); a 5 percent fall in the finish grade away from the foundation, or a stricter local code, applied over 6 to 10 feet; at least 8 inches of exposed foundation after final grading; capillary breaks between foundation and framing, under slabs and on footings; a vapour barrier directly beneath a slab; perimeter drainage below the top of the footing; basement and crawl space floors above the 100-year flood level and the water table. Lead-Safe Renovations for DIYers (https://www.epa.gov/lead/renovation-repair-and-painting-program-do-it-yourselfers, last updated 20 August 2026, read 2026-10-04 for How a Building Stands Up): "If your home was built before 1978, it may have lead-based paint"; a renovation in a pre-1978 home with lead-based paint "can easily create dangerous lead dust"; EPA recommends hiring a lead-safe certified contractor. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check of How a Building Stands Up: Learn About Asbestos (https://www.epa.gov/asbestos/learn-about-asbestos, last updated 13 July 2026, read 2026-10-04): the list "Where asbestos may be found", including "Textured paint and patching compounds used on walls and ceilings" and "Attic and wall insulation produced containing vermiculite"; fibres released by "building or home maintenance, repair, and remodeling". Protect Your Family from Exposures to Asbestos (25 June 2026) re-read the same day: "Generally, you can't tell whether a material contains asbestos simply by looking at it, unless it is labeled."; "If you suspect material contains asbestos, don't touch it."; "Taking samples yourself is not recommended."; samples by a trained and accredited asbestos professional; removal and major repair by people trained and qualified in handling asbestos. Read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out, Repairing a Building and Salvage and Reuse: Moisture Control Guidance for Building Design, Construction and Maintenance, EPA 402-F-13053, December 2013 (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2014-08/documents/moisture-control.pdf): "In most climates, rain is the largest source of water in buildings."; water runs downhill, wicks upward ("When water is in tiny pores, gravity is not the most important force acting on it.") and "may travel many feet along the bottom of a floor joist or roof truss before collecting in a drop big enough to fall."; Table 1-1 (shingling or sealing; overhangs, copings and drip edges as capillary breaks); downspouts to sloped leaders at 5 percent extending at least 10 feet from the foundation; roof maintenance: inspect semi-annually and soon after heavy winds or rains, do not rest ladders against gutters, granules in gutters, moss and lichen removed with a water hose and nozzle sprayed down the slope (under "Special Considerations for Asphalt Shingle Roofs", so asphalt only; nothing on pressure washers), do not chip ice from a blocked drain, a logbook and roof map; failure to correct roof and ceiling problems quickly "can cause additional damage". Read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out after its fact check: Learn About Asbestos lists "Attic and wall insulation produced containing vermiculite"; Protect Your Family from Asbestos-Contaminated Vermiculite Insulation (last updated 17 April 2026, https://www.epa.gov/asbestos/protect-your-family-asbestos-contaminated-vermiculite-insulation): "a pebble-like, pour-in product and is usually gray-brown or silver-gold in color"; leave it undisturbed in the attic or walls; do not store boxes or other items in an attic that contains it; do not let children play there; do not attempt to remove it yourself; hire a professional asbestos contractor for renovation that would disturb it. Lead-Safe Renovations for DIYers (https://www.epa.gov/lead/lead-safe-renovations-diyers, last updated 20 August 2026; the old renovation-repair-and-painting-program-do-it-yourselfers URL redirects there): assume lead if the age is unknown; set up, N-100 respirator suggested, mist, HEPA, wash, clean twice; the rule generally not for homeowners in their own homes except rentals, child care and resale. Reduce the Risk of Lead Exposure at Home (https://www.epa.gov/lead/reduce-risk-lead-exposure-home, last updated 19 August 2026; the protect-your-family-sources-lead URL now redirects there): lead paint in good shape usually not a problem; refinishing old furniture among the jobs that expose people. Lead Test Kits (https://www.epa.gov/lead/testkits, last updated 6 November 2025): no kit meets both criteria; recognised kits reliable only for a negative result when used by trained professionals. Learn About Asbestos (last updated 13 July 2026) and Protect Your Family from Exposures to Asbestos (25 June 2026) re-read. Chromated Arsenicals (CCA) and Creosote pages (both last updated 22 December 2025): CCA in decks and play sets before 2004, homeowner products discontinued December 2003, not reused as mulch, never burned at home, goggles and dust mask when sawing; creosoted railroad ties reused as landscape timbers, no health risks of concern found for the general public, never burned at home; reuse of either not regulated under pesticide law. Safe Disposal of Pesticides (last updated 25 June 2026): "Never reuse empty pesticide containers. Pesticide residues can contaminate the new contents and cause serious harm." Appliance Disposal (last updated 8 July 2026) and Prohibition on Venting Refrigerants (8 December 2025): mercury, oils and PCBs in older appliances; R-290 propane in some new ones; isobutane R-600a in household refrigerators exempt from the venting rule; a professional such as an appliance repair shop to recover refrigerant. Waste Management Hierarchy (last updated 19 December 2025) and Sustainable Management of Construction and Demolition Materials (18 March 2026): reuse most preferred; deconstruction; commonly reused C&D materials. WaterSense Fix a Leak Week re-read (13 March 2026): the two-hour meter test, the 10-minute dye test, 9,300 gallons a year, one drip a second over 3,000 gallons a year. A Brief Guide to Mold re-read: "Do not paint or caulk moldy surfaces."; renters report leaks. Protect Your Home's Water (https://www.epa.gov/privatewells/protect-your-homes-water, last updated 26 February 2026, read 2026-10-04): slope the ground so runoff drains away from a well; check safe distances from a well with the local health department or environmental agency. Read 2026-10-04 for Pottery and Firing, from AP-42, Compilation of Air Emissions Factors: Section 11.25 Clay Processing (January 1995, https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-10/documents/c11s25.pdf): the definition of clay; kaolin, ball clay, fire clay (withstands 1,500 C) and common clay (vitrification point below 1,100 C). Section 11.3 Brick and Structural Clay Product Manufacturing (August 1997, https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-10/documents/c11s03.pdf): firing in six steps; firing zone about 2,000 F; 20 to 50 hours to dry, fire and cool; fluorine released as HF at 500 to 600 C. Section 11.7 Ceramic Products Manufacturing (May 2025, https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-06/c11s07_2025_final.pdf): earthenware, stoneware, chinaware and porcelain; drying and differential shrinkage; presinter thermal processing and bisque firing; glazes maturing at 600 to 1,500 C; firing at about two-thirds of the melting point; short firing gives porous ware. The 2020-10 URL for c11s07 returned an error page; the 2025 final is current. Read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning: 6 Steps for Safe & Effective Disinfectant Use, one-page sheet, April 2020, written during the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2020-04/documents/disinfectants-onepager.pdf): step 1, check that the product is EPA-approved by its registration number at epa.gov/listn; then read the directions, pre-clean with soap and water, contact time with the surface kept wet, gloves and handwashing, lids closed and out of reach of children. Read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species and Rats, Flies, Mosquitoes and Ticks: Introduction to Pesticide Labels (https://www.epa.gov/pesticide-labels/introduction-pesticide-labels, last updated 2 June 2026): "It is a violation of Federal law to use this product in a manner inconsistent with its labeling."; "the label is the law". In Case of Pesticide Emergency (https://www.epa.gov/rodenticides/case-pesticide-emergency, 28 July 2026): call 911 if unconscious, having trouble breathing or convulsions; the label's first aid; 1-800-222-1222. About Rats and Mice (10 June 2026): the Norway rat, roof rat and house mouse as non-native pests; native rodents feed predators. Restrictions on Rodenticide Products (8 September 2026) and Safely Use Rodent Bait Products (29 September 2026): consumer products only as ready-to-use bait stations; second-generation anticoagulants for professional and agricultural markets only; store out of reach and never next to food; remove dead rodents promptly. Tips for Hiring a Rodent Control Professional (29 January 2026): ask to see the licence; the state pesticide regulatory agency. Asthma Triggers: Gain Control (https://www.epa.gov/asthma/asthma-triggers-gain-control, 6 July 2026): cockroach droppings and saliva as asthma triggers; clean, airtight containers, sealed cracks; insecticides harm people too. Added after the fact check (read 2026-10-04): Restrictions on Rodenticide Products, second-generation anticoagulants "more likely than first-generation anticoagulants to be able to kill after a single night's feeding" and longer in animal tissues, so "no longer are registered for use in products geared toward consumers"; consumer bait stations contain bromethalin, chlorophacinone or diphacinone; bromethalin, cholecalciferol and zinc phosphide are not anticoagulants, "Each is toxic in other ways."; professional and agricultural products "are not to be sold in “consumer” stores". Read 2026-10-04 for Wells and Groundwater: Protect Your Home's Water (last updated 26 February 2026): annual tests for total coliform, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH, and when to test at once; after a flood, "Get assistance from a well or pump contractor to clean and disinfect your well before turning on the pump." (added after the 2026-10-04 fact check); a certified driller for new wells, changes and closing; sloping the ground away; no wastes in dry or abandoned wells; never cutting the casing below ground; inspecting casing, cap and seal; keeping maintenance records. What to Do After the Flood (816-F-05-021, listed as updated October 2024 on the page What to Do With Your Private Well After a Flood, last updated 18 June 2026): do not turn on a flooded pump; wiring checked before restarting, and "Get assistance in turning the pump on from a well or pump contractor"; "If pumps are not cleaned and properly lubricated they can burn out."; "Rubber boots and gloves are not adequate protection from electric shock." (the last three added after the 2026-10-04 fact check); wells over 10 years old or under 50 feet deep likely contaminated; the one-gallon bleach disinfection procedure, 6 to 24 hours, a bacteria test 7 to 10 days later; drilled, driven and bored wells best disinfected by a contractor.

sources.name: United States Geological Survey
sources.note: Elevation, hydrography, geology and streamflow. The terrain under the canonical world comes from here. Topographic maps (read 2026-10-03): the FAQs What is a topographic map?, How current are US Topo maps? (a three-year production cycle) and How do I find, download, or order topographic maps? (free downloads through topoView, The National Map Download Client and the Map Locator), all undated; and the US Topo Map Symbol Guide (1:24,000, one inch represents 2,000 feet; perennial and intermittent stream symbols; contour interval always noted below the bar scale). Also read 2026-10-03: Fact Sheet 035-01, Finding Your Way with Map and Compass (March 2001, https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2001/0035/report.pdf): a compass "does not really point to true north, except by coincidence in some areas"; a map's declination "may not be current"; subtract when the magnetic north arrow is right of true north, add when left; stay away from pocket knives, belt buckles, railroad tracks, trucks and electrical lines. Its contact details are out of date. FAQs: How much distance does a degree, minute, and second cover on your maps? (updated 17 March 2023: at 38 degrees north a degree of latitude about 69 miles, of longitude 54.6 miles); How large is the NAD 27 to NAD 83 shift? (updated 18 July 2025: 10 to 100 ground metres in latitude and longitude in the conterminous 48 states, around 200 metres in UTM); What does the term UTM mean? (updated 17 March 2023: 60 zones each 6 degrees wide, numbered east from 180 degrees; MGRS the military version; neither more accurate than the other). usgs.gov FAQ pages refuse a plain scripted download but load with browser request headers. Water Science School pages read 2026-10-03 (they load with browser request headers): Specific Heat Capacity and Water (dated 24 August 2026: 4,184 joules to warm a kilogram of water 1 C against 385 for copper; oceans and lakes moderate climate, Nebraska against Oregon); Evaporation and the Water Cycle (8 June 2019: evaporation removes heat, leading to a net cooling; the alcohol wipe); Sublimation and the Water Cycle (8 June 2019: heat of vaporization 540 calories a gram or 2,260 kilojoules a kilogram, about five times the heat to warm water from freezing to boiling; 80 calories a gram to melt ice). FAQ: Are there geologic maps or publications for where I live? (https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/are-there-geologic-maps-or-publications-where-i-live, undated, read 2026-10-04 through a page summary): the National Geologic Map Database lists maps from many sources; state geological surveys; detailed geologic mapping not complete for the whole country, but maps available for most locations. Read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You (browser request headers): Open-File Report 2008-1292, Landslides Mapped from LIDAR Imagery, Kitsap County, Washington, by McKenna, Lidke and Coe, 2008 (https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2008/1292/downloads/OF08-1292.pdf; its own suggested citation prints the number as 2007-1292): the Puget lobe and the youngest advance and retreat about 18 to 16 ka; Vashon till over advance outwash and, in many areas, a fine-grained unit that more recent mapping suggests "may be, or may correlate with, the Lawton Clay Member of the Seattle area" (corrected after the 2026-10-04 fact check, which found the earlier wording stated the Lawton Clay as fact for Kitsap); the Lawton Clay described regionally as a laminated silt- to clay-rich lake deposit under the advance outwash; the map unit Qls, which the report credits to the 1:100,000 surficial map by Yount, Minard and Dembroff (USGS Open-File Report 93-233, 1993), not to its own map (attribution corrected after the same check); debris topples and falls "that initiate at the tops of coastal bluffs"; basaltic Gold and Green Mountain hills at about 500 m; about 77 percent of mapped landslides involving advance outwash; the perched-water explanation and the later emphasis on erosion at the base of slopes. FAQs What are igneous rocks?, What are sedimentary rocks? and What are metamorphic rocks? (undated). Fact Sheet 2018-3054, Divisions of Geologic Time (August 2018, https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2018/3054/fs20183054.pdf): Holocene from 0.0117 Ma, Pleistocene and Quaternary from 2.58 Ma, Tertiary from 66.0 Ma, the map symbols T and Q. National Cooperative Geologic Mapping Program page (undated): the NGMDB as "the authoritative, comprehensive National Archive for maps and reports about the Nation's geology"; mapView (https://ngmdb.usgs.gov/mapview/, in beta). The Geology of Radon (general interest publication, Government Printing Office imprint 1992, https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/7000018/report.pdf): most rocks and soils 1 to 3 ppm uranium, some rock types up to 100 ppm; soil uranium about that of its rock; radon moving more readily through coarse sand and gravel than clay; coarse glacial deposits among places with high indoor radon; the volcanic basalts of the Pacific Northwest coastal mountains low in uranium; all houses should be measured. Study Estimates about 2.1 Million People using Wells High in Arsenic (news release, 18 October 2017): arsenic presumed natural, from rocks and minerals; Washington among the places listed; "the only way for them to be certain of what's in their water is to have it tested." Water Science School, Sinkholes (17 September 2026): soluble rocks; Florida, Texas, Alabama, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee and Pennsylvania; human-induced sinkholes; Dover, Florida, January 2010. Read 2026-10-04 for Wells and Groundwater: Water Science School, Where is Earth's Water? (https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/where-earths-water, dated 6 June 2018, read 2026-10-04 through a page reader because the site refused a direct download): over 68 percent of fresh water in ice and glaciers; "Another 30 percent of freshwater is in the ground."; rivers and lakes about 1/150th of one percent of all water (added after the 2026-10-04 fact check, for Wells and Groundwater). Aquifers and Groundwater and Groundwater Decline and Depletion (both dated 17 September 2026): the water table and aquifers; recharge rates differ; "pumping your well too much can even cause your neighbor's well to run dry if you both are pumping from the same aquifer"; the cone of depression; groundwater moving metres a day or centimetres a century; artesian aquifers; groundwater as the drinking water of about half the population and nearly all the rural population; depletion and its effects, streams fed by groundwater, salt water drawn inland. Scientific Investigations Report 2014-5106 (Welch, Frans and Olsen, first posted 10 June 2014), abstract: the Kitsap Peninsula like an island; glacial aquifers and till; seasonal water-level changes of 1 to about 20 feet, 33 in bedrock; the 2012 water budget (66 percent to streams, about 4 to wells, 30 to Hood Canal and Puget Sound). NWIS groundwater site inventory for Kitsap County (3,856 wells with a depth; median 109 feet, quartiles 47 and 228, our count). Read 2026-10-04 for Water and Wind Power: daily mean discharge at Chico Creek near Bremerton, gauge 12072000 (15.3 square miles; 6,119 days, 1 July 1947 to 29 September 1950 and 1 April 1961 to 1 October 1974, with no record between (the gap found by the 2026-10-04 fact check; the guide had said every day from 1947 to 1974); monthly means about 92 cfs in January and 2.0 cfs in August, minimum 0, our calculation), through the USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov) because the older waterservices statistics and daily-value services returned 503 that day. Water Science School, Water Density (https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/water-density, dated 24 August 2026), read 2026-10-04 for Floating and Boats: water roughly 1 gram per millilitre, varying with temperature and dissolved substances; its table (62.424 pounds per cubic foot at 39.2 F, 62.300 at 70 F, credited to the Bureau of Reclamation's Ground Water Manual, 1977); ice about 90 percent as dense as water, about 10 percent of an iceberg above the water line; ocean water denser than pure water.

sources.name: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
sources.note: National Ocean Service facts, both last updated 23 September 2026 and read 2026-10-03: What is latitude? (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/latitude.html: latitude measures distance north or south of the equator; each degree about 111 kilometres; a second about 30.7 metres) and What is longitude? (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/longitude.html: longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian; a degree about 111 km at the equator, 56 km at 60 degrees, zero at the poles; GPS zero 102 m east of the Greenwich markers; each hour of difference equals 15 degrees of longitude; a smartphone position good to about 5 metres). Read 2026-10-04 for Reading the Weather: Understand Forecast Information (https://www.noaa.gov/understand-forecast-information, last updated 30 April 2026): "In general, a Watch means impacts are possible; a Warning means impacts are expected or happening."; enable Wireless Emergency Alerts. NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Red sky at night, sailor's delight (https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/about/redsky/index.html, undated): high pressure traps aerosols that redden sunrise and sunset; weather moves west to east in the mid-latitudes; "Note that this only works in the belt of westerlies, from about 30 degrees to 60 degrees latitude in both the northern and southern hemispheres."; reversed in the trade wind belt. Also from Understand Forecast Information, quoted after the fact check (2026-10-04): "A Tornado Watch means a tornado is possible: know your safe place and be ready to act quickly if a Warning is issued. A Tornado Warning means a tornado is happening or about to happen - immediately seek shelter in your safe place!"

sources.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
sources.note: Climate normals and the GHCN station record. The authority for frost dates and precipitation. Geomagnetism Frequently Asked Questions (undated, read 2026-10-03; parts of it describe the 2020 to 2025 model epoch and are out of date, so cite only its general statements): a compass points along the local horizontal field, not at a single point; declination may be considerably different a mile or two away; rare local anomalies of more than 10 degrees; models revised at least every five years. Also used (re-read 2026-10-03): declination defined as the angle between magnetic north and true north, positive east and negative west; "There is no simple equation connecting latitude and longitude to declination"; the online calculator takes a location or a US zip code; true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination with west negative; northern and southern hemisphere compasses balanced differently; stray fields from power lines not in the models; the Minnesota anomaly of 16 degrees east a few miles from 12 degrees west. 1991-2020 monthly normals for Bremerton, WA (station USC00450872, https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-monthly/1991-2020/access/USC00450872.csv, re-read 2026-10-04): 56.93 in (1,446 mm) a year, 79.7 percent of it October through March; January mean high 8.1 C and low 2.0 C; July 0.83 in (21 mm). 1991-2020 normals for Bremerton, WA (USC00450872), monthly and annual/seasonal CSV files, read 2026-10-04: January mean 41.1 F (maximum 46.6), December 40.3 F, December to February 41.2 F with mean minimum 35.3 F and mean maximum 47.2 F, annual 52.3 F, annual snowfall 3.0 inches.

sources.publisher: NOAA Office of Response and Restoration
sources.note: Sulfur datasheet (https://cameochemicals.noaa.gov/chemical/4562, undated, read 2026-10-04 for Soil Chemistry): flammable; burns with a pale blue flame that may be difficult to see in daylight; produces toxic sulfur dioxide; reacts violently with strong oxidizing agents, with dangerous reactions listed for chlorates, perchlorates and calcium hypochlorite. Many reactivity entries are credited to outside handbooks; quote only the database's own short phrases. Sodium Hydroxide, Solid (https://cameochemicals.noaa.gov/chemical/9073, undated, read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning): used in cleaning compounds and drain cleaners; dissolution in water can liberate enough heat to cause steaming and spattering and ignite adjacent combustible material (credited on the page to "[Haz. Chem. Data 1966]", which the page does not expand; an earlier note here called it the Coast Guard's CHRIS data, which the page does not say, corrected 2026-10-04; restated); readily absorbs moisture to give caustic semi-solids that attack aluminium and zinc with flammable hydrogen; reacts rapidly and exothermically with acids; strong corrosive action on tissue (USCG, 1999); NIOSH's full first aid text (NIOSH, 2024), including occasionally lifting the lower and upper lids while irrigating; molecular weight 40. The old datasheet number 1491 returns 404.

sources.name: National Weather Service
sources.note: National Weather Service Flagstaff pages, undated, read 2026-10-03: How Do Rainbows Form? (https://www.weather.gov/fgz/Rainbow: the 42 degree rainbow ray; stand with the sun to your back and the rain in front; the sun below 42 degrees; the secondary bow at about 50 degrees with colours reversed) and Why Is The Sky Blue? (https://www.weather.gov/fgz/SkyBlue: white light a combination of colours; Rayleigh scattering of violet and blue; red sunrises and sunsets). The Rainbow page also says that if the sun is more than 42 degrees above the horizon no rainbow will be visible. Lightning (read 2026-10-03, undated pages): Understanding Lightning: Thunder (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder): thunder heard only about 10 miles from the strike; about 5 seconds to travel a mile, divide by 5 for miles; be in a safe place while counting; a crack or click means nearby, a rumble at least several miles away; the channel runs many miles and the nearest part is heard first. Lightning Safety Overview (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-safety-overview): "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!"; substantial buildings and hard-topped vehicles are safe, rain shelters, small sheds and open vehicles are not; indoors, do not touch anything plugged into an electrical outlet, plumbing or corded phones (cell and cordless phones are safe), keep away from outside doors and windows, and do not lie on a garage floor; wait 30 minutes after the last lightning or thunder. Heat Safety Tips and Resources (https://www.weather.gov/safety/heat, undated, read 2026-10-03): it is never safe to leave a child, disabled person or pet locked in a car, even in winter; lock cars if there is a toddler in the household; children can die in 10 minutes; young children and infants less able to adapt to heat. JetStream, the National Weather Service online weather school, now hosted at https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream (weather.gov/jetstream URLs redirect there), read 2026-10-04 for Reading the Weather. Each page carries its own last-updated date: Air Pressure (10 July 2026: inches of mercury and millibars, 29.92 in and 1013.2 mb; conversion to sea level; the daily cycle lowest around 4 a.m./p.m. and highest around 10 a.m./p.m.; Brewer's 1848 barometer rules, including "Its motion upwards, indicates the approach of fine weather; its motion downwards, indicates the approach of foul weather."; "In the tropics, except for tropical cyclones, there is very little day-to-day pressure change, and none of the rules apply."); Origin of Wind (3 April 2023: a west wind blows from the west; Coriolis right in the north and left in the south; clockwise around highs, counter-clockwise around lows, slightly across the isobars); Ten Basic Clouds (28 March 2023; its definitions come from the WMO International Cloud Atlas, so restate them); Lightning Safety (22 June 2026: "If you hear thunder, then lightning is near."; "Lightning can strike more than 10 miles away from the location of rainfall."; safe and unsafe shelters; detailed forecasts accurate only out to seven days at best); Flood (2 June 2023: six, twelve and twenty-four inches of moving water; nearly half of flash flood deaths vehicle-related); NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards (8 September 2023); Types of Weather Phenomena (20 September 2023: mist and haze by the 3 F spread; hail of 1 inch or more severe; the squall). Glossary entries (forecast.weather.gov/glossary.php, undated): dew point and dew point depression, backing, veering. SKYWARN (https://www.weather.gov/skywarn/, undated): volunteer spotters, free training of about two hours. Heat Safety (https://www.weather.gov/safety/heat) re-read 2026-10-04: "It is NEVER safe to leave a child, disabled person or pet locked in a car, even in the winter." Read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of Reading the Weather: What to do During a Tornado (https://www.weather.gov/safety/tornado-during, undated): at home in a tornado warning, a basement, safe room or interior room away from windows; outside, a sturdy building at once, sheds, storage facilities, mobile homes and tents not safe; a vehicle not safe, drive to the closest shelter, or get down and cover your head, or leave it for a ditch or ravine. NWS Birmingham, What Constitutes a Severe Thunderstorm? (https://www.weather.gov/bmx/outreach_svr, undated): severe means at least one of "Hail that is one (1) inch in diameter or larger" or "Winds of 58 miles per hour (mph) or greater"; lightning alone does not make a storm severe. JetStream Types of Weather Phenomena on the squall: "the term 'squall' only refers to the wind speed increase, not any other associated weather." JetStream Lightning Safety: do not wait for the rain to start before seeking shelter, and do not leave shelter just because the rain has ended. Turn Around Don't Drown (https://www.weather.gov/safety/flood-turn-around-dont-drown, undated, read 2026-10-04): "A mere 6 inches of fast-moving flood water can knock over an adult." How Powerful Is Lightning? (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-power, undated, read 2026-10-04): "A typical lightning flash is about 300 million Volts and about 30,000 Amps. In comparison, household current is 120 Volts and 15 Amps." Cold Water Hazards and Safety (https://www.weather.gov/safety/coldwater, undated) re-read 2026-10-04 for Floating and Boats: cold shock a drowning risk "even for confident swimmers in calm waters"; a life jacket significantly increasing survival; cold shock as severe at 50 to 60 F as at 35 F; gasping triggered by water as warm as 77 F (25 C), and gasping and rapid breathing during the first 2 to 3 minutes or more (the Coast Guard's guide says cold shock passes in about a minute; the Library gives both); physical incapacitation; "Always dress for water temperature, not for air temperature."; carrying an EPIRB, PLB or VHF radio and filing a float plan; the Coast Guard guidelines, "If you can swim to safety, stay calm and do so.", "If you cannot swim to safety, conserve energy and heat and await rescue.", the H.E.L.P. position and the huddle. Its line that Pacific Northwest ocean temperatures may stay in the 60s year round does not match NOAA's Puget Sound record and is not used; its rewarming steps are credited to the Red Cross and are not quoted. Turn Around Don't Drown re-read the same day for Navigating Without Instruments and What to Do When You Are Lost. Read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of the navigation guides, for What to Do When You Are Lost and Floating and Boats: Lightning Tips (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-tips, undated): "If you hear thunder, lightning is close enough to strike you."; safe shelter a substantial building with electricity or plumbing or an enclosed, metal-topped vehicle with windows up; no place outside safe; the last-resort tips for someone caught outside with no safe shelter nearby, "Immediately get off elevated areas such as hills, mountain ridges or peaks", "Never lie flat on the ground", "Never shelter under an isolated tree", "Never use a cliff or rocky overhang for shelter", "Immediately get out and away from ponds, lakes and other bodies of water", and away from conductors such as barbed wire fences and power lines. Lightning Safety Outdoors (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-outdoors, undated): nothing substantially lowers the risk outside; avoid open fields, hilltops and ridge tops; stay away from tall, isolated trees, and in a forest stay near a lower stand of trees; a group spreads out; away from water, wet ropes and metal; on the water, the vast majority of lightning injuries and deaths on boats on small boats with no cabin, do not go out if thunderstorms are forecast, and if you cannot get back to land, drop anchor and get as low as possible. Its advice to camp in a valley or ravine in an open area is not used: the lost-person guide keeps people out of ravines and creek beds, for the Army survival manual's cold-air and flash-flood reasons. Cold Water Hazards and Safety re-read the same day: its examples of dressing for water temperature (wet suit, dry suit, immersion suit, survival suit, exposure coveralls).

sources.note: National Cancer Institute, SEER Training Modules, Anatomy and Physiology (https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/, undated web course, read 2026-10-04 for How Your Body Works): cells, tissues, organs and systems, with the stomach as the organ example; ten major systems; homeostasis and Claude Bernard; life depends on water, oxygen, nutrients, heat and pressure; body functions least efficient in infancy and old age; capillaries; the sinoatrial node at 70 to 80 impulses a minute; "Without blood, the human body would stop working."; nerve impulses start a breath every 3 to 5 seconds; nervous system sensory, integrative and motor; hormones act over minutes, hours or weeks; the six activities of the digestive system; the urinary system keeps body fluids within normal limits, makes erythropoietin and renin, and if it fails other organs cannot compensate; the skin as an excretory organ; the lymphatic system's three functions and edema; the skeleton about 20 percent of body weight, calcium storage, red marrow; nearly 85 percent of body heat from muscle contraction. National Cancer Institute, Symptoms of Cancer (https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/diagnosis-staging/symptoms, updated 16 May 2019, read 2026-10-04): see a doctor about symptoms lasting a couple of weeks or not better after a few weeks; most often caused by something else; cancer often does not cause pain; the list of changes (lumps, sores that do not heal, moles, cough or hoarseness, bleeding, bowel and bladder changes, fatigue, fever or night sweats, weight change).
