McColloch, Home Storage of Vegetables and Fruits, Farmers' Bulletin 1939, revised June 1960 (scan at https://archive.org/details/CAT87205380, carrying the National Agricultural Library stamp "Do not assume content reflects current scientific knowledge, policies, or practices."; read 2026-10-04 for Cold Storage Without a Fridge): basement storage rooms, cellars, pits and their ventilation; min-max thermometers; home storage impractical for most produce unless kept below 40 F, and elaborate storage unless winters average 30 F or lower; an underground cellar strong enough for its earth roof; odours (apples and pears, dairy and eggs); crop by crop. Its carbon tetrachloride fumigation of beans is obsolete and must not be repeated (see atsdr).

sources.name: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.note: Read 2026-10-04 for Cold Storage Without a Fridge (fsis.usda.gov loads with full browser request headers): "Danger Zone" (40 F - 140 F) (last updated 28 June 2023): bacteria grow fastest from 40 to 140 F, doubling in as little as 20 minutes; never out of refrigeration over 2 hours, 1 hour above 90 F; cold food at or below 40 F. Refrigeration and Food Safety (last updated 23 March 2015): game in caves and snow and harvested ice; 40 F or below; pathogens that do not change taste, smell or appearance; Listeria in the cold; appliance thermometers. Keep Your Food Safe During Emergencies (last updated 7 August 2013): the 4-hour refrigerator and 48 or 24-hour freezer; coolers with ice at 40 F or below; dry ice and its caution; do not put food in the snow, make ice; never taste; the lists of foods to discard and foods that need no refrigeration; flood water. Shell Eggs from Farm to Table (last updated 20 November 2024): refrigerate eggs as soon as possible; a cold egg left out can sweat; not out more than 2 hours.

sources.name: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
sources.note: Conservation Practice Standard, Livestock Pipeline, Code 516, NRCS Vermont, January 2021 (https://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/api/CPSFile/29283/516_VT_CPS_Livestock_Pipeline_2021_pdf, read 2026-10-04): friction and minor losses; plastic pipe working pressure limited to 72 percent of its rating; backflow prevention or an air gap at least twice the inside diameter or 1 inch; air release and vacuum relief to prevent air locking; "Design the pipeline to remain below the hydraulic grade line during operation."; filling a closed pipe faster than 1 foot per second needs special provisions; a flushing valve at the distant end or low point; draining when freezing is a hazard; trench safety, buried utilities, protection from water blowing from valves; the landowner obtains all permissions. Practice 533, Pumping Plant, cost scenarios, NRCS North Carolina, FY2015, compiled 7 November 2014 (https://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/references/public/NC/CostSenarios533PumpingPlant.pdf, read 2026-10-04), scenario #2, Water Ram: a ram uses the energy of moving water to lift part of it; bypass water easily 90 percent; a 2-inch ram with 10 gpm in and 10 feet of drop supplies about 1.0 gpm about 50 feet higher; may need fencing from cattle. Wording checked 2026-10-04: "The landowner and/or contractor is responsible for locating all buried utilities in the project area"; trench safety is listed under "Ensure safe conditions by--" with no party named; the device-or-air-gap rule applies "between pump discharge and the pipeline", and separately "Use approved backflow prevention devices on all pipelines where back flow may contaminate the source water supply or ground water." Read 2026-10-04 for Life in Soil, Soil Chemistry and The Ground Under You (nrcs.usda.gov PDFs load only with full browser request headers): Soil Quality Test Kit Guide (Agricultural Research Service and NRCS Soil Quality Institute, July 2001, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/Soil%20Quality%20Test%20Kit%20Guide.pdf): the earthworm test (a square foot dug 12 inches deep, the optional mustard solution of 2 tablespoons in 2 litres) and its interpretation (about 10 per square foot good in farmland, rarely over 20 in cultivated ground, up to about 50 in grassland; patchy counts; not all soils have earthworms); tillage killing about 25 percent and recovery within a few years; earthworms absent below pH 3.5, scarce to 4.5, most between 5.0 and 7.4; the slake test and its stability classes 0 to 6; "Binding of soil particles must constantly be renewed by biological processes."; fungal hyphae, fibrous roots and polysaccharides binding macroaggregates; biological activity doubling per 10 C (a steeper factor below 15 C); maximum microbial activity at about 60 percent water-filled pores; nitrogen fertilizers reducing earthworms; all soils contain some salts, salt-affected soils largely in the western arid and semiarid regions, EC 0 to 0.8 dS/m in a 1:1 soil-water mix acceptable for general crop growth. Soil Quality Indicators: Soil pH (April 2011, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/soil_ph.pdf): sources of acidity; acidification by leaching and crop removal; soluble aluminium below pH 5; arid soils neutral or alkaline; calcareous against granitic parent material; the nutrients deficient in acid and in very alkaline soils; many crops best at pH 6 to 7.5; microbial pH ranges (bacteria 5 to 9, fungi 2 to 7); nitrification and nitrogen fixation inhibited by low pH; field-specific lime requirement; the relative yield table adapted from Smith and Doran 1996. Rangeland Soil Quality: Soil Biota (information sheet printed 2017, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-12/Rangeland_Soil_Quality_Soil_Biota.pdf): what soil biota are; the soil food web; bacteria and fungi the bulk of the biota; immobilisation and mineralisation; nitrogen-fixing nodules; mycorrhizal fungi as an extended root system; water films, cysts; compaction, erosion, fire and the relative effects of pesticides. Its sentence that denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates "into nitrites and ammonia" is not used (the AWMFH gives nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas). Soil Tech Notes 11A, Biological Underground Community (NRCS Illinois, undated, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-09/SoilTechNote11A.pdf): decomposers, grazers and predators, litter transformers and mutualists; a single tillage killing as many as 25 percent of earthworms; bacterial activity highest at 68 to 104 F, pH 6 to 8 and 50 to 60 percent water-filled pores. Soil Biology Classroom Activities (draft dated February 2001, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-10/Three_Soil_Biology_Classroom_Activities.pdf): the night crawler introduced from Europe; forests without earthworms; the buried-material rot comparison; 500 to 200,000 arthropods a square yard; bacteria most active at 70 to 100 F; high C:N limiting microbes. Soil Health on Cropland (undated page, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/soil/soil-health/soil-health-on-cropland): the four principles (minimize disturbance, maximize soil cover, maximize biodiversity, maximize continuous living roots); "Tillage can destroy soil organic matter and structure along with the habitat that soil organisms need."; cover crops trapping nitrogen; root exudates feeding microbes. Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651 (directives.nrcs.usda.gov): Chapter 5, Role of Soils in Manure Management (issued August 2012, Amend. 61): exchangeable cations and anions; "Plants obtain many of their nutrients from soil by an electrochemical process called cation exchange. This process is the key to understanding soil fertility."; bentonite about 800 m2 a gram; typical CEC 6.3 for sand and 27.2 for clay/loam; ammonium held weakly; practices that raise CEC; nitrate leaching; phosphorus adsorption; potassium mobility; salinity; SAR above 13. Chapter 11, Waste Utilization (issued September 2013): the nitrogen pathways, denitrification to nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas, microbial activity almost ceasing below 41 F, ammonia loss from manure on hot dry soil within 24 hours, about half of added soluble phosphate immobilised within the first day, excess potassium, and lb P x 2.3 = lb P2O5, lb K x 1.2 = lb K2O. Inoculation of Legumes (Virginia Field Office Technical Guide reference, undated, https://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/references/public/va/Inoc_of_legumes.pdf): "Specific species of Rhizobium bacteria are required for specific species of legumes."; the inoculation groups; what reduces fixation (including nitrogen generally over 20 lb an acre and low pH); handling inoculant; pink nodules. Bismarck Plant Materials Center newsletter, Inoculating Legume Seeds (April 2025, volume 25, issue 3; the year is not printed and comes from the file creation date and the text, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/plantmaterials/ndpmcnl14228.pdf): when a legume is first planted in a field the right rhizobia may be absent, so an inoculant is often recommended. National Range and Pasture Handbook, Title 190, Part 645, Subpart H, Livestock Nutrition, Husbandry, and Behavior (190-645-H, June 2022, https://directives.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files2/1712930386/33922.pdf), read 2026-10-04 for How Animals Work, Keeping Animals and Animal Health and Disease: maintenance energy; walking on slopes costing 12 to 20 times more; lactation the greatest nutritional stress, peak milk 30 to 45 days after calving, milk 80 to 88 percent water, dairy goats lactating about 284 days; pregnancy needs greatest in the last third; body condition scores (1 to 9 for beef cattle and horses, 1 to 5 for sheep and goats; BCS 5, at least 14 percent fat, at calving; does 3 to 3.5); "Animals are more sensitive to the lack of water than food."; 10 percent dehydration severe, 20 percent fatal; green forage 70 to 90 percent water, hay and concentrates 7 to 15; metabolic water about 110 g from 100 g of fat and 55 g from carbohydrate; the routes of heat loss, insulation reduced by wind and wet; the thermoneutral zone (horses about 41 to 77 F, foals 60 to 72, pigs 50 to 75 with a body temperature of about 102 F, most poultry 60 to 75 with a body temperature of 105 to 107 F; Table H-2 for cattle, calves, sheep and goats extracts with its rows misaligned and is not used); evaporation the only cooling when the air is hotter than the body; intake down 50 percent in the first 8 days of heat; protein needed by rumen micro-organisms, which adjust to the feed; grazing 4 to 9 hours a day for cattle and 9 to 11 for sheep and goats, ruminating 4 to 9 and 7 to 10; swine and poultry 5 to 20 percent of needs from forage; Table H-12 animal units (26 lb oven-dry or 30 lb air-dry forage a day per AU; goat 0.15 and 3.9 lb, sheep 0.20 and 5.2 lb, horse 1.25 and 32.5 lb; beef cow intake 1.5 to 3.5 percent of body weight); Table H-14 water (sheep and goats 1 to 4 gallons a day, swine 1.5 to 3, beef cattle 6 to 18, horses 8 to 12, dairy cattle 10 to 30, poultry twice the feed weight; lactating dairy cows 30 to 50); testing new water sources, nitrites; warm drinking water in winter; Table H-18 salt by species, salt kept away from water; copper toxic to sheep; monensin fatal in sheep, turkeys and horses; prussic acid after freezing, wilting or crushing; grass tetany; avoiding overgrazing; pastures rested 20 days and grazed no closer than 4 inches, 30 to 45 days and 4-inch stubble against the barber pole worm in goats; the FAMACHA eyelid score and the five-point check, faecal egg counts, changing the active ingredient; Table H-19 heat periods and gestation (horses 336 to 340 days, 320 to 380 in the horse text; cattle 283; sheep 142 to 150; goats 151, about 150 in the goat text; its heat-cycle column, garbled by pdftotext -layout but legible with -raw or -table: horses 22 days, cattle 19.5, sheep 17, goats 20 to 22, used since the 2026-10-04 fact check), sow gestation about 115 days, Table H-20 ages of puberty; horses living 20 to 25 years, over 30 possible; behaviour (instinct, habituation, imprinting, classical and operant conditioning, elimination counts, diet selection). The handbook reproduces some figures from copyrighted sources (the FAMACHA chart, body condition drawings): restate them, never copy the figures. NRCS Illinois, Practice Specification, Fence (Code 382), Electric Fence Specifications, May 2019 (https://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/api/CPSFile/5591/382_IL_PS_Fence-Electric_Fence_Specifications_2019, read 2026-10-04): livestock trained to the fence with at least 12 hours of exposure, most trained in 48; sheep and goats clean shorn first; barbed wire never electrified; energizers installed to the maker's recommendations and grounded; ground rods at least 25 feet from water lines, well casings and other grounding systems, never into an existing ground system; interior fences at least two thirds of shoulder height. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check (handbook re-read 2026-10-04 with pdftotext -raw and -table, which keep the tables in order): Table H-2, typical thermoneutral zones, cattle 41 to 68 F, calves 50 to 68, sheep 70 to 88, goats 50 to 68; the goat text gives 50 to 68 too; the sheep text calls its zone 'almost 20 degrees higher than for most other farm animals', probably an adaptation to the wool, and says 'Without wool, a sheep's energy requirements would be higher.', with wind breaks, shade structures and dry ground recommended; Table H-14's footnote, 'During heat stress situations, these upper limits can increase dramatically'; the 30 to 50 gallons a day for lactating dairy cows is in the dairy section and is not a heat figure; sheep water 'Requirements increase greatly during late gestation and lactation.'; poultry, 'During periods of extreme heat stress, water requirements may easily quadruple.'; 645.0807, grazing systems that disrupt the internal parasite cycle. Its monensin line ('fatal in sheep, turkeys and horses') overstates turkeys against 21 CFR 558.355, which approves monensin for growing turkeys and warns only about mature ones: cite the regulation for monensin, and the handbook for sheep only. NRCS Illinois fence specification, also used: 'All energizers require an external lightning arrestor.'; more ground rods for the arrestor than for the energizer, at least 50 feet from the energizer ground rods; a surge or spike protector between a 120- or 240-volt energizer and its power supply. Soil Survey Staff, Soil Taxonomy, Second Edition, 1999, Agriculture Handbook 436 (https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-06/Soil%20Taxonomy.pdf, read 2026-10-04): soil temperature swings fade with depth; a single reading at 6 m within 1 C of the yearly mean; the yearly mean soil temperature commonly estimated as the yearly mean air temperature plus 1 C, and for some areas by adding "2 or even 3 oC (rather than 1 oC)" (wording corrected after the 2026-10-04 fact check).

sources.name: Complete Guide to Home Canning, Agriculture Information Bulletin 539
sources.note: The tested process times. Deviating from them is how botulism happens, which is why this is one of the few sources a lethal-hazard topic may rest on alone. Hosted by the National Center for Home Food Preservation since USDA NIFA stopped serving it; the work itself is USDA and public domain. Guide 1, Principles of Home Canning (https://nchfp.uga.edu/papers/guide/GUIDE01_HomeCan_rev0715.pdf, file marked as revised July 2015, read 2026-10-03): "Do not alter vinegar, food, or water proportions in a recipe or use a vinegar with unknown acidity."; "Use only recipes with tested proportions of ingredients."; jams and jellies one batch at a time, because increasing the quantities often results in soft gels; do not reduce the sugar in traditional recipes. Guide 1 re-read 2026-10-04 for Salvage and Reuse: Mason jars "may be reused many times, requiring only new lids each time"; metal containers used only once; most commercial mayonnaise or salad dressing jars usable with new two-piece lids for acid foods, with more seal failures and breakage, and not recommended for a pressure canner; other commercial jars that cannot take two-piece lids not recommended at all; gaskets in unused lids good for at least 5 years from manufacture; no old, dented or deformed lids.

sources.name: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
sources.note: Defend the Flock, read 2026-10-04 with full browser headers (aphis.usda.gov refuses a plain scripted request): How To Spot Sickness (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/defend-the-flock/how-to-spot-sickness, last modified 21 September 2026): the signs of illness in a flock (sudden or more deaths; no energy or appetite; fewer, soft-shelled or misshapen eggs; swelling of head, neck, eyelids, comb, wattles or shanks and purple colouring; gasping, nasal discharge, sneezing; stumbling, twisted neck; greenish watery diarrhoea) and "Report any sick or dying birds to your State veterinarian or to USDA by calling toll-free 1-866-536-7593". Biosecurity Basics (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/defend-the-flock/biosecurity-basics, last modified 29 September 2026): clean clothes, shoes and tools, washed hands, visitors limited, birds protected from pests and wildlife. Read 2026-10-04 for Keeping Animals and Animal Health and Disease: Foot-and-Mouth Disease (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/cattle/foot-and-mouth, last modified 30 July 2025): cloven-hoofed animals; not a human health or food safety threat; fever, blisters on tongue, lips, mouth, mammary glands and hooves, sticky foamy saliva, lameness, abortion, low milk, heart disease and death in newborns; only a laboratory can tell it from other blistering diseases; report immediately; declare farm visits abroad and keep from livestock for 5 days. Scrapie (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/sheep-goat/scrapie, last modified 29 June 2026): a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy; 2 to 5 years to signs; the signs; no treatment; a closed herd; confining and cleaning up after lambing and kidding, no milk or colostrum from possibly exposed animals to lambs or kids; owners contact their veterinarian; APHIS pays for testing of up to 30 animals per flock per year. National List of Reportable Animal Diseases (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/surveillance/reportable-diseases, last modified 18 September 2026): "For after hours and weekends, call the FAD Hotline at 866-536-7593." Biosecurity: Protecting Your Livestock and Poultry, Veterinary Services factsheet, March 2007, read from the copy hosted by the Texas Animal Health Commission (https://web.tahc.texas.gov/news/brochures/USDABrochure_LivestockPoultryBiosecurity.pdf): new and commingled animals segregated for 30 days as a rule of thumb; visitors, cleanliness, not hauling disease home, not sharing equipment; assess health daily; report serious or unusual problems without waiting; the USDA hotline 1-866-536-7593. Regulations cited through ecfr: 9 CFR 79.2, 86.5 and 166. Scrapie page re-read 2026-10-04: 'Maintain a closed herd with no external contact with sheep or goats. Minimize outside purchases of sheep or goats to reduce the risk of scrapie exposure.'; 'Select replacement animals from another closed herd that has measures in place to prevent scrapie introduction or that are genetically resistant.'; reduce commingling at markets, fairs and exhibits. Human Food Waste and Swine: Protecting the Health of the U.S. Swine Industry, APHIS-24-022, April 2024 (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/shpa-human-food-waste-and-swine.pdf, read 2026-10-04 through the web reader, because aphis.usda.gov refused scripted downloads): garbage is 'human food that contains meat or has come in contact with meat during the food preparation process'; FMD, ASF and CSF could be brought into the United States through contaminated meat; 'Pigs should never have access to uncooked garbage.'; 25 states listed where garbage feeding is prohibited. Small Farm and Pet Pig Owners: 7 Ways to Protect Pigs from African Swine Fever, undated (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/small-farm-and-pet-pig-owners-7-ways-to-protect-pigs-from-asf.pdf, read the same way): do not feed pigs garbage or let them eat trash; the virus can survive for months in pork and pork products; keep all outside food products away from pigs. What Swine Growers Need to Know about Garbage Feeding, November 2019 (fs-swine-producers-garbage-feeding.pdf) agrees and is not cited. Read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species: Spotted Lanternfly (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/slf, last modified 26 August 2025): native to Asia, Pennsylvania 2014, 19 states and DC; eggs on any hard surface; egg masses of 30 to 50 eggs like grey putty then cracked mud; park 15 feet from trees in a quarantine zone; check vehicles; smash eggs into a bag of hand sanitizer or rubbing alcohol. Emerald Ash Borer (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/eab, last modified 23 April 2026): Michigan 2002, 38 states and DC; spread by people in firewood, logs and nursery stock; the signs; buy local or certified heat-treated firewood; 1-866-322-4512; the domestic quarantine removed by a rule effective 14 January 2021. How USDA Fights Invasive Pests (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/hungry-pests/what-to-do, last modified 1 October 2026): report what you see; State Plant Health Directors. Feral Swine (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/operational-wildlife-activities/feral-swine, last modified 31 August 2026): "a dangerous and destructive invasive species"; at least $3.4 billion a year, $2.5 billion in agriculture; 8 percent with brucellosis; the signs; sighting reports. Feral Swine Damage to People and Pets (last modified 24 February 2026): at least 30 viral and bacterial diseases and nearly 40 parasites; gloves and cooking to 160 F; attacks on farmers, golfers, hikers and picnickers; aggression raised by handouts and waste. Added after the fact check (read 2026-10-04): Asian Longhorned Beetle (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/alb, last modified 17 September 2026): "please don't move firewood out of quarantined areas"; "Follow State and Federal laws. Laws limit moving tree material and untreated firewood in case ALB is inside."; hotline 1-866-702-9938. Asian Longhorned Beetle Regulated Articles, 7 CFR 301.51-2 (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/asian-longhorned-beetle-regulated-articles_1.pdf, last update 16 June 2016; the list 7 CFR 301.51-2 incorporates by reference to the APHIS website): "1. Firewood (all hardwood species), and green lumber and other material ... of the following genera", Fraxinus (ash) among them. So the 2021 removal of the emerald ash borer quarantine did not end federal rules on moving firewood.

sources.name: Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material, FPL-GTR-282
sources.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory
sources.note: Species-by-species strength, stiffness, shrinkage and decay resistance. The authority for anything made of wood. FPL-GTR-282 is dated March 2021. Chapter 8, Fastenings, by Douglas R. Rammer, read 2026-10-03 from the chapter PDF (https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr282/chapter_08_fpl_gtr282.pdf) because the whole-book URL returned a service-unavailable page that day: withdrawal and lateral loads; withdrawal as low as 25 percent after moisture cycling; penny sizes obsolete in favour of length and diameter; end grain withdrawal 50 to 75 percent of side grain; lead holes; toenailing; screw and lag screw lead holes; screws and lag screws turned, never hammered; bolt hole fit and spacing; retightening bolts in green timber during the first year. Also from chapter 8 (re-read 2026-10-03): nails of copper, silicon bronze and 300 series stainless have performed well in ACA and CCA treated wood, and 300 series stainless also in copper azole and ACQ; a joist hanger and its fastener should be the same metal type. Read 2026-10-03 from the FPL-GTR-282 chapter PDFs. Chapter 14, Biodeterioration of Wood (Arango, Lebow and Glaeser): fungi need mild temperatures, moisture and air; decay only above fibre saturation (average 30%), the 20% air-dry margin, wood kept air dry will not decay and present decay will not progress; too wet to decay; optimum 25 C, slow below 10 and above 30 C (printed with the mismatched conversion 95 F; 30 C is 86 F), ceasing at 2 or 38 C; mould and stain affect strength only slightly, their effect usually confined to appearance and to shock resistance or toughness, and incipient decay may hide in stained areas; brown, white and soft rot; dry rot a misnomer, water-conducting fungi; strength losses over 50% by 10% weight loss, and visible decay means greatly reduced strength; building rules (8 in and 6 in soil clearances, 12 to 18 in foundations, 18 in crawl space clearance, a 2 ft overhang, plumbing leaks, stumps and debris); repairs start with the moisture; the climate index for decay hazard, the Gulf States and Mississippi; subterranean and dry-wood termites, carpenter ants, carpenter bees, marine borers (untreated pilings on the Pacific, Gulf and South Atlantic coasts destroyed in a year or less); fumigation only by licensed professional fumigators. Chapter 15, Wood Preservatives (Kirker and Lebow): use categories UC1 to UC5; the treatment tag; cut surfaces, end grain and fastener holes need supplemental on-site treatment, copper naphthenate at 1 to 2 percent copper, not a restricted-use pesticide but to be handled as an industrial pesticide; treated wood must not be burned in open fires, stoves, fireplaces or residential boilers. Chapter 16, Finishing Wood (Hunt): weathering defined; UV breaks down surface lignin; about 6 mm lost per century; the cedar sunburn test (16 weeks of exposure, repaint within 3 years; 1 week, peeling after 13; unexposed, good after 20); mildew does not decay wood directly; paint stripping; lead paint not sanded, power washed, blasted or heated, lead fumes at about 370 C (700 F); lead paint still made for steel products; blowtorch fires smouldering for hours. Chapter 10, Wood Adhesives: Bond Formation and Performance, by Charles R. Frihart and Christopher G. Hunt, read 2026-10-04 from the Forest Service Treesearch copy (https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62250.pdf; record https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/62250) because the FPL chapter URL returned a 502 that day: the chain of links; wetting and penetration two to six cells deep; wood failure as the standard; solidification by solvent loss, cooling or reaction, full strength over hours to days or weeks; surfaces within 24 hours, knife-cut best, glazing, the 20 and 40 second water drop test; teak extractives; metals and plastics; 6 to 14 percent moisture, 5 to 12 indoors; Table 10-1 (PVA "joints yield under continued stress", PVAx, polyurethane, epoxy, resorcinol, contact, construction mastic up to 1/4 inch gaps, hot melt, animal glue); structural, semi-structural, non-structural, exterior and interior; pot life, open, closed and clamp time; pressure and starved joints, glue lines of 0.08 to 0.15 mm; clamp time from minutes to 24 hours; sunken joints and 7 days at room temperature; edge-grain joints as strong as wood, tongue and groove for alignment, end-grain butt joints at about 25 percent, scarf and finger joints at 10 times the area and 1 in 12, up to 90 percent; end-to-edge joints needing interlock and protection from moisture change; construction adhesive with nails or screws, not counted in design; uncured adhesives, epoxy amine hardeners as skin sensitizers, isocyanates and occupational asthma, low flash point solvents, fine dust. Added after the fact check (same reading): formaldehyde hardener for resorcinol, phenol, melamine and urea adhesives "is a severe irritant"; the less flammable formulations based on chlorinated solvents: "Solvents in these adhesives are generally toxic, but harmful effects can be avoided by providing adequate ventilation and following the manufacturer's safety instructions."; the adhesive must "wet," or completely cover the wood surface "at the molecular scale" (not microscopic). Read 2026-10-04 for How a Building Stands Up, Foundations and Ground and Framing a Building, from the chapter PDFs (chapters 16 and 17 returned the service-unavailable page that day): chapter 6, Commercial Lumber, Round Timbers, and Ties (Senalik and Farber: Table 6-6 standard sizes under PS 20; lengths given as actual, commonly in 2 ft multiples; dry lumber at most 19 percent moisture; S-DRY, S-GRN and KD; what a grade stamp carries, and grade lost to storage or handling or changed by reworking); chapter 7, Stress Grades and Design Properties (Senalik and Farber: the visual sorting criteria; knots worse in tension; decay severely restricted); chapter 9, Structural Analysis Equations (Lo Ricco, Amini and Rammer: beam deflection, moment of inertia, bending and shear stresses, notches and holes, creep, ponding, column buckling and Euler's formula, lateral torsional buckling and deck restraint); chapter 15, Wood Preservatives (Kirker and Lebow, both FPL: use categories UC3 above ground and UC4 ground contact; the end tag; higher retention for house foundations). Chapters 6, 7 and 9 each have a university co-author (Mississippi State University; Colorado State University), so the guides restate them rather than quote them; chapter 15 is quoted. Chapter 15 re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of Foundations and Ground: Table 15-6 (summary of the AWPA use category system) places "Permanent wood foundations, building poles, horticultural posts, crossties and utility poles (high decay areas)" in UC4B, ground contact or fresh water for critical components or difficult replacement. Chapter 14 re-read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out, Repairing a Building and Salvage and Reuse, from the Treesearch copy (https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62262.pdf; the FPL chapter URL redirected to a Forest Service landing page that day): "wood will not decay if it is kept air dry, and decay already present from prior infection will not progress."; decay detectable only microscopically at 10 percent weight loss, by which strength losses may exceed 50 percent, and "It may be assumed that wood with visually discernible decay has been greatly reduced in all strength values."; "Serious decay problems are almost always a sign of faulty design or construction, lack of reasonable care in the handling the wood, or improper maintenance"; design, work quality and maintenance of roofs critical "particularly at roof edges and points where roofs interface with walls", a 0.6 m (2 ft) overhang with gutters and downspouts kept free of debris; plumbing leaks undetected for long periods; the repair rule (correct the moisture; dry lumber if eliminated, treated or decay-resistant heartwood if not); termite shelter tubes, swarms and shed wings, probing with a pick or knife; carpenter ants and porch-roof leaks; "Fumigation is very dangerous and should be conducted only by licensed professional fumigators."; air-drying yards on well-drained ground, debris and weeds removed, piling that dries fast and protects against wetting. The fpl.fs.usda.gov chapter addresses redirected to research.fs.usda.gov on 2026-10-04; chapters 4 and 5 were read that day for Floating and Boats from https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62243.pdf and https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62244.pdf. Chapter 4 (Glass and Zelinka): Table 4-1, average moisture content of green wood (coast Douglas-fir heartwood 37 and sapwood 115 percent; western redcedar 58 and 249; red alder sapwood 97, heartwood not given), with considerable variation between trees; the fibre saturation point averaging about 30 percent; maximum moisture content (equation 4-3); the moisture content at which wood sinks, 100(1 - Gb)/Gb (equation 4-4); liquid water replacing the air in the cells up to the maximum; specific gravity unchanged above about 30 percent; density including water, equation 4-14 and Table 4-6a. Chapter 5 (Senalik and Farber), Table 5-3b specific gravities: coast Douglas-fir 0.45 green and 0.48 at 12 percent; western redcedar 0.31 and 0.32; red alder 0.37 and 0.41.

Read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species: Clean, Drain, Dry (https://www.fws.gov/story/clean-drain-dry, published 7 October 2021, modified 17 September 2024): the steps; hot water of at least 120 F, avoiding the skin; dry at least five days or towel-wipe; bleach and other chemicals not recommended on boats and gear; dispose of bait in the trash; report with an exact location and a photograph. Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force, Ways to get involved (https://www.fws.gov/program/aquatic-nuisance-species-task-force/get-involved, undated): report to the state natural resource agency or the USGS form; never move water, animals or plants between waters; never release aquarium fish, animals or plants; "If you don't know it, don't grow it!". Invasive Zebra Mussels Found in Moss Balls (https://www.fws.gov/story/2021-03/invasive-zebra-mussels-found-moss-balls, dated 12 March 2021, modified 17 September 2024): confirmed 2 March 2021, 46 states by 27 April 2021, no known introduction; destroy by freezing 24 hours, boiling 1 minute, bleach at 1/3 cup per gallon for 10 minutes or undiluted vinegar for 20; dispose sealed; household drain, never a storm drain; what zebra mussels do.

sources.name: United States Department of Energy
sources.note: DOE Fundamentals Handbooks, written to train facility operators with no background; Distribution Statement A, approved for public release; hosted at energy.gov under /sites/default/files/2026-04/. Material Science (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93 and /2-93) and Chemistry (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93) are cited in Metals and Alloys. Read 2026-10-03 for Heat and How It Moves: Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Flow, Volume 1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, June 1992): heat as energy in transit, the Btu, sensible and latent heat ("When latent heat is added, no temperature change occurs"), the specific heat of water as 1 Btu per lbm per F, saturation temperature rising with pressure (212 F at 14.7 psia); Volume 2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, June 1992): temperature and heat defined, the Second Law and the two metal blocks, conduction (temperature difference and the resistance of the medium), convection (natural and forced; the stagnant film and fluid velocity) and radiation (mostly infrared; the fireplace in the line of sight; no medium needed; the cloud over the sun; emissivity). Read 2026-10-03 for Rust, Rot and Decay: Chemistry, Volume 1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93; its cover is dated January 1993), Module 2, Corrosion: corrosion defined; "Even though corrosion cannot be eliminated, it can be controlled"; general corrosion of iron needs metal and water and an oxide-forming reaction; a loose or defective oxide film lets corrosion continue; oxygen, temperature (a rate doubling per 20 to 50 F rise, a rule of thumb written for plant water) and dissolved salts raise the rate; chloride ions cause pitting of iron and steel; pits form under mounds of oxide; pitting and crevice corrosion mean rapid penetration with little loss of mass. WINDExchange, Small Wind Guidebook (https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/windexchange/small-wind-guidebook, modified 26 August 2026, read 2026-10-04 for Water and Wind Power): the power formula and the exponent of 3; Cp 0.25 to 0.45 against a maximum of 0.59; annual energy 0.01328 D^2 V^3; a typical home at 10,649 kWh a year; at least 10 mph for grid-connected and 9 mph for off-grid hybrid systems; airport data at about 30 feet, hub-height wind 15 to 25 percent higher; flagging; a year of measurement; 30 feet above obstacles within 300 feet (tower section) and within 500 feet (siting section); turbulence costing 15 to 25 percent; rooftop vibration and turbulence; most zoning height limits 35 feet; tilt-down and guyed towers, guy radius one-half to three-quarters of the height, aluminium towers prone to cracking; the installer questions; overspeed governing; the NEC; interconnection agreements, IEEE 1547, PURPA; the danger to line workers; hybrid systems and the seasons. The Energy Saver micro-hydropower pages it once sat beside are retired (see doe-energy-saver); use doe-microhydropower-handbook and usbr for hydro.

sources.name: Federal Emergency Management Agency
sources.note: Corrosion Protection for Metal Connectors and Fasteners in Coastal Areas, NFIP Technical Bulletin 8 (June 2019, read 2026-10-03): structural failures frequently at connections rather than framing members; CCA removed in 2004 and some replacement preservatives more corrosive; stainless or hot-dip galvanised fasteners for treated wood; higher retention corroding faster; fasteners and connectors of similar metals; corrosion dramatically higher near the coast; G185 or heavier galvanising; routine inspection. The bulletin also carries ASCE and ICC material used with permission: rely only on FEMA's own text. National Incident Management System, Third Edition, October 2017 (https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/fema_nims_doctrine-2017.pdf, read 2026-10-04): management by objectives, "Establishing specific, measurable objectives"; "Every incident should have an action plan; however, not all incidents need written plans."; "The optimal span of control for incident management is one supervisor to five subordinates", a guideline, with the factors that change it; "Unity of command means that each individual only reports to one person."; plain language and clear text "is a matter of public safety"; check-in, checkout and accountability; transfer of command with a briefing; the Safety Officer, who "stops and/or prevents unsafe acts", with ultimate responsibility for safe conduct resting with the Incident Commander and supervisors at all levels. Catalog of FEMA Building Science Resources, FEMA P-787, Sixth Edition, January 2022 (https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_building-science-catalog_12-29-21.pdf, read 2026-10-04 through the web reader because fema.gov refuses scripted downloads): its entry for FEMA P-774, Unreinforced Masonry Buildings and Earthquakes (October 2009), says URM buildings are "typically the most vulnerable to earthquake damage" among structures in use in US communities. Snow Load Safety Guide, FEMA P-957, January 2013 (read 2026-10-04 from the GovInfo copy, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-HS5_100-PURL-gpo59955/pdf/GOVPUB-HS5_100-PURL-gpo59955.pdf): most buildings not at risk of snow failure and removal often more hazardous than beneficial; 3 to 21 psf per foot of fresh snow, ice a little under 5 psf per inch and about 57 psf per foot; roof snow not equal to ground snow; wood and steel deflecting visibly before failure; the warning signs of overstress; prompt evacuation and a qualified design professional; removal by a licensed, insured roofing contractor, and the safety and method rules for removal. Ready.gov, Earthquakes (https://www.ready.gov/earthquakes, last updated 9 September 2026, read 2026-10-04): "If you are in a damaged building, go outside and quickly move away from the building. Do not enter damaged buildings." The Home Builder's Guide to Coastal Construction (FEMA P-499, December 2010) could not be read on 2026-10-04: fema.gov refuses scripted downloads and the file is too large for the web reader; the load path material in How a Building Stands Up comes from the Building America page instead. FEMA P-957 re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of How a Building Stands Up: "When using a non-metallic snow rake, be aware that roof snow can slide at any moment."; "Use a non-metallic snow rake for steep roof slopes if possible. Metal snow rakes can damage roofing material and should be avoided. Snow removal can be conducted from the ground, removing the risk to people on a hazardous roof."; sliding snow on "porch/sunroom roofs and entrance canopies". Read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out and Repairing a Building: Snow Load Safety Guide, FEMA P-957, January 2013 (GPO copy https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-HS5_100-PURL-gpo59955/pdf/GOVPUB-HS5_100-PURL-gpo59955.pdf): homeowners among its intended users; fresh snow 3 to 21 psf per foot, ice a little under 5 psf per inch and about 57 per foot; the ice dam mechanism; "Small disrepairs can propagate into much larger issues."; repairs beyond the homeowner's ability "can cause additional damage"; the warning signs of overstress; evacuate and call a qualified design professional; removal by a licensed, insured roofing contractor; from the ground with a non-metallic rake; sliding snow; at least 2 inches left; no picks; icicles; buried skylights. Wind Retrofit Guide for Residential Buildings, FEMA P-804, first edition, December 2010 (WBDG copy https://www.wbdg.org/FFC/DHS/fema_p_804.pdf; written by URS Corporation authors for FEMA): three areas typically vulnerable (coverings, openings, load path connections); the Hurricane Ike house destroyed at an estimated 50 mph. The second edition (April 2023) exists but fema.gov returned Access Denied to scripted downloads that day, so it was not read. Ready.gov (FEMA): Safety Skills (https://www.ready.gov/safety-skills, last updated 20 March 2026: gas, water and electricity shut-offs; "only a qualified professional can turn it back on") and Floods (https://www.ready.gov/floods, last updated 27 August 2026: do not touch wet electrical equipment or touch electrical equipment while standing in water; turn off the electricity if it is safe to do so). Ready.gov Pets and Animals (https://www.ready.gov/animals, last updated 20 March 2026, read 2026-10-04), tips for large animals: identification for every animal; evacuate early with primary and secondary routes mapped; vehicles, trailers and experienced handlers and drivers; destinations with food, water, veterinary care and handling equipment; if evacuation is not possible, decide whether to move large animals to a barn or turn them loose. Ready.gov Floods re-read 2026-10-04 for Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops ("Do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Turn off the electricity to prevent electric shock if it is safe to do so."; underground or downed power lines can electrically charge the water), and Power Outages (https://www.ready.gov/power-outages, last updated 4 June 2026: generators and fuel outdoors at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; keep a generator dry; heavy-duty extension cords to appliances). Re-read 2026-10-04 after the electricity fact check: Ready.gov Power Outages, "Generators and fuel should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows, doors and attached garages." and "Install working carbon monoxide detectors on every level of your home." (also: carbon monoxide detectors with battery backup in central locations on every level); Ready.gov Floods, avoid wading in floodwater, "Underground or downed power lines can electrically charge the water."

sources.name: United States Fire Administration
sources.note: Smoke alarm care (page last reviewed 28 September 2026: test monthly, batteries yearly, replace the alarm every 10 years), heating fire safety (last reviewed 4 May 2023: chimneys and heating equipment cleaned and inspected each year by a professional) and the clothes dryer fire safety flyer (undated: clean the lint filter before and after each cycle). Fireplace and Wood Stove Safety card (https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/fireplace_woodstove_safety_card.pdf, undated, read 2026-10-03): do not burn paper in a fireplace or wood stove; put ashes in a metal container with a lid, outside at least 10 feet from the home. Cooking fire safety (https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prevent-fires/cooking/, page last reviewed 28 September 2026, read 2026-10-03): cooking by far the leading cause of home fires and home fire injuries; stand by your pan; turn the burner off at smoke or boiling grease; pot handles towards the back; a pan lid or baking sheet to cover a pan fire. Cooking Fire Safety flyer (https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/cooking_fire_safety_flyer.pdf, undated): an oven fire, turn it off and let it cool; if the flames escape the oven, leave and call 911. Heating fire safety re-read 2026-10-04: anything that can burn at least 3 feet from all heat sources; never use an oven to heat your home; space heaters off when leaving the room or going to bed; portable heaters 3 percent of home heating fires in 2017 to 2019 but 41 percent of the fatal ones. Cooking fire safety re-read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning (rendering fat): stand by your pan; turn the burner off at smoke or boiling grease; a pan lid or baking sheet to cover a pan fire, which will put it out. Portable Heater Fire Safety flyer (https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/portable_heater_fire_safety_flyer.pdf, undated, read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows): "Plug space heaters directly into wall outlets, don't use an extension cord or power strip."; space heaters on a solid, flat surface, at least three feet from things that can burn.

sources.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.note: NIST Handbook 133-2026 (December 2025): net weight is the commodity exclusive of wrapping materials. Weighing and Scales FAQs (updated 6 March 2026): commercial scales must meet state law, all 50 states have adopted Handbook 44, and a scale must be inspected and approved by the state before commercial use. The FAQ names "an active NTEP Certificate of Conformance as proof that it is compliant with NIST Handbook 44" as the most important aspect for a commercial scale. Technical Note 1297 (Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994), appendix D: random and systematic error. Its definitions reproduce the international vocabulary of metrology (VIM), so restate them rather than quoting. CODATA value, speed of light in vacuum (https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?c, 2022 CODATA recommended values, read 2026-10-03): 299 792 458 m/s, exact. Culinary Measurement Tips (https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/culinary-measurement-tips, created 1 March 2023, updated 29 April 2026, read 2026-10-03): measuring ingredients by mass with a kitchen scale is a best practice to improve recipe accuracy; convert a traditional recipe by measuring with its own tool and weighing the result in grams. Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (2008 edition; web chapters created 2016 and updated 18 August 2025, read 2026-10-03): section 8.3, Weight (weight as a force, in newtons; a 10 kg copper sphere weighs about 98 N on the Earth's surface; in everyday use weight is a synonym for mass, as in "the briefcase weighs 6 kg"; make clear which meaning is intended) and Appendix B.9 (1 pound-force = 4.448 222 N; 1 kilogram-force = 9.806 65 N; 1 pound-force foot = 1.355 818 N m). Marshall, R. D., Pfrang, E. O., Leyendecker, E. V., Woodward, K. A. and others, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, National Bureau of Standards Building Science Series 143, issued May 1982 (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/BSS/nbsbuildingscience143.pdf, read 2026-10-04): 113 dead and 186 injured as counted in the report, and in those terms "the most devastating structural collapse ever to take place in the United States"; the most probable cause, insufficient load capacity of the box beam-hanger rod connections; the change in hanger rod arrangement that essentially doubled the load on the fourth floor connections; minimal capacity as built. A later account (see asce) gives the final toll as 114. Read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows: National Bureau of Standards, Copper Wire Tables, Handbook 100, issued 21 February 1966 (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/hb/nbshandbook100.pdf; tables 5, 6 and 11, standard annealed copper by AWG: at 20 C, 16 gauge 4.02 ohms per 1,000 feet and 13.2 per km, 14 gauge 2.52 and 8.28, 12 gauge 1.59 and 5.21, 10 gauge 0.9988 and 3.277; at 75 C, 16.0, 10.1, 6.34 and 3.985 per km; the layout extraction misaligns rows, so read the raw text). CODATA value, elementary charge (https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?e, 2022 CODATA): 1.602 176 634 x 10^-19 C, exact.

sources.name: National Center for Home Food Preservation
sources.note: USDA-funded and its recommendations trace to USDA research, but the site itself is the university's. Where a process time appears in both, cite usda-canning-guide so the number can ship.

sources.name: American Red Cross
sources.note: Congressionally chartered under 36 U.S.C. ch. 3001, which does not make it a federal agency. Its training materials are ordinary copyright.

sources.name: World Health Organization
sources.note: Most WHO publications are CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. The non-commercial clause is incompatible with a bundle anyone may redistribute, so cite, never copy.

sources.name: Poison Control, the National Capital Poison Center
sources.note: A nonprofit, not a government body. The US helpline number 1-800-222-1222 is a fact and may be stated anywhere. Gasoline siphoning can cause pneumonia, by Rose Ann Gould Soloway (https://www.poison.org/articles/siphoning-gasoline, undated, read 2026-10-04 through a page summary): siphoning petrol by mouth can let it into the lungs, causing pneumonia, coma and death; its advice is not to siphon by mouth. Restate; do not quote.

sources.name: Rutgers Water Resources Program
sources.publisher: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

sources.name: University of Minnesota Extension
sources.note: A state university, so restate the fact, never the wording. Varnum, A. (Extension livestock veterinarian) and Florentino, S., Managing barberpole worms in sheep and goats, reviewed 2026 (https://extension.umn.edu/small-farms/managing-barberpole-worms-sheep-and-goats, read 2026-10-04): internal parasites a leading cause of death for sheep and goats in the United States; resistance documented across every class of chemical dewormer, so eradication is no longer a realistic goal; larvae persist on grass up to 2 months in warm weather and 6 months or more in cooler weather; eggs on grass become infective larvae in 5 days; move animals off before the forage is shorter than 6 inches; rest pastures grazed in Minnesota summers at least 2 months; grazing adult cattle or horses after sheep or goats, and haying, clear larvae; deworming a whole flock leaves resistant worms to breed; combine pasture management, breeding for resistance and targeted treatment; sometimes there are no visible signs.

sources.name: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife
sources.note: A state agency, so 17 U.S.C. 105 does not apply and Washington waives nothing by statute. Cite it for the fact, write the sentence ourselves. Where a topic is not specifically about Washington, cite the role state-fish-wildlife instead. Statutes read 2026-10-04 for Water and Wind Power: RCW 77.55.011(11) (a hydraulic project defined), 77.55.021(1) (a permit before work starts) and 77.57.070 (fish guards or screens on diversions from waters with game fish, plans approved first).

sources.name: The state cooperative extension service
sources.note: Each state's land-grant university runs one, and its advice is the locally correct advice. Resolved per place through data/locales/<id>/locale.json.

sources.name: The state fish and wildlife agency
sources.note: Seasons, limits, protected status and what may be taken. Different agency in every state, same question everywhere.

sources.name: The state health department's marine biotoxin programme
sources.note: Whether shellfish may be taken today. This is the one authority a player must check live rather than read once, which is why it is a role carrying a live URL per place.

sources.name: The state or county noxious weed control board
sources.note: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board pages read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species (state copyright, restated only): Washington's Noxious Weed Laws (https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/washingtons-noxious-weed-laws, undated): RCW 17.10 the basic weed law; Class A eradication required, Class B control depending on region and county, Class C not required by the state but possibly by a county; the WSDA quarantine list, seed packets and wildflower mixes, civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation; 38 of 39 counties with weed boards. Noxious Weeds FAQ (undated): Class A the least likely to be seen and the most important to report. Controlling Noxious Weeds (https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/control-and-disposal, undated): identify, check the requirement, integrated control, licensed applicators for some herbicides, work in sections, revegetate.

sources.name: A soil testing laboratory
sources.note: Usually the state extension service's lab. The point of citing it is that the answer comes from testing your own ground, not from reading.

sources.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
sources.note: Occurrence records: what has actually been observed at a given place. Licences vary per dataset and include non-commercial terms, so records are fetched when a player asks and cached on their machine.

sources.name: iNaturalist
sources.note: Photographs and research-grade observations. Per-observation licences vary and many are non-commercial.

sources.name: OpenStreetMap
sources.note: Roads, buildings and coastline detail. ODbL share-alike would attach to anything we shipped it inside, so it is fetched and cached instead.

sources.name: Wikipedia
sources.note: Useful as a starting point and never as the authority for a hazardous claim. Fetched, never bundled.

sources.name: NASA Technical Reports Server
sources.note: NASA-authored publications such as Reference Publication 1228 (Fastener Design Manual) are federal works and quotable. CONTRACTOR reports hosted on NTRS are not: the Materials Data Handbooks (CR-123772 for 6061, CR-123773 for 7075) carry NTRS metadata belongsToUsGov false, so they are cited under nasa-contractor-reports as facts only. Check the stiType before quoting anything from NTRS. RP-1228 (Barrett, March 1990, with an erratum of 17 June 2008) read 2026-10-03: thread friction coefficients from 0.04 to 1.10 and torque tables adjusted for them; not torquing close to yield; the helical spring lock washer flat and without locking ability once tightened; galvanic corrosion and which metal should be the larger; rivets weak in tension and not watertight without seals. Its tool-accuracy tables and Appendix A (bolthead markings) are credited to outside sources: restate those, do not quote them.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service
sources.note: Forest ecology, fire behaviour and the Missoula Technology and Development Center testing reports. If You Get Lost (https://www.fs.usda.gov/visit/know-before-you-go/if-you-get-lost, page last modified 4 December 2023, read 2026-10-03): "As soon as you realize you may be lost: stop, stay calm, stay put."; think, observe, plan; stay put unless very confident of the route; stay in place at nightfall, when injured or near exhaustion. Also used from If You Get Lost (re-read 2026-10-03): the essentials, including a compass you know how to use; GPS devices that lose signal or battery and cell phones that likely will not work for lack of signal; give someone the exact details of your trip; do not walk aimlessly; following a drainage downhill only as a very last resort that could be very dangerous. Also used (re-read 2026-10-03): the trip-details list ends "do not go alone", and the Observe step says "If you are on a trail, stay on it." Handtools for Trail Work, re-read 2026-10-04 for Organising Shared Work and Teaching What You Know: "Such knowledge cannot come from a manual. Ask experienced crew members for help."; "Productive, safe crews depend on each member being alert, informed, and caring."; be aware of nearby workers, carry tools at your side with blades forward, a central drop point for tools; hardhats, gloves and safety glasses; training for crosscut saws and "Be sure you are properly trained and certified before cutting either standing or fallen trees."; for chopping, swing clearance, stable footing, "Chop only when you are clear of other workers.", stance and distance, and "Stand so a glancing blow won't strike you."; "Always maintain safe distances between workers." The PDF is two-column, so check a quotation against a plain (non-layout) text extraction. Re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check: "Pass tools so others avoid grasping a cutting edge. Never throw a tool."; the central drop point is there "so tools are less likely to be lost" (keeping tools out of walkways is our own reason, labelled so in Organising Shared Work). Read 2026-10-04 for Life in Soil: Invasive jumping worms can change their world (feature, 22 April 2022, https://www.fs.usda.gov/features/invasive-jumping-worms-can-change-their-world): native earthworms absent from the northern United States because of the last ice age; jumping worms eating the forest litter layer; arriving in potted plants from the early 1900s; spread in mulch, potting mixes, potted plants, moved leaves and municipal leaf compost; "The best way to prevent future invasions is to avoid moving earthworms around." Anderson, L. O. and Heyer, O. C., Wood-Frame House Construction, Agriculture Handbook No. 73, Forest Products Laboratory, February 1955 (read 2026-10-04 from the djvu text of https://archive.org/details/WoodFrameHouseConstruction; that item's catalogue lists the authors of a later revision, but the scan is the 1955 edition, and the guides cite it as 1955): foundation walls high enough above grade to see termite tubes; 18 inches of crawl space clearance under the joists; footings transmitting the load to the soil, complying with local code, below the frost line and at least 6 inches thick; foundations below fill to undisturbed earth; an over-dug footing filled with concrete, never dirt; the footing rule of thumb for firm soil. The handbook was later revised; 1955 figures that modern codes have changed, such as anchor bolt spacing, were not used. Wood-Frame House Construction (1955) re-read 2026-10-04 for Framing a Building: pipe notches in the top or bottom of joists "should not be more than one-sixth of the joist depth and should be located only in the end third of the span"; ceiling joists "also serve as tension members to resist the thrust of the rafters of pitched roofs"; rafters "should not be erected until ceiling joists are fastened in place, as the thrust of the rafters will otherwise tend to push out the exterior walls." Read 2026-10-04 for Salvage and Reuse: Falk, Maul, Cramer, Evans and Herian, Engineering Properties of Douglas-fir Lumber Reclaimed from Deconstructed Buildings, Research Paper FPL-RP-650, Forest Products Laboratory, July 2008 (https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/33418.pdf): mean bending strength about 25 percent below in-grade data of the same species, stiffness about 10 percent higher; nail holes reduce strength when closely spaced or split, mainly at the tension edge; 980 of 1,078 pieces graded as Douglas fir confirmed by the Wood Identification Unit; grade stamps infrequent on the World War II-era lumber; deconstruction damage about one grade (Falk and others 1999b); recommendations: regrade reclaimed lumber before reuse, accept some species mixing, put edge-nail holes in the compression zone; reclaimed timber for timber framing usually regraded with designs approved by a licensed engineer. Two of the five authors were not federal employees (a private structural engineer and a University of Wisconsin professor), so Salvage and Reuse restates the findings rather than quoting. One Moving Part: The Forest Service Ax Manual, Bob Beckley, project leader, National Technology and Development Program, 1823-2812P-NTDP, October 2020 (https://www.fs.usda.gov/t-d/pubs/pdfpubs/pdf18232812P/1823-2812P_AxManual_508_10-21-20c_150dpi.pdf; the fs.usda.gov host without www refused the TLS handshake), read 2026-10-04 for Making a Tool: hickory preferred, oak and ash suitable; grain parallel to the head; runout; red, white and mixed hickory of equal strength per FPL research; chapter 10, hanging an ax: three criteria, trial fit, rasp only inside the eye, seat with a wooden or rubber mallet on the heel, never pound the head with a metal hammer, alignment checks, a wooden wedge about 3 inches long into one-half to three-quarters of the head's depth, no linseed oil on the wedge, no metal crosstie wedges, pinning about one-fifth up the head, linseed oil on the handle. Some fractions in the text (how much handle to leave above the head) are lost in text extraction and were not used. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check: chapter 9, "Leave the top of the handle (where it fits inside the ax head) free of oil or ensure that it is completely dry before inserting it into the ax head. Oil is a lubricant and can cause the ax head to slip on the handle."; chapter 10, the wedge is about 3 inches long "depending on the depth of the ax eye"; chapter 12, "If the head becomes loose, you may be tempted to soak the ax in water to make the handle swell. This temporary fix is ill advised." (the swollen wood is crushed and the head ends up looser), and the fix is to reset the wedge with a mallet or replace it with a thicker wooden wedge. This contradicts the older Handtools for Trail Work (2005, 0523-2810-MTDC), which gives soaking as a temporary field fix; Making a Tool follows the 2020 manual. Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course: Student's Guidebook, 2006 Edition, 0667-2805-MTDC, December 2006 (https://www.fs.usda.gov/t-d/pubs/pdfpubs/pdf06672805/pdf06672805dpi300.pdf), read 2026-10-04 for Power Tools: a 16 to 32 hour course; personal protective equipment; how chaps stop a chain by pulling fibres into the drive sprocket; most chain contact injuries on the left leg; kickback the most powerful reactive force, the upper quadrant of the bar nose, the uncontrolled arc toward the sawyer, and the ways to avoid it. The kickback zone figure is credited to Blount, Inc. and is not reproduced. The PDF is two-column: check quotations against the text, not the layout. If You Get Lost re-read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost and Navigating Without Instruments: advance planning and the essentials (food and water, a compass you know how to use, maps, boots and layers, a blanket, flashlight and matches); exact trip details and "do not go alone"; a positive mental attitude as the most important tool; STOP (Stop: "stop, stay calm, stay put. Panic is your greatest enemy."; Think: "Do not move at all until you have a specific reason to take a step."; Observe: "Do not walk aimlessly.", stay on a trail, a drainage downhill only as a very last resort that could be very dangerous; Plan: stay put unless very, very confident, and in place at nightfall, when injured or near exhaustion); self-rescue tips (rest before exhausted, rest 30 minutes after eating, the signs of dehydration, no hiking 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on hot days). The page's metadata gives its last modification as 4 December 2023.

sources.name: MedlinePlus
sources.publisher: US National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health
sources.note: SPLIT LICENCE, AND THE HALF WE ACTUALLY CITE IS THE COPYRIGHTED HALF. MedlinePlus states that the A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia, which is every /ency/ URL, is copyrighted and licensed only for use on MedlinePlus. All the first-aid and symptom content lives under /ency/. Public domain covers the health topic summaries, medical test pages, genetics pages, recipes, videos and illustrations carrying an NLM watermark; those may be quoted and bundled with the attribution MedlinePlus asks for. Default to restating the fact in our own words, which is what use: facts means, and never paste /ency/ prose into a shipped document. This entry read public-domain-us-gov / verbatim / bundle true until 2026-09-15, which told seven guides the opposite. Sodium hydroxide poisoning (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002487.htm, reviewed 8 April 2025, read 2026-10-04 through a page reader for Soap, Lye and Cleaning; /ency/, so restated only): products containing it include drain cleaners, oven cleaners, hair straighteners and metal polishes; no vomiting unless poison control or a provider says so; water or milk right away unless a provider says otherwise, but not when vomiting, convulsions or decreased alertness make swallowing hard; flush skin or eyes at least 15 minutes; after an exposure, call the local emergency number (such as 911) or Poison Help; what to have ready when calling. Read 2026-10-04 for How Your Body Works, restated only: Vital signs (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002341.htm, reviewed 1 January 2025): resting adult ranges, blood pressure 90/60 to 120/80, breathing 12 to 18 a minute, pulse 60 to 100, temperature 97.7 to 99.1 F averaging 98.6 F. Pulse (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003399.htm, reviewed 1 January 2025): wrist and neck methods; sit or lie down for the neck and never both sides at once; 10 minutes' rest; ranges by age, athletes 40 to 60; a change from your normal rate as a sign. Anaphylaxis (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000844.htm, reviewed 20 January 2026): causes, signs, call 911, help with epinephrine, nothing by mouth and no pillow when breathing is hard, scrape a stinger. Dehydration health topic summary (https://medlineplus.gov/dehydration.html, last updated 29 December 2023): causes, who is at risk, signs in adults and young children, when to get help right away.

sources.name: DuPont technical guides (Kevlar, Nomex)
sources.note: The manufacturer of the aramid fibre a wick is made of, and the only party who publishes its decomposition and continuous-service temperatures. Cite the named guide, never "an SDS": an SDS with no product named is not a citation, which is what placeholder-manufacturer-sds exists to record.

sources.name: Peer-reviewed literature (cited per paper in the document)
sources.note: Individual papers are cited in full in the document that uses them. This entry exists so a topic can record that some of its claims rest on primary literature rather than on an agency, without pretending one journal is an institution.

sources.name: ENERGY STAR
sources.note: Recommended insulation R-values by climate zone, air sealing, and window performance. An EPA programme, so public domain, which matters now that DOE Energy Saver is gone. Maintenance Checklist (undated, read 2026-10-03): annual pre-season contractor check-ups, and air filters inspected, cleaned or changed monthly by the owner.

sources.name: Building America Solution Center
sources.publisher: US Department of Energy, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
sources.note: Building-science guidance and the county-by-county climate region tables. The technical half of what Energy Saver used to cover. Continuous Load Path Provided with Connections from the Roof through the Wall to the Foundation (https://basc.pnnl.gov/resource-guides/continuous-load-path-provided-connections-roof-through-wall-foundation, last updated 6 December 2022, read 2026-10-04): the definition of a continuous load path; vertical loads including wind uplift, horizontal loads in and out of plane; connections as the weakest link and progressive failure; loads routed around openings and headers bearing on the studs beside them; hurricane straps, hold-downs and bolts; the residential code's nailing schedule and prescriptive braced wall lines and panels; a licensed structural engineer for the connections in hurricane-prone regions. Its figures and its summaries of the model codes and IBHS standards are other people's material: quote only the page's own sentences. Look for Missing Roof and Wall Flashing, a DIY guide (https://basc.pnnl.gov/diy-guides/look-missing-roof-and-wall-flashing, last updated 2025-09-11 per the page footer, read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out): drip edge along roof edges, into not behind the gutter; step flashing upper over lower, under the siding, an inch or so visible; kick-out flashing and the wall damage without it, field-made kick-outs often too small; boot or collar flashing worked in as if it were a shingle; valley flashing as a self-adhered membrane in the valley under the underlayment and roofing, with an open metal valley (a wide, flattened W) optionally on top, so only the metal can be seen; caulk-only vents checked every two years or so; gutters cleaned twice a year near trees, branches trimmed back; downspout extensions left disconnected after mowing; hire a contractor if flashing is missing. PNNL is operated for DOE by a contractor and the page carries figures credited to private firms, so the guide restates it rather than quoting. The page footer reads: "This content is a work created with funding provided by the United States Department of Energy under Contract no DE-AC05-076RL01830 for the operation of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory." That is a contractor's work, the same situation as hud-rrig, so Roofs and Keeping Water Out lists it under "facts restated", not under public domain (fact check, 2026-10-04). OPEN QUESTION, not settled here: the same notice also appears on Proper Solar Orientation (checked 2026-10-04), so it is probably site-wide, while this entry is still marked public-domain-us-gov / verbatim and Choosing Where to Build quotes that page. Whether the whole Solution Center should move to licence unknown / use facts needs its own dated finding.

sources.name: Federal Trade Commission
sources.note: 16 CFR 460, the R-value Rule, is why an insulation label may not advertise R-value per inch. Consumer advice pages (read 2026-10-03): How To Avoid a Home Improvement Scam (July 2022), How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Fake Check Scams (June 2025), Mobile Payment Apps (May 2022), and Auto Warranties and Auto Service Contracts (April 2024; a dealer may not deny warranty coverage because maintenance was done by someone else). Auto warranties exception, verbatim: "But if the warranty says that the work will be done for free, the dealer or manufacturer can make you use repair facilities it chooses"; without maintenance records "your claim might be denied". Home improvement page: "Consider only contractors who are licensed and insured", the licence number in the contract, and the three-business-day right to cancel a contract signed at home. Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising, 16 CFR 255.2 (read 2026-10-03 in the eCFR): "Consumer endorsements themselves are not competent and reliable scientific evidence"; testimonials read as typical; disclaimers such as Results not typical do not cure them; disclose the generally expected result; reviews not to be distorted. Read 2026-10-04 for Making an Agreement That Holds: Cosigning a Loan FAQs (https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/cosigning-loan-faqs, April 2024): "When you cosign a loan, you agree to be responsible for someone else's debt."; the lender must give the Notice to Cosigner under the Credit Practices Rule (16 CFR 444.3, see ecfr), though not for some real estate purchases; cosigning gives no title or ownership; property offered as security can be lost; the loan counts as the cosigner's obligation even if paid on time; ways to protect yourself; release needs both the lender and the borrower, and is unlikely. Re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check: on asking the lender for the total you might owe, "The lender doesn't have to do this, but might, if you ask."; on copies of the loan papers, "The lender doesn't have to give you these papers, so you might have to get copies from the borrower." The Credit Practices Rule reaches only lenders and retail installment sellers within the FTC's jurisdiction (16 CFR 444.1, see ecfr), and 15 U.S.C. 45(a)(2) (see us-code) leaves banks, savings and loan institutions and federal credit unions outside it, so a co-signer may never be given the Notice. The home improvement page re-read the same day: "Don't sign a document you haven't read, is in a language you don't understand, or that has blank spaces."; "Don't let anyone pressure you into signing any document."; "Never transfer your deed to anyone without consulting an attorney, a knowledgeable family member, or someone else you trust."; follow a call with a letter by certified mail with a return receipt; "Many disputes can be resolved at this level." Read 2026-10-04: Threading Your Way Through the Labeling Requirements Under the Textile and Wool Acts (undated): generic fibre names and percentages by weight listed in descending order of predominance. Clothes Captioning: Complying with the Care Labeling Rule (undated, https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/clothes-captioning-complying-care-labeling-rule): makers and importers must attach care instructions to clothing that cause no substantial harm if followed and warn about procedures that would harm the product. Dates found on the pages, 2026-10-04: Threading Your Way is dated July 2014, with notes that it was edited in October 2020 and January 2025; Clothes Captioning is dated May 2014.

sources.name: Consumer Product Safety Commission
sources.note: Injury data by product, and the safety standards themselves. Cite a proposed rule for its data, never as if it were in force. Also cited: Publication 5123 Portable Generator Hazards (102021), Publication 5126 Walk-Behind Power Mower Fact Sheet (052016), and Publication 254 Guide for Resale Stores and Product Resellers (012013 RV 052014: selling recalled products is unlawful, including at yard sales). Publication 254 also lists children's metal jewellery over 100 ppm lead, and children's products and painted furniture over the lead limits, as not to be sold; resellers need not test but cannot knowingly sell them. Staff report CPSC/EXHR/TR--15/001, Preliminary Evaluation of Anchoring Furniture and Televisions Without Tools (May 2015; produced by staff and not reviewed or approved by the Commission), read 2026-10-03: drywall anchors strongest in shear and weakest pulled straight out; drywall typically unable to take the 50 lb pull of the voluntary standard, so kits supply a wood screw for a stud; the 50 lb based on a 95th percentile five-year-old; no strength requirement for the wall anchor. News release 25-409 (29 July 2025): anchor TVs and furniture such as bookcases and dressers securely to the wall; the mandatory clothing storage unit stability standard in effect from September 2023. cpsc.gov refuses scripted downloads; both were read through the web reader. The release also says to keep cable cords out of reach of a TV that cannot be anchored, not to store toys and remotes where children may climb for them, and to store heavier items on lower shelves (re-read 2026-10-03). Sunlight focused by glass (read 2026-10-03 through a page summary, as cpsc.gov refuses scripted downloads): recall 09-073, Hallmark Jumbo Snowman Snow Globes (23 December 2008: in sunlight the globes can act as a magnifying glass and ignite nearby combustible materials; two reports) and release 01-092, Brinkmann outdoor solar lights (22 February 2001: a beveled lens that can act as a magnifying glass; five reports of grass and mulch fires). Button Cell and Coin Battery Information Center (https://www.cpsc.gov/Safety-Education/Safety-Education-Centers/Button-Cell-Coin-Battery-Information-Center, undated, read 2026-10-03 through the web reader): if a button cell or coin battery is swallowed, immediately seek medical attention; the National Battery Ingestion Hotline (800-498-8666) and the Poison Help Line (800-222-1222); a button cell can burn through a child's throat or esophagus in as little as two hours; tape used cells and take them to a battery-collection center. Read 2026-10-03: Publication 5098, Avoiding Tap Water Scalds (printed with the code 032012): third-degree burns in most adults at 150 F in 2 seconds; burns, degree not stated, at 140 F in 6 seconds and 130 F in 30; third-degree burns possible at 120 F in 5 minutes (wording corrected after the 2026-10-04 fact check); most injuries among the elderly and children under five; hand-test bath water; never leave a child alone in the bathroom. Holiday cooking news release 26-093 (19 November 2025, read through the web reader because cpsc.gov refuses scripted downloads): stand by your pan; smother a grease fire by sliding a lid over the pan and turning off the burner; never use water on a grease fire; turn pot handles inward; have a fire extinguisher nearby; keep children and pets at least three feet from the cooking area. Release 25-409 is dated 29 July 2025 on cpsc.gov (re-read 2026-10-03) and 28 July 2025 on its anchorit.gov copy. Read 2026-10-04: Publication 5013, Prevent Child In-Home Drowning Deaths (printed with the code 032012, https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/PreventChildInHomeDrowningDeaths.pdf): 5-gallon buckets a serious threat to toddlers; pails, coolers, sinks, fish tanks and landscape ponds; "Be sure all containers with liquids are emptied immediately after use." News release 21-030, Sound the Alarm: Pants Do Catch Fire (12 November 2020, read through a page summary): seniors 16 percent of the population and 77 percent of clothing fire deaths; pants, then shirts, nightgowns and robes; 22 percent of senior clothing fire injuries from cooking fires; "Keep sleeves and dangling clothing components away from the cooktop."; "Stop (don't run), drop and roll. Cover your face. Roll until the fire is out." Publication 5013 also: "A solar cover can allow children to slip into the water while the cover appears to stay in place, hiding the child."; "Always secure the safety cover on your spa or hot tub." What Is a GFCI?, Publication 099, printed with the code 092010 (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/099_0.pdf, re-read 2026-10-04 for Stone, Clay and Earth): GFCI protection especially "where electrical equipment is near water"; portable GFCIs where installed ones are not practical; consider portable protection with electric tools (drills, saws, sanders) for do-it-yourself work in and around the house. Publication 099, What Is a GFCI? (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/099_0.pdf, printed with the code 092010), read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You (the PDF downloaded with browser request headers and matched byte for byte against an earlier copy): ground fault protection "especially for circuit outlets in particularly vulnerable areas such as where electrical equipment is near water"; portable GFCIs "even if a GFCI is not installed on the circuit"; consider portable GFCI protection "With electric tools (drills, saws, sanders, etc.) for do-it-yourself work in and around the house"; test after installation, at least once a month, after a power failure and according to the manufacturer's instructions. Read 2026-10-04 for Salvage and Reuse: Publication 5073, Freezer, Dryer, Cooler and Refrigerator Entrapment Deaths to Children (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/fridge.pdf, printed with the code 009611 032012; downloaded with browser request headers): victims mostly four to seven, often playing hide-and-seek; the surest method is to take the door off; unlawful in many local jurisdictions to discard a refrigerator with its door on; the Refrigerator Safety Act. Publication 254 re-read the same day (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/ResellersGuide_0.pdf): the crib standard of 28 June 2011, destroy older cribs without written proof of compliance, no drop-side crib can comply even with new hardware, 35 crib deaths from structural problems between November 2007 and April 2010, "When in doubt, throw it out!", illegal to sell any recalled product.
