Read 2026-10-04 for Pottery and Firing, Soap, Lye and Cleaning, and Making a Tool: Art and Craft Safety Guide, Publication 5015, published with The Art & Creative Materials Institute, Arts, Crafts & Theater Safety, Inc. and The National Art Education Association, undated (its references run to 2006, the latest being ACMI (2006); the PDF at https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/5015.pdf is a 2021 scan): Ceramics and Clay (what clay and glazes can contain; premixed clays; finish green ware damp; "When cleaning do not sweep dust. Use a wet mop, rags, and/or a vacuum with a HEPA filter system."; NIOSH-approved respirators; a glaze labelled food safe is not lead-free; do not mix glazes; label lead pieces; "When spraying glazes use a spray booth equipped with a fan that exhausts to the outside."; test ware even when given to family and friends; pug mills, slab rollers, extruders and wheels; kilns: local or state authorities, mechanical ventilation to the outdoors, emissions, infrared goggles or a welding shield, GFCI outlets; salt kilns and building codes; raku outdoors only); Metals (forging: metal fumes, carbon monoxide, infrared radiation, ventilation, carbon monoxide alarms, earplugs, infrared goggles or a face shield); Woodworking (wood dust, sensitising hardwoods, occupational exposures to some hardwood dusts "have been associated with cancer of the nasal cavities and sinuses" (IARC, Group 1); added after the 2026-10-04 fact check). Home Electrical Safety Checklist, Publication 513, July 2008 (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/513.pdf, read 2026-10-04 for Making a Tool): install the correct size of fuse, an electrician to identify an unknown size, the wrong size can let too much current flow and overheat the wiring. 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(5) (read in the eCFR 2026-10-04): special packaging for household sodium or potassium hydroxide, dry forms at 10 percent or more and all other forms at 2 percent or more. Carbon Monoxide Questions and Answers re-read 2026-10-04 for How Your Body Works: early symptoms like the flu without the fever; high levels can confuse people before milder symptoms; when the alarm sounds, move outside, call 911 or the fire department, count heads, do not re-enter until responders allow it, and do not try to find the source. Publication 5123 also read 2026-10-04 for Wells and Groundwater and Water and Wind Power: never power house wiring by plugging a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding"), an electrocution risk to utility workers and neighbours on the same transformer. Read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows, Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops and Power Tools: Publication 513 re-read in full (bulb wattage; heaters; adapters and ground pins; cords frayed, stepped on, under furniture, wrapped, nailed or stapled; 16 AWG handles 1,375 W; too much current makes wires hot; extension cords not as safe as house wiring; outlets warm, loose plugs, outlets not working; a loose connection cannot carry much current without getting hot; GFCIs and AFCIs tested monthly; exercising breakers yearly with compressor appliances off; power tools with three-prong plugs or double insulation; wet and immersed tools; outdoor cords; pools). The PDF text layer drops the fi and fl ligatures (fre, fow); quotations restore them. Publication 099 re-read: who may install a GFCI outlet, and the footnote that the NEC may be adopted into law by states, counties or local jurisdictions and is revised every three years, whose text layer interleaves it with a second footnote and was reconstructed letter by letter. Repairing Aluminum Wiring, Publication 516, June 2011 (https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/516.pdf): homes before 1972 with aluminium branch wiring 55 times more likely to have an outlet connection reach Fire Hazard Conditions; deterioration raising resistance and causing overheating; aluminium wiring from 1965 to the mid 1970s; the warning signs; DO NOT TRY TO DO IT YOURSELF; Al or Aluminum marked on the cable jacket; copper 14 and 12 AWG for 15 and 20 A circuits; COPALUM installed only by electricians trained by the maker; modifications performed and inspected under local regulations. Hanway, Massie and Seebruck, Electrocutions Associated With Consumer Products: 2011-2020, November 2023, a staff report not reviewed or approved by the Commission (https://cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/Electrocutions-2011-to-2020.pdf): about 100 consumer product electrocutions a year in 2018 to 2020; fractal wood burning, often by tampering with microwaves, the most frequent product in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Publication 5123 re-read: heavy-duty outdoor cords rated above the load, all three prongs; backfeeding also bypasses household circuit protection; keep the generator dry. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check of the electricity guides. Publication 5123: carbon monoxide poisoning the first hazard named, and most generator incidents reported to the CPSC involving CO from generators used indoors or in partly enclosed spaces; the danger label required on portable generators made or imported on or after 14 May 2007 ("Using a generator indoors CAN KILL YOU IN MINUTES."; "NEVER use inside a home or garage, EVEN IF doors and windows are open."); never in homes, garages, basements, crawlspaces or sheds, even with fans or open doors and windows, CO lingering for hours after shutdown; battery-operated or battery-backup CO alarms, batteries tested monthly; "DO NOT DELAY" in getting to fresh air; shock risk in wet conditions, an open canopy and a dry surface. Publication 516: "failing aluminum-wired connections seldom provide easily detected warning signs"; a permanent repair recommended for aluminium wiring not remediated; a copper shortage in the mid 1960s, homes before 1965 unlikely to have aluminium branch wiring, cable from 1965 to the mid 1970s possibly aluminium; only three approved permanent repairs (complete copper replacement, the COPALUM connector, and the AlumiConn connector as the next best alternative where COPALUM is not available); twist-on connectors and CO/ALR devices not permanent repairs. Publication 099: a GFCI receptacle can replace an ungrounded two-slot receptacle, with its supplied "NO EQUIPMENT GROUND GFCI PROTECTED" label. The 2023 table saw supplemental proposal was withdrawn on 29 September 2025; see federal-register.

sources.name: US Department of Housing and Urban Development
sources.note: 24 CFR 3280, the manufactured home construction standards, carries thermal numbers that are quotable because they are regulation. 24 CFR 3285.203, in the Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards, requires drainage to slope at least one half inch per foot away from the foundation for the first ten feet (read in the eCFR 2026-10-03). Read 2026-10-04 in the eCFR (versioner API, issue of 1 October 2026; the sections last amended 16 August 2016) for Foundations and Ground: 3285.201 (firm undisturbed soil or fill compacted to 90 percent; organic material removed), 3285.202 (bearing capacity determined before building; the table of allowable pressures from rock at 4,000 psf and more down to 1,000 psf; the 1,500 psf default; a registered professional for peat, organic clays, uncompacted fill or unusual conditions; values not adjusted for overburden, embedment, water table or settlement), 3285.204 (six mil polyethylene under an enclosed crawl space, joints overlapped 12 inches, except in arid regions) and 3285.312 (footing materials, 6 inch poured concrete at 3,000 psi; a footing under every pier; footings below the frost line, with the local authority or a registered professional for its depth; monolithic slabs and insulated foundations above it designed by a registered engineer or architect; the table of footing capacities, reduced by the footing's own weight). Residential Rehabilitation Inspection Guide, February 2000 (https://www.huduser.gov/Publications/PDF/rehabinspect.pdf, read 2026-10-04): prepared for HUD's Office of Policy Development and Research by the National Institute of Building Sciences under contract, with some illustrations and an appendix used by permission, so the guides restate it and do not quote it; signs of structural distress, settlement and its causes, reading cracks, piers, wood structural problems, roof spreading, holes and notches in framing, checking members when loads are increased, and the seismic and wind conditions it sends to a structural engineer. Re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of Foundations and Ground: 24 CFR 3285.203(c), all drainage sloped "a minimum of one-half inch per foot away from the foundation for the first ten feet"; 3285.312(a)(2)(ii) and (iii), wood footings treated "for Use Category 4B ground contact applications" and "Cut ends of pressure treated lumber must be field-treated"; the minimum thicknesses in the table to 3285.312 (the 24 by 24 inch footing under an 8 by 16 inch pier is 8 inches thick on 1,500 and 2,000 psf soil) and its note 1, sizes based on the area (in square inches) and the "shear and bending required for the loads shown".

sources.name: Joint Trauma System Clinical Practice Guidelines
sources.note: Trauma and burn care written for austere settings with limited evacuation, which is closer to the reader we are writing for than a hospital protocol is.

sources.name: Radiation Emergency Medical Management
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services

sources.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
sources.publisher: A partnership of US, Canadian and Mexican agencies, hosted by USGS
sources.note: The accepted binomial and its authority. What makes a species claim checkable rather than a common name that means three different plants in three counties.

sources.name: Fire Effects Information System
sources.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station
sources.note: Species reviews with habitat, fire ecology, wildlife use and human use, each with its own literature citations. The deepest public-domain species source there is.

sources.name: United States Naval Observatory Astronomical Applications
sources.note: Sunrise, sunset and twilight for a given point and date. The authority behind a locale daylight table.

sources.name: Canada's Drug Agency (formerly CADTH)
sources.note: Rapid evidence reviews. Not a US federal body, so cite the finding and write the sentence ourselves.

sources.name: American Burn Association
sources.note: The burn-centre referral criteria. A professional society, so ordinary copyright.

sources.name: NC State Extension
sources.note: The Extension Gardener Handbook is unusually complete on soils and plant nutrition. Copyrighted by the university: cite it, restate the fact.

sources.name: The state water resources agency
sources.note: Water rights, well permits and the exemptions. In the western United States, whether you may legally take water is a real constraint and the answer is different in every state.

sources.name: The state or local electrical permit and inspection authority
sources.note: Electrical permits, inspections and the licensing of electrical contractors and electricians. Who it is differs by place: a state agency, a city or county building department, or in some places a utility (in Washington, L&I except in the 25 cities and the Tacoma Power service area that inspect for themselves; see wa-lni). Mapped for Silverdale in data/locales/silverdale_wa/locale.json (2026-10-04) to the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries, Electrical Program (wa-lni).

sources.name: US Food and Drug Administration
sources.note: Regulates what may be sold as soap, as a drug and as a food, so it is the authority for what a label is allowed to claim as well as for what is in the bottle. The FDA Food Code page (content current as of 17 September 2026) describes the Code as a model that local, state, tribal and federal regulators use to write their own food safety rules. Laser Toys: How to Keep Kids Safe, Consumer Update (https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/laser-toys-how-keep-kids-safe, content current as of 11 December 2023, read 2026-10-03): a beam in the eye can instantly cause damage, often without immediate pain; reflections off shiny surfaces still hazardous; never aim at a person, animal, vehicle or aircraft (pointing a laser at an aircraft is a federal crime); no laser pointers for children; no laser over 5 mW or without its power on the label; consult a health care professional at once for a suspected eye injury. Also from Laser Toys: "Vision can deteriorate slowly and, therefore, may go unnoticed for days." Read 2026-10-03: Disposal of Unused Medicines: What You Should Know and Dispose "Non-Flush List" Medicine in Trash (both content current as of 31 October 2024: take-back first, then the flush list, then the trash steps); Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps (10 August 2023) and DOs and DON'Ts of Proper Sharps Disposal (28 April 2021); Infant Formula Safety: Do's and Don'ts (https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/infant-formula-safety-dos-and-donts, content current as of 31 May 2023): no homemade formula; the water and scoops on the label, the maker's scoop, water first; liquid concentrate mixed with an equal amount of water; ready-to-feed needs no mixing. Microwave Ovens (https://www.fda.gov/radiation-emitting-products/resources-you-radiation-emitting-products/microwave-ovens, content current as of 12 October 2023, read 2026-10-03): super-heated water does not appear to be boiling and can erupt when disturbed; adding instant coffee or sugar before heating greatly reduces the risk; follow the manual's heating times; most microwave injuries are heat burns from hot containers, overheated foods or exploding liquids. What You Need to Know About Egg Safety (https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/what-you-need-know-about-egg-safety, content current as of 5 March 2024, read 2026-10-04): store eggs promptly in a clean refrigerator at 40 F or below, checked with a thermometer, in the carton, used within 3 weeks for best quality; cook until yolk and white are firm and egg dishes to 160 F; treated (for example pasteurized) eggs for raw or undercooked recipes; the carton safe handling statement. Read 2026-10-04 for Keeping Animals and Animal Health and Disease: FDA Announces Transition of Over-the-Counter Medically Important Antimicrobials for Animals to Prescription Status, CVM Update, 12 June 2023 (prescription labels from 11 June 2023, old OTC stock allowed to deplete); GFI #263: Frequently Asked Questions for Farmers and Ranchers (content current as of 22 May 2024: food and companion animals, the species list, buying from suppliers with a prescription, the VCPR); Antibiotic Stewardship: Sheep and Goats, CVM leaflet, undated (https://www.fda.gov/media/162073/download: talk to your vet before your livestock are sick, build a VCPR, set treatment protocols); T.A.L.K. Before You Treat (https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/animal-health-literacy/talk-you-treat, content current as of 16 May 2018): the withdrawal time "is the time from when the animal was last treated with the drug to when the animal can be slaughtered for food or the animal's milk or eggs can go to market"; Talk, Ask, Look, Keep. Regulations cited through ecfr: 21 CFR 530 and 589.2000. Read 2026-10-04 for Pottery and Firing: Questions and Answers on Lead-Glazed Traditional Pottery (https://www.fda.gov/food/environmental-contaminants-food/questions-and-answers-lead-glazed-traditional-pottery, dated November 2010, content current as of 27 October 2017): earthenware porous and glazed to hold food or liquid; lead bound into the glaze only when fired properly; old kilns contaminating lead-free pottery; a child with lead poisoning may not look or act sick; the problem types; lead-testing kits; warning stamps on decorative pieces (the FDA's example joins "Not for Food Use" and "May Poison Food" with an em dash, so the guide restates it rather than quote it, as the Library ships no dashes); "no amount of washing, boiling, or other process can remove lead from pottery." Read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning: Frequently Asked Questions on Soap (https://www.fda.gov/cosmetics/cosmetic-products/frequently-asked-questions-soap, content current as of 20 August 2024): ordinary soap from fats or oils and an alkali such as lye; no lye remains when made properly; lye once extracted from wood ashes; most cleansers are synthetic detergents; the three-part definition of 21 CFR 701.20; true soap regulated by the CPSC; cosmetics, MoCRA registration and listing, drugs; natural and organic undefined. The older soap URL under /cosmetics/cosmetics-labeling/soap returned page not found that day.

sources.name: National Park Service
sources.note: Visitor safety guidance written for people who are actually outside in the conditions described, which makes it unusually practical on cold, heat, water and wildlife. Park-specific pages are often better than the general ones. Ten Essentials (https://www.nps.gov/articles/10essentials.htm, last updated 28 May 2026, read 2026-10-03): navigation as a map, compass and GPS; know how to use them before going out; bring a physical map as a back-up and an extra phone battery; tell someone where you are going and when to expect you back. The other nine essentials it lists: sun protection, extra clothing, illumination, first-aid supplies, fire, repair kit and tools, nutrition, hydration and emergency shelter. Preservation Briefs from Technical Preservation Services, each stating that it is not copyrighted, read 2026-10-04: Brief 5, Preservation of Historic Adobe Buildings, de Teel Patterson Tiller and David W. Look, August 1978 (https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1739/upload/preservation-brief-05-adobe.pdf): adobe of sand, clay, water and often straw; straw for even shrinkage, not strength; the clay-to-sand ratio; air-curing 4 weeks or longer; shrinking and swelling with water content, weaker when wet; moisture the main cause of decay; roofs, regrading, coving, footing drains, mud plaster; cement stucco and cement or lime mortar incompatible with unstabilized adobe; professional help for structural problems. Brief 2, Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings, Robert C. Mack and John P. Speweik, October 1998 (https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1739/upload/preservation-brief-02-repointing.pdf): new mortar softer and more permeable than the masonry units and the historic mortar; hardness not a measure of appropriateness; joints sacrificial; more lime softer, more cement harder; lime carbonating for many years; misting and burlap while it cures; use within about 30 minutes. Brief 2 was written by private architects under contract; quote it sparingly. Rocky Mountain National Park, Hypothermia (https://www.nps.gov/romo/planyourvisit/hypothermia.htm, last updated 6 March 2026, read 2026-10-04): "Avoid clothing that will absorb and hold water, like cotton and jeans." Brief 5 also, re-read 2026-10-04: "never replace adobe mud mortar with lime mortar or portland cement mortar"; portland cement or lime mortars make the bricks, the weaker material, crack, crumble and eventually disintegrate; "Today, cement and lime mortars are commonly used with stabilized adobe bricks, but cement mortars are incompatible with unstabilized adobe"; footing drain trenches about 2 to 2 1/2 feet wide and several feet deep at the base of the walls. Yellowstone National Park, Safety in the Park (https://www.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/safety.htm, last updated 28 July 2026, read 2026-10-04): "Always stay at least 100 yards (91 m) away from bears, wolves, and cougars, and at least 25 yards (23 m) away from all other animals, including bison and elk."; back away if an animal comes closer; cow elk protective around calves in spring (May to early July); never feed wildlife, because animals dependent on human food may become aggressive and have to be killed, and animals carry diseases. Pottery of the Ancestral Pueblo, lesson plan for teachers (https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/pottery-of-the-ancestral-pueblo.htm, last updated 24 February 2025, read 2026-10-04 for Pottery and Firing): coiling and scraping, gourd or wood scrapers and polishing stones; every added piece "MUST be scored and slipped"; vocabulary for fire cloud (fired outdoors), leather hard, paste, smothering with powdered fuel such as manure, and temper ("gritty material added to clay to prevent a piece from shrinking or breaking as it dries or is fired"). The lesson has typographical slips ("pt" for pot), so quote it sparingly. Brief 5 re-read the same day for "they do not permanently harden". Species Spotlight: Giant Hogweed (https://www.nps.gov/articles/species-spotlight-giant-hogweed.htm, last updated 13 June 2018, read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species): carrot family; up to 15 feet tall, leaves 5 feet wide; sap and sunlight cause severe blistering, eyes temporary or permanent blindness, inhaled sap respiratory problems; Federal Noxious Weeds List; up to 5 years to clear a colony; never mow or weed-whack; gloves, sleeves, pants, shoes and eye protection; wash sap off and keep the skin out of the sun for a couple of days; bag flower heads; local authorities or a professional. Read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost. Outdoor Emergency Plan (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/healthandsafety/upload/NPS-Outdoor-Emergency-Plan-508c.pdf, undated; the PDF was created 21 June 2023): "Help can take hours or days depending on your location, weather, and resources."; before the trip, a map, the 10 essentials, a whistle ("Blowing a whistle helps people find you and saves your energy from yelling."), a mirror, bright clothing and a trip plan with a trusted contact; if lost, stop and breathe, find your location, retrace your steps if safe, call 911 with GPS coordinates, the trail, the last known location, landmarks, clothing, equipment and medical conditions, stay put ("Move only if there is an immediate threat to your life."); waiting (shelter, inventory, layers; no fire at high fire risk or in wildland fire season; whistle three times, a break, three times again; the SOS flash; a mirror for aircraft; a shape from shelter or rocks); injuries, and sending two or more people for help while the rest stay with the injured person; Hug-A-Tree in the Junior Ranger Park Explorer. Trip Planning Guide, December 2022, with Trip Plan form 10-1700 Rev 3/23 (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/healthandsafety/upload/Trip-Planning-Guide-Package-508c.pdf): a trusted contact who is not going, asked to call authorities and share the plan if you are not back on time; a whistle especially with children; sticking to the plan or telling the contact; turning around; checking in afterwards; the contact's two steps; parks do not accept trip plans. Rocky Mountain National Park, Search and Rescue (https://www.nps.gov/romo/search_and_rescue.htm, last updated 31 March 2012): searches begin at the last known location; the search area growing dramatically every hour; quick and accurate reporting keeping it small; searchers spreading out, yelling and whistling; children who fear being in trouble; "If you get lost, stay put so you can be easily found." Ten Essentials re-read the same day (last updated 28 May 2026); the page credits the ten-category system to The Mountaineers.

sources.name: ASHRAE Standard 62.2, Ventilation and Acceptable Indoor Air Quality in Residential Buildings
sources.publisher: American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers
sources.note: The standard that governs how much a dwelling must be ventilated, and the one most building codes adopt by reference. Copyrighted and sold, like NFPA 30: state the requirement in our own words and never reproduce its tables. Where a federal regulation says the same thing, cite the regulation instead (HUD 24 CFR 3280 carries ventilation requirements that are quotable).

sources.name: The regional air quality agency
sources.note: Declares burn bans and publishes the local air quality. A burn ban is a legal prohibition with a date on it, so this is one of the authorities a reader must check on the day rather than read once. Different body in every region.

sources.name: Published alloy and fibre data (unresolved)
sources.note: Stands in for a real citation that was never made. Replace with nasa-contractor-reports for the 6061 and 7075 Materials Data Handbooks (CR-123772 and CR-123773, cited as facts because they are contractor reports, not federal works), a named producer data sheet such as kaiser-aluminum-technical or alleima-technical, doe for the general mechanical-property tables, fpl-wood-handbook for wood, and a named manufacturer technical guide for aramid fibre. An earlier version of this note named mil-hdbk-5, which is not an id in this registry: its link answered 200 with a publisher homepage and it was removed.

sources.name: Manufacturer safety data sheet (product unnamed)
sources.note: An SDS is only a citation once the product and manufacturer are named. Until then it points at nothing. For fuel properties, niosh-pocket-guide and cameo-chemicals say the same things and are public domain.

sources.name: US military technical and training manuals
sources.note: Works of the US government, so public domain under 17 USC 105 and quotable in the bundle. The hand-tool and shop manuals (TM 9-243 Use and Care of Hand Tools and Measuring Tools, TC 9-524 Fundamentals of Machine Tools) are the most thoroughly illustrated free instruction on these subjects that exists, written to teach a skill to somebody with no background, which is our reader exactly. Treat the equipment-specific volumes with more care: a manual written for one machine in one decade is not general guidance. FM 5-426 Carpentry (3 October 1995, approved for public release, distribution unlimited; copy at archive.org) is the source for building layout: batter boards, the 6-8-10 and diagonal methods, plumbing posts, stairs as a right triangle and the rafter table. TM 9-243 is a joint Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps manual (also Navy M6290-AJ-MAN-010, Air Force TO 32-1-101, Marine Corps TM 10209-10/1) dated 12 December 1983 (the date on its title page; recorded here as 1984 until the 2026-10-04 fact check); the archive.org copy (use-and-care-of-hand-tools-and-measuring-tools-1983) is the Navy June 1992 reissue, NAVEDTRA 12085, with Change 1. Its chapter 20 also says to make certain no one is under a vehicle being raised, and to be aware of the capabilities of the jack, especially its load capacity. FM 3-25.26 Map Reading and Land Navigation (20 July 2001, approved for public release, distribution unlimited; archive.org MManuals copy, read 2026-10-03) is the source for map reading: marginal information, scale and bar scales, map colours, contour lines and terrain features, azimuths and the declination diagram, compass separation distances, orienting a map, terrain association, handrails, catching features and attack points. Its later editions (FM 3-25.26 of 2005, TC 3-25.26 of 15 November 2013) are not public release. Also read 2026-10-03: FM 5-426 chapter 2, Hardware (nails, screws, lag screws, bolts; the three-times nail length rule) and TM 9-243 chapters 21, 22 and 25 (hammer, screwdriver and wrench safety; torque wrenches as calibrated precision instruments for final tightening). FM 21-76 Survival (Headquarters, Department of the Army, 5 June 1992; also Marine Corps MCRP 3-02F; copy at archive.org MManuals/UsMarineCorps-Survival-Mcrp3-02f.pdf, read 2026-10-03): chapter 18 field-expedient direction finding (shadow-tip and arc methods, watch method, moon, Big Dipper, Cassiopeia, Southern Cross, improvised compass, moss not accurate, slopes and wind), chapter 7 lighting tinder with a convex lens, chapter 19 signal mirrors (flashes reported up to 160 km in ideal conditions; never hold the beam on a cockpit). The 1992 edition carries no distribution restriction; its 2002 successor, FM 3-05.70, is cited nowhere because available copies are restricted to US government agencies and their contractors (a determination dated 5 December 2003). FM 3-25.26 (2001) chapters 3, 4, 9 and 11 also cited for the datum note, geographic and grid coordinates, the lensatic compass and steering marks. Opticalman 3 & 2, NAVEDTRA 10205-B (Naval Education and Training Program Development Center, revised 1979, US Government Printing Office; read as the scanned ERIC ED185315 copy at https://archive.org/details/ERIC_ED185315): reflection, refraction, the indices of air, water and crown glass, the critical angle of water, porro prisms, curved mirrors, the principal focus, real and virtual images, magnifying power and the dioptre. The OCR is poor, so restate it rather than quote. Corrections after the 2026-10-03 fact check: FM 3-25.26 section 9-5 limits the watch method to the north temperate zone ("In the north temperate zone only") with a separate south temperate zone form, and says the shadow "may move either clockwise or counterclockwise" depending on location and season, so FM 21-76's clockwise rule is used only outside the tropics. The FM 21-76 scan read (MCRP 3-02F) shows no date in its text; 5 June 1992 is from the publication record. FM 21-76's silk-or-hair way of magnetising a needle is cited as its claim and flagged in the guide as unreliable (friction makes static charge, not magnetism). Opticalman page 4-17: convex mirror images are virtual, erect and reduced in size, never as large as the object. NEETS Module 10, Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, NAVEDTRA 14182, September 1998, Distribution Statement A (copy in the Internet Archive NEETSModules collection, read 2026-10-03): sound needs a source, a medium and a detector, and the bell in a jar from which the air is pumped; hearing range about 20 to 20,000 Hz; wavelength is velocity over frequency; doubling loudness takes about a tenfold increase in intensity; sound in air 1,087 ft/s at 32 F, 1,100 for practical purposes; table of speeds in water (about 4,600 to 4,950 ft/s) and steel (about 16,400 to 16,850 ft/s; the table's temperature column is scrambled in the scan, so quote ranges, not pairs), solids about 15 times air; refraction makes sound travel farther with the wind; echo, reverberation (thunder drawn out), resonance (the barrel), the Doppler effect (the train whistle). FM 5-428 Concrete and Masonry, 18 June 1998, approved for public release, distribution unlimited (https://archive.org/details/FM_5_428_C_M_1998, read 2026-10-03): the water-cement ratio decides strength, about 2.5 gallons per sack to hydrate, 4 to 7 gallons per sack in economical mixes, the Corps of Engineers watertightness limits of 5.5 gal/sack (W/C 0.48) and 5 gal/sack (0.44); a 94 lb sack equal to 1 loose cubic foot; clinker heated to 2,600-3,000 F; damp sand bulking and care proportioning by volume; weight the most reliable measure; the 1:2:3 method "regardless of the units of measure used"; hand mixing; mortar types by volume (Type N 1:1:6) and conversion to weight with 94, 50 and 85 lb per cubic foot. Read 2026-10-03 for Force, Levers and Mechanical Advantage and for Rust, Rot and Decay: Basic Machines, NAVEDTRA 14037, Nonresident Training Course, February 1994, Naval Education and Training Professional Development and Technology Center, Distribution Statement A (archive.org item navedtra-14037-basic-machines-1994, a text PDF): six simple machines but only two basic principles, the lever and the inclined plane; the three classes of lever with the wheelbarrow, the forearm, the 9-foot bar and the paint tin lid; curved arms; mechanical advantage as resistance over effort for all machines; blocks and tackle (count the parts at the movable block; multiply stacked tackles; the rope as the limiting factor; the 600-pound, 75 percent example); the wheel and axle, moments, the pole carried by two sailors, wrenches and torque wrenches; the inclined plane, wedge and screw jack (about 20 percent efficient, held by friction); work, friction and efficiency; force, the spring scale, pressure and snowshoes. FM 5-125, Rigging Techniques, Procedures, and Applications, 3 October 1995, with Change 1 of 23 February 2001, approved for public release (archive.org item fm-5-125-rigging-techniques-procedures-and-applications-1995): a force is a push or pull; safe working capacity is breaking strength over a factor of safety of at least 4, with the 1-inch Manila example and the diameter-squared rule of thumb; knots, sharp bends and shock loading can cut strength up to 50 percent; about 10 percent of the load in friction per sheave; dead or rotten trees and stumps snap suddenly as anchors; skids kept at a low angle, rollers, cribbing and jacking in stages; fibre rope stored dry against mildew and rot, inspected inside and destroyed when bad; nylon resists rot; wire rope cleaned, lubricated and stored against corrosion; chains lubricated, not painted. TM 9-243 also cited: chapter 25, page 25-13 (do not extend a wrench handle to increase leverage; penetrating oil on rusted nuts and time to soak); chapter 28 (do not oil files); chapter 37, page 37-4 (remove rust with fine aluminium oxide abrasive cloth; a thin film of oil against rust; rust-preventive compound for long storage); chapter 42, page 42-2 (bars: body weight on the long section, a block as a fulcrum near the point; bars are heavy, may slip, and bend under extra heavy work). Read 2026-10-04 for Glue and Joints: FM 5-426 chapter 6, Rough Framing, Connections (weak points at connections and poor workmanship, quoted; the butt joint the weakest; the miter very weak; the lap the strongest; the half-lap relatively strong and easy), and TM 9-243 chapter 19, Clamps (C-clamps; hand screw clamps for holding wood while gluing, jaws parallel; an opening 1 1/2 to 2 inches wider than the work; brass shims or wooden blocks for glass and highly polished surfaces; even pressure; never tightened with wrenches or bars), from the archive.org full text. The Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews (AAR), US Army Combined Arms Center - Training, Training Management Directorate, Fort Leavenworth, December 2013 (superseding the August 2012 guide; read 2026-10-04 from the copy NWCG hosts at https://fs-prod-nwcg.s3.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2023-06/army-leaders-guide-to-aar.pdf): an AAR as a professional discussion that lets people discover for themselves what happened; four parts (what was supposed to happen, what happened, what was right or wrong, how the task should be done differently); "The AAR is not a critique."; concentrate on what went wrong, not the person responsible, naming the duty position rather than the person. TC 25-20 (1993), its predecessor, could not be fetched (DTIC under maintenance on 2026-10-04). Read 2026-10-04 for Moving Water Without Power: TM 5-297, Well Drilling, War Department, 29 November 1943, as digitised by the Government Publishing Office (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-W-3317fdebba68d1dec72e414a9a999a8f/html/GOVPUB-W-3317fdebba68d1dec72e414a9a999a8f.htm): wells raised by suction pumps, "the depth to water must not exceed 20 to 25 feet"; pitcher pumps of the suction type; a Eureka cylinder or similar pump near the water level for deeper water; a foot valve in the suction pipe so a pump need not be primed each time it is shut off. Read 2026-10-04 for Stone, Clay and Earth (FM 5-428 from the copy at https://vulcanhammer.net/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/fm5_428.pdf): chapter 8 rubble stone masonry (with or without mortar, "but for strength and stability use mortar"; limestone, sandstone, granite and slate; "No stones should be larger than what two persons can handle easily."; the largest stones in the footing; bonding stones through the wall; horizontal bed joints; each stone on its broadest face; moistening porous stones; lifting clear to reset; workmanship the main factor); chapter 1 (sand and stone or gravel 60 to 80 percent of the volume of normal concrete); chapter 2 (portland cement heated to 2,600 to 3,000 F to form clinker; aggregates clean, hard, strong and durable); chapter 5 (hydration ceasing for good once the water is removed; curing usually 3 days to 2 weeks); chapter 7 (mortar used within 2 1/2 hours at 80 F or above and 3 1/2 hours below; never frozen). TM 9-243 chapter 2, eye protection against flying objects such as chipped concrete and wood, and chapter 21, sledge and club hammers. Read 2026-10-04 for Fibre, Cord and Textiles: FM 5-125 chapters 1 to 4 (Manila from abaca, 4 to 15 foot fibres; sisal about 80 percent as strong as Manila; tarred hemp about 80 percent of untarred; coir a quarter as strong as hemp and floating; cotton and jute; nylon nearly three times as strong as Manila; each element twisted the opposite way; the overhand knot reducing a straight rope by 55 percent; the square knot not holding when wet or of different sizes; sheet bends, bowline, clove hitch, round turn and two half hitches, timber hitch; whipping; care, inspection and destroying bad rope; sling leg tension, the 1,800-pound example and the critical angle; dead or rotten anchors); FM 21-76 chapter 12, lashing and cordage (the pull, twist-and-roll and overhand-knot tests; the two-strand twisting drawing; sinew; inner barks of linden, elm, hickory, white oak, mulberry, chestnut and red and white cedar) and its list of nettles, milkweeds, yucca and linden inner bark for cordage. Corrections after the fact check, 2026-10-04: TM 5-297 is also on govinfo as the scanned book (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-W-3317fdebba68d1dec72e414a9a999a8f/pdf/GOVPUB-W-3317fdebba68d1dec72e414a9a999a8f.pdf); the text version cited above was re-fetched the same day and does carry chapters 4 and 5, including paragraph 130. The foot valve sentence is about the pump that keeps a dug well dry while it is dug. The Eureka cylinder sentence is conditional: "If 2-inch or larger pipes are used". Paragraph 130, pitcher pumps: most have a tilting check valve that drains the pump when the handle is raised to its highest point; a foot valve "prevents convenient drainage. Foot valves, therefore, are not installed where either the pump or the suction line is exposed to freezing temperatures."; a good pump may lift 28 feet or more but "allowance must be made for elevation above sea level, friction, presence of air in the water, and eventual wear"; reduced capacity past 22 feet of suction lift plus friction for plunger pumps; "the handle is likely to fly up when released during the downstroke" when the lift is too great. FM 5-428 paragraph 8-46: one bonding stone for every 6 to 10 square feet of wall; "Offset each head joint from adjacent head joints above and below it as much as possible". FM 21-76: the scan's authentication page carries the date, its text layer reading "5 JUNE *992". TM 9-243 chapter 2 re-read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You: eye protection needed against flying objects including chipped concrete; "It is absolutely necessary for you to use eye protection devices such as helmets, handshields, and goggles during eye-hazard operations." The 12 December 1983 date for TM 9-243 (checked again 2026-10-04 after a fact check could not see it): the scanned title page reads "Washington, DC, 12 December" with no legible year, and the DA Form 2028 printed at the back of the manual gives "12 Dec 83" on its publication date line, on each copy of the form in the scan. archive.org's catalogue entry for the same scan (its djvu text is the file that was read, the same size to the byte) gives 1984-12-12, from the uploader's note "This was published 12 Dec. 1984 and reissued June 1992."; the guide follows the manual's own form and says so. Read 2026-10-04 for How a Building Stands Up, Foundations and Ground and Framing a Building: FM 5-426 chapters 2 (the 2 x 4's nominal and dressed size; No. 2 common for framing; the board foot formula), 4 (foundations varying with use, soil-bearing capacity and material; wall foundations for heavy loads or low supporting strength; posts 6 to 10 feet apart; braces for wood posts 3 feet or more above ground; steel reinforcement in concrete walls), 5 (the form work cautions: protruding nails the principal cause of accidents, mud sills under shoring, no large panels raised in heavy gusts, shoring braced), 6 (connections as the usual weak points and a sign of poor workmanship; end grain, butt and lap joints; compression splices worthless in tension or bending; the platform frame; sills; girders: depth better than width, double the depth for four times the safe load, bearing at least 4 inches on posts; the planks example and the girder's load area; dead and live load, live load allowances governed by local regulations; joists at 16 or 24 inches, crown up, doubled under partitions, notched no more than a third at supports, bridging lines over 8 and 16 feet; studs, plates, corner posts, bearing and nonbearing partitions, trimmers and the jack stud, let-in, cut-in and diagonal sheathing bracing), 7 (rafters resting on and nailed to the plate; the collar tie keeping the building from spreading; long spans sagging; the truss definition) and 8 (window openings: doubled studs, a header, doubled and trussed when wide). FM 5-410 Military Soils Engineering, 23 December 1992 with Change 1 of 4 June 1997, approved for public release (https://archive.org/details/ost-military-doctrine-fm5_410, djvu text read 2026-10-04): highly organic soils (Pt) and their field identification; high-clay soils that swell when compacted dry and wetted; frost action needing a water supply and a long enough freeze, silts and fine silty sands most susceptible, coarse material with little or no fines little affected; retaining walls, like other structures, founded below frost penetration. FM 5-426 Carpentry chapter 7, Roof Systems and Coverings, read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out (same archive.org copy): asphalt and asbestos-cement coverings the most frequent on pitched roofs, built-up roofing on flat or nearly flat roofs; 1 x 3 strip shingles laid 5 inches "to the weather" with 7 inches overlapped; felt underlay with a 2-inch top lap and 4-inch side lap; nails about 6 1/2 inches from the butt, covered by the next course, and in the reroofing section about 3/4 inch above the cutout sections (the two figures disagree on a modern three-tab shingle, so the guide defers to the printed nail line); no roofing unless the sheathing is absolutely dry; flashing and "the lines along which adjoining roof surfaces intersect"; ridges and hips moderately subject to leakage, valleys more; shingle tins and side flashing; practically all difficulties with asphalt shingles on Army buildings from nailing too high. Read 2026-10-04 for Making a Tool. TM 9-243 (archive.org full text, the 1992 NAVEDTRA reissue): files: never without a handle where designed for one (the tang can cause serious injury), never for prying ("The body of the file is hard and very brittle. A light bending force will cause it to snap."), never hammered (it may shatter); screwdrivers not for prying, punching, chiselling, scoring or scraping, nor near a live wire or to test a circuit; wrench handles never extended for leverage and wrenches never struck with hammers; NEVER USE DAMAGED TOOLS; replace a hammer with a worn, dented or chipped face. TM 9-237 Welding Theory and Application, Departments of the Army and the Air Force, 6 November 1967 (https://archive.org/download/TM9-237/TM9-237_djvu.txt): low (up to 0.30 percent), medium (0.30 to 0.45), high (0.45 to 0.90) carbon and tool steels (0.60 to 1.70) and their uses; the spark test for low and high carbon steel; low carbon steel, wrought iron and steel castings cannot be hardened; high carbon steel hardened at a good red and quenched in water; the 0.35 percent rule; never heat near the melting point; annealing, hardening and tempering (370 to 750 F, sometimes 1,100); a pyrometer wherever possible because estimating temperature by colour is not accurate; poisonous fumes from galvanised and plated parts; Table IV (very deep straw 480 F for punches, dies, knives and reamers; peacock or full purple 540 F for augers and cold chisels for steel; bluish purple 550 F for axes, cold chisels for iron, screwdrivers and springs; the OCR garbles brown yellow's figure). Navy Electricity and Electronics Training Series, Module 1, Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, NAVEDTRA 14173, and Module 2, Introduction to Alternating Current and Transformers, NAVEDTRA 14174, both September 1998, Distribution Statement A (Internet Archive NEETSModules; archive.org/download returned a server error on 2026-10-04 and the files came from the item's ia800504/ia600504 servers), read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows and Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops: current, the ampere, difference of potential and the water-tank comparison, the ohm, resistance and its four factors, Ohm's law, power, the watt-hour, 746 watts to the horsepower; current rather than voltage the measure of shock intensity, about 1, 10 and 100 mA at 60 hertz, body resistance as low as 300 ohms, fatalities from 30 volts, the signs of malfunction and "Do not operate faulty equipment."; Module 2: effective (rms) value and the 1.414 peak factor, and the nominal US household supply of 120 volts at 60 Hz (assignment question 1-50). Parts of both text layers use a font shifted 29 code points and were decoded before reading. Module 1 gives 6.28 x 10^18 electrons per coulomb, which is wrong (1/e is 6.24 x 10^18); do not use that figure. Read 2026-10-04 for Navigating Without Instruments, What to Do When You Are Lost and Floating and Boats. FM 3-25.26 (2001): 5-8 (time and distance, D = R x T, 4 km/h and 12 km in 3 hours); 6-8 and 6-9 (resection with two or three known points, modified resection on a linear feature); 9-2c (no compass more than 3 degrees out); 9-4e (the deliberate offset, "Ten degrees is an adequate offset for most tactical uses.", about 18 metres per degree per 1,000 metres); 8-7b (orienting an aerial photograph by its shadows: "On average, the amount of variation in shadow fall per hour is 15 degrees.", reasonably accurate within three hours of noon and to be corrected for season and latitude beyond that); 11-6a, Moving by Dead Reckoning (its two fundamental steps; pacing, odometer or elapsed time; errors compounding over distance; steering marks, never walking with the compass open, back azimuths to a mark behind, a person sent ahead; detours, counting only forward paces, returning to the line; the deliberate offset; accumulated error, a single distant steering mark dangerous, counts begun anew at each confirmed position, marks close together in darkness and fog); 11-6c, combining techniques ("either or both could be lost or destroyed"); 11-7, night navigation (dead reckoning the basic technique, several compasses, smaller steps and a night pace count). FM 21-18, Foot Marches, 1 June 1990, approved for public release, distribution unlimited, superseding the 1971 edition (read from https://www.elon.edu/assets/docs/rotc/FM%2021-18%20Foot%20Marches.pdf): the normal pace of 30 inches at 106 steps a minute; rate, distance and time; rates of march including short halts and minor delays; appendix A's sample unit procedure, 4.0 km/h on roads and 2.4 km/h cross-country by day, 3.2 and 1.6 by night (the rates table in chapter 3 is an image and was not read). FM 21-76: chapter 4 ("Although you can live several weeks without food, you need an adequate amount to stay healthy."); chapter 5, shelters (too large the most common error; insulating material against heat lost to the ground; site selection: suitable for signalling, falling dead trees, flash floods, avalanche and rockslide, below the high water mark, low ground collecting cold air; the evasion rule BLISS); chapter 16, sea survival (throwing a life preserver on a line as the best rescue; the strength of a panic-stricken person; the body's natural buoyancy in sea water; H.E.L.P.; heat exchange about 25 times faster in water); chapter 19, signalling (three fires in a triangle and three columns of smoke as international distress signals; the mirror caution; whistles heard up to 1.6 km in documented cases; conserving and warming radio batteries). FM 21-76 also says about 50 percent of body heat is lost through the head and that a person at rest loses as much as 80 percent of body heat to the ground; the Library does not use either figure. US Navy Surface Warfare Officers School, Damage Control Training, Stability and Buoyancy Lessons, Lesson Topic 4.1, Principles of Stability, undated, read 2026-10-04 in the copy hosted by the Federation of American Scientists (https://man.fas.org/dod-101/navy/docs/swos/dca/stg4-01.html), which is not itself a government site, so it is restated: the laws of buoyancy; a ton of steel as a cube and as a hull; displacement; the centre of buoyancy moving with the waterline and toward the low side; the centre of gravity moving toward weight added, away from weight removed and with weight shifted; the metacentre and the righting arm; positive, neutral and negative stability; load lines varying with water density. FM 21-76 chapter 13, Desert Survival, read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of What to Do When You Are Lost: "Do not ration your water! If you try to ration water, you stand a good chance of becoming a heat casualty."; drinking at regular intervals, sipping even when the supply is low; find shade, put something between you and the hot ground, limit your movements. Its chapter 4 says to ration water sensibly until a source is found, provided water losses are kept to a minimum; the Library gives the hot-weather rule because heat is where rationing does harm.

sources.name: State health department, wastewater and water reuse programme
sources.publisher: varies by locale, see locale.json authorities
sources.note: There is no federal greywater regulation. EPA runs research and a summary service and says plainly that states hold this, so a guide that cites only EPA for greywater has cited nobody with authority over the reader. The existing state-health-biotoxin role is scoped to marine biotoxins and cannot stand in for this.

sources.name: Local health jurisdiction
sources.publisher: varies by locale, see locale.json authorities
sources.note: The county or district health department is the body that actually permits a septic system, a well or a greywater system, and it is the one a reader has to telephone. It is also the level at which a state rule may simply not be implemented locally, which is not the same as the activity being prohibited.

sources.name: State natural resources or public lands agency
sources.publisher: varies by locale, see locale.json authorities
sources.note: Harvest rules differ per land category and the differences are not small: a national PARK and a national FOREST are different regimes, and state land is a third. Cite the category the reader is standing on.

sources.name: Tribal government
sources.publisher: varies by locale, see locale.json authorities
sources.note: Treaty-reserved rights are law and are co-managed with the state, not a courtesy and not a historical note. Where a guide touches who may take fish, shellfish or game, the tribal government whose usual and accustomed area covers the place is an authority on it. Represent what the nation itself publishes; do not characterise treaty rights from secondary sources.

sources.name: Federal Aviation Administration advisory circulars and handbooks
sources.note: AC 43.13-1B, Acceptable Methods, Techniques and Practices for Aircraft Inspection and Repair, is the most careful free writing on metal repair, fastening and corrosion that exists, because the consequence of getting it wrong is a crash. Aviation tolerances are tighter than a homestead needs, so take the method and the reasoning rather than the acceptance limits. Aviation Weather Handbook, FAA-H-8083-28B, signed and published 2 April 2026 (landing page last updated 13 April 2026; https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook), read 2026-10-04 from the PDF for Reading the Weather: temperature-dewpoint spread (6.6); local winds, sea and land breezes (10.6); fronts and their passage, warm fronts at 10 to 25 mph, cold fronts at 25 to 30 mph and up to 60 (11.3); fog seldom forming at a spread above 2 C (4 F), radiation, valley and advection fog (18.1); gust fronts often moving far ahead of the precipitation, up to 15 mi, marked by a line of dust or a shelf or roll cloud (19.2.1.1); thunderstorm ingredients, the three-stage cell life of about 30 minutes, the gust front, multicell clusters and lines (22); the pressure rising or falling rapidly remark at 0.06 inch an hour with a change of 0.02 inch (24.4.3.13.21). It was prepared under FAA contract DTFAWA-15-D-00031 with AvMet Applications and carries credited photographs, so restate its text rather than quote it. Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 6, section 2 (https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap6_section_2.html; the AIM index lists the web edition as effective 9 July 2026), read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost: under the National Search and Rescue Plan the Coast Guard coordinates maritime and the Air Force inland search and rescue; "Search efforts are often wasted and rescue is often delayed because of pilots who thoughtlessly takeoff without telling anyone where they are going."; an Air Force review of 325 missions in which 36 hours normally passed before family concern started an alert for people with no flight plan; body signals, "Stand in the open when you make the signals."; figure 6-2-6, the ground-air visual code for use by survivors (V require assistance, X require medical assistance, N no, Y yes, an arrow proceeding in this direction, SOS if in doubt; symbols of fabric, wood or stones, as much colour contrast as possible, at least 10 feet high), read from the figure's SVG rendered in a browser because its text is drawn as shapes. The AIM's own text is a federal work and is quoted.

sources.name: Penn State Extension
sources.note: Strong on food preservation and storage. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording. Check the scope of what you take, because an extension article written about canning jars is not a general rule about food. Clothes Moth, by Steve Jacobs, revised January 2013, page updated 12 May 2026 (https://extension.psu.edu/clothes-moth, read 2026-10-04): webbing and casemaking clothes moths; larvae feeding on wool, fur, feathers and hair, often under cuffs and collars; the webbing clothes moth leaving cotton and synthetics alone unless stained with food or body oils; launder or dry-clean and store airtight; vacuum, as larvae can live on shed pet hair under baseboards and in air return vents; never apply pesticides to clothing or bedding. Clothes Moth also: the casemaking clothes moth attacks plant-derived materials as well, dried herbs, tobacco, tea, hemp and seeds among them (restate, never quote).

sources.name: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
sources.note: Strong on grain storage, food safety and the growth conditions of spoilage organisms. A state university, so restate rather than quote. Steil, A. and Naeve, L., Using Wood Ashes in the Home Garden (https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/using-wood-ashes-home-garden, last reviewed February 2025, read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning): ash 5 to 8 percent potash varying with wood type; wood ashes can be caustic, so long sleeves and pants, gloves, eye protection and a mask; never ash from treated or painted wood or garbage.

sources.name: Washington State Department of Health
sources.note: A STATE agency, so 17 USC 105 does not cover it and nothing from it may be quoted verbatim into the bundle: restate the fact. Carries the fish consumption advisories, the shellfish biotoxin programme and the greywater rules. Check publication dates: the Puget Sound fish advisory most often cited is from 2015 and sits on a legacy URL.

sources.name: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.note: The source of the Dietary Reference Intakes, so every RDA, AI, UL and EAR in this Library ultimately comes from here even when it is read off an NIH fact sheet, and NIH says so on those sheets. NOT a federal work: the National Academies are a private non-profit chartered by Congress, and their reports are copyrighted, so restate. Many reports are readable free at nap.nationalacademies.org. Cite the report and its year, because the DRI panels revise.

sources.name: University of Georgia Extension
sources.note: Strong on pruning, propagation and southern horticulture. Scope-check anything seasonal: Georgia is not the Pacific Northwest. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording. Management Guide for the Backyard Flock, Circular 969, by Claudia Dunkley (published with minor revisions 16 September 2026; first published 1 November 1999), read 2026-10-04 at https://fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/C969/management-guide-for-the-backyard-flock/: 3 to 3.5 square feet a laying bird; litter; brooding at 90 F the first week, down 5 F a week to five weeks, a cardboard ring; layer ration from 18 weeks; breeds; feed the greatest cost; treats limited to 10 to 20 minutes; 20 hens drink about a gallon a day in cool weather; drinkers scrubbed daily; hens lay without roosters; a nest box for every four or five hens, checked twice a day; 14 to 16 hours of light; rodent control. Its claim that a poultry house must stay at least 70 F is written for Georgia and is not used. C969 also advises against hardwood shavings as litter: mould can grow in hardwood shavings that have composted in storage and, inhaled, cause a serious brain infection in chicks or their human caretakers (used in Chickens and Eggs after the fact check).

sources.name: Utah State University Extension
sources.note: Good on seedling culture and arid-climate growing. The arid part is the scope word to watch when reading it here. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording.

sources.name: University of Illinois Extension
sources.note: Strong on field crops and vegetable culture. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording.

sources.name: Colorado State University Extension
sources.note: Strong on food preservation, and the source of blanching material already cited in this Library. Altitude is the scope word: Colorado guidance often assumes it. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording.

sources.name: University of Missouri Extension
sources.note: General horticulture and food preservation. A state university, so NOT public domain: restate the fact, never the wording.

sources.name: United States federal and military specifications
sources.publisher: US Department of Defense and General Services Administration, distributed through the DLA ASSIST database
sources.note: QQ-P-416F (cadmium plating: 450 F limit, vapour warning, Type II chromate colours), MIL-DTL-5541F (chromate conversion coatings on aluminium, unpainted coatings lose protection from 140 F), MIL-T-6736B (4130 tube minimums, 1965) and MIL-DTL-5002F (10 May 2022: no cadmium on or in contact with titanium; section 3.6.7(a) no silver or silver plating on or in contact with titanium parts and fasteners, and no silver-plated hardware, clamps, tools, fixtures or jigs in titanium fabrication or assembly; Table I note 2/ adds silver not against titanium above 350 F in service; cadmium to 450 F, zinc coatings to 500 F). Some were read through mirrors (anoplex.com, an everyspec copy); the specifications themselves are federal works, Distribution A. MIL-DTL-5002E (12 July 2011, superseded by F; read on everyspec, cited only for history: its section 3.6.12(a) limited the silver ban to titanium above 350 F / 177 C, citing silver embrittlement). Kept separate from dod-technical-manuals, which is the teaching-manual series.

sources.name: US Customs and Border Protection
sources.note: Informed compliance publication, Fiber Trade Names and Generic Terms, June 2006: the authoritative brand-to-fibre list (Dacron, Polartec, Supplex, Orlon, Kanekalon and so on). CBP itself warns the list is not exhaustive, and several brands map to more than one fibre. Wood Packaging Materials (https://www.cbp.gov/border-security/protecting-agriculture/wpm, last modified 2 January 2026, read 2026-10-04 for Salvage and Reuse): ISPM 15 treatments, HT with a 56 C core for at least 30 minutes, MB methyl bromide fumigation for at least 16 hours, DH dielectric heating to a 60 C core for one minute; the stamp carries the IPPC symbol, a two-letter country code, a facility identifier and the treatment code.

sources.name: Defense Visual Information Distribution Service
sources.note: Military public-affairs news. Cited for the April 2006 Marine Corps ban on polyester and nylon athletic wear in Iraq. Check each item's credit line: most DVIDS material is a federal work, but individual items can carry third-party rights.

sources.name: Bureau of Reclamation
sources.note: Research and Development Office project 8623 (FY2015), Potentiodynamic Polarization Testing of Zinc Anodes in Natural Waters: zinc anodes passivate in some fresh waters, and Reclamation tends to use magnesium anodes. Related record: data.usbr.gov/catalog/8513 (S&T Project 22021). Hydroelectric Power (booklet, https://www.usbr.gov/power/edu/pamphlet.pdf, undated; the PDF was made in April 2008; read 2026-10-04): output set by discharge and head; "More head or faster flowing water means more power."; theoretical horsepower = flow (cfs) x head (feet) / 8.8; one horsepower is 746 watts. Svoboda, Riley and Gee, Scoping Report: Public Safety of Low-Head Hydraulic Structures, Final Report ST-2017-1799-01, September 2017, read 2026-10-04 in the copy at https://damfailures.org/sites/default/files/wp-pdf/10-Reclamation-Scoping-Report.pdf because the Reclamation research site was down for maintenance: dangerous currents and hydraulic forces downstream of low-head structures.

sources.name: NASA contractor reports (via the NASA Technical Reports Server)
sources.note: Materials Data Handbooks: Aluminum Alloy 6061 (CR-123772, May 1972) and 7075 (CR-123773, April 1972), by Western Applied Research & Development under contract NAS8-26644 for Marshall Space Flight Center. NTRS metadata: stiType CONTRACTOR_REPORT, belongsToUsGov false, copyright determination GOV_PUBLIC_USE_PERMITTED. Not federal works under 17 USC 105, so cite facts in our own words and copy no text until the redistribution terms are confirmed. NASA-authored publications (Reference Publications such as RP-1228) stay under nasa-ntrs.

sources.name: Oak Ridge National Laboratory technical reports (via DOE OSTI)
sources.publisher: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, through the DOE Office of Scientific and Technical Information
sources.note: ORNL-TM-4396 (Swindeman, Feb 1974), type 304 plate: only the abstract was read, which says the measured yield was near the 30,000 psi minimum ASTM A 240 specifies. A contractor-operated national laboratory's report is not automatically a 17 USC 105 federal work, so licence stays unknown and use facts until a specific report's status is checked.

sources.name: Health Canada
sources.note: Industry Guide to the Flammability of Textile Products (modified 2026-03-05): three flammability groups, weight and weave, raised-fibre surface flash, the blend scaffolding effect. A foreign government work under Crown copyright, so facts only.

sources.name: UK Health and Safety Executive
sources.note: Lead in construction: keep heat guns below 500 C on lead paint. A foreign government work (Crown copyright, generally under the Open Government Licence); treated as facts per the rule for non-federal government.

sources.name: California Division of Occupational Safety and Health
sources.note: N95 Mask Commonly Asked Questions (Feb 2021): N95s do not protect against gases or vapours. A state work, so facts only.

sources.name: Code of Maryland Regulations 03.03.05.03, Specifications for Kerosene (ASTM D-3699)
sources.publisher: State of Maryland (read via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
sources.note: A state regulation, not a federal work, so 17 USC 105 does not apply and it is use: facts. The readable source for ASTM D3699 figures from the older edition Maryland adopted: flash point 38 C (100 F) minimum for 1-K and 2-K, sulphur 0.04 and 0.30 percent maximum, end point 300 C.

sources.name: Portland Fire & Rescue, Fire Marshal's Office policy FIR 3.07, Fire Performance Art
sources.note: A city work, not federal, so facts only. Revised 2018-08-02, reviewed 2019-12-30, read in full 2026-09-24. Fuel list, gasoline ban, kerosene outdoors only, 1 gal maximum, no glass, age 18 (16-18 by exception), 20 ft distance, two safety personnel, snug natural-fibre or fire-resistant clothing and no synthetics for performers and spotters, spotter's wet cotton towel of at least 15x24 in or a wool or Nomex blanket or duvetyne, 2A-10BC extinguisher per spotter, 5 gal water bucket for cooling burns, aramid plus fibreglass wicks recommended, sprinklers and a 12 ft minimum ceiling for indoor venues, NFPA 160 among its references.

sources.name: Seattle Fire Department, Permit Conditions 2511, Fire Performance
sources.note: A city work, so facts only. Rev. March 2025, based on the 2021 Seattle Fire Code. No Class I liquids (gasoline, white gas) without prior approval, only Class II or higher; two 2A-40BC extinguishers; a 2.5 gal bucket of water for the flame devices; 15 ft clear area; no fire breathing; snug natural-fibre clothing for performers and spotters (the sentence is garbled in the original and is read as an outright ban on synthetics); cites NFPA 160.

sources.name: Utah State Fire Marshal, Artisan's and Performers Safety Standards (compilation)
sources.publisher: Utah Department of Public Safety, State Fire Marshal's Office
sources.note: A state work, so facts only. Describes itself as a compilation, not a code. Chapter 9 on fabrics and costumes is consistent with other sources; its fuel chapters contradict themselves, so cite those with care. Sections 18.10 to 18.12 (stop rolling once a blanket is ready; open the blanket afterwards) and chapter 8 on substance abuse. It reprints third-party text (NAFAA Rev 2.1; the Home of Poi clothing Q&A and flame test in Appendix B): cite that material to its original author.

sources.name: ASTM International standards
sources.note: Paywalled; cite figures as facts, never copy tables. D3699 Standard Specification for Kerosine (current edition D3699-25, May 2025; the public scope was read directly, the 38 C flash minimum through maryland-comar). B338, B348/B265, B210/B483, B221, A269/A213/A554, A240, A666, A513, B107, B88: specification minimum strengths, mostly read as reprinted by producers (Kaiser, Totten). B633-19 electrodeposited zinc on iron and steel (type II coloured chromate; hexavalent-free passivates defined separately as types V and VI), read from a finisher's reprint.

sources.name: SAE Aerospace Material Specifications
sources.note: AMS 4944/4945 (grade 9 CWSR titanium tube), AMS 5643 (17-4PH bar).

sources.name: British and European Standards (BS EN)
sources.note: BS EN 755-2, 6082-T6 extruded tube minimum.

sources.name: ANSI C80.3, Electrical Metallic Tubing
sources.note: EMT dimensions (1/2 in trade size 0.706 in OD x 0.042 in wall). Not read directly: the dimensions come from the North American EMT table on Wikipedia, which does not name the standard.

sources.name: International Residential Code
sources.note: IRC 2021 R305.1 minimum ceiling height (7 ft).

sources.name: ASME B1.1 Unified Inch Screw Threads
sources.note: Standard 60-degree thread form, external thread depth about 0.61 of pitch. Used only for arithmetic; paywalled and not read directly. ASME conference papers are cited under peer-reviewed-literature.

sources.name: DNV recommended practices (DNV-RP-F107, Risk Assessment of Pipeline Protection)
sources.note: Classification society standard. DNV-RP-F107 (2001) Eq. 3 gives the dent energy of a pipe under a knife-edge impact after Wierzbicki and Suh (1988); expanded, the diameter cancels and the force for a given dent depth scales with yield x wall^1.5. Used for the staff dent index from 2026-09-25.

sources.name: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
sources.note: 84th ed. (2003) vapour pressure of the metallic elements (1 Pa temperatures: Cd 257 C, Zn 337 C) and melting points (Zn 419 C, Pb 327 C). Read as transcribed on Wikipedia's data page, which is itself cc-by-sa; cite the CRC as the authority and copy no tables.

sources.name: Metallic Materials Properties Development and Standardization (MMPDS)
sources.publisher: Battelle Memorial Institute, under FAA sponsorship
sources.note: MMPDS-04 (2008) figure on 6061-T6 strength after elevated-temperature exposure, read by eye and marked approximate wherever used. Successor to the public-domain MIL-HDBK-5, but MMPDS itself is sold and is not a federal work.

sources.name: Kaiser Aluminum tube and pipe data sheets
sources.note: Drawn tube minimums (ASTM B210/B483), densities, moduli, conductivities, corrosion and cold-workability ratings; 7068 brochure (strength loss at 150 C). Note the 7075 MPa column misprint documented in the research notes (alloys-final.json).

sources.name: Alleima titanium grade 9 datasheet and Safety Information Sheet
sources.note: SIS (Nov 2023): massive titanium not combustible, fines self-ignite, powder auto-ignition 250 C, melting at 1900 K, no water or CO2. Datasheet (Ti Grade 9 tube and pipe, updated 2025-05-09): modulus, strength at temperature from its graphs, usable to about 427 C (800 F) where oxidation begins, springback about twice that of stainless.

sources.name: Haynes International Ti-3Al-2.5V brochure
sources.note: Grade 9 developed for seamless tubing; heat-treatment range 371-790 C; standard 3/4 in walls.

sources.name: Fine Tubes titanium alloy data sheets
sources.note: Grade 5 annealed tube minimum (700 MPa); grade 9 thermal conductivity 7.6 W/(m K) and expansion 7.9 um/m per C.

sources.name: TIMET Titanium Design and Fabrication Handbook for Industrial Applications, and TIMETAL datasheets
sources.note: Titanium's tendency to gall; clean with non-chlorinated solvents before heating and after chlorinated cutting fluids; extremely hot grinding sparks and brilliant torch-cutting discharge; the TIMETAL grade 12 modulus.

sources.name: Zapp Titanium Grades 1-4 datasheet
sources.note: Last revised January 2022. CP titanium conductivity 22 W/(m K) at room temperature, melting about 1660 C, grade 2 strength at 315 C.

sources.name: Carpenter Technology alloy data sheets
sources.note: CP Ti Grade 4 data sheet (undated, accessed 2026-09-24): bar/plate minimum, hot strength, 204 C service limit, galling tendency, and a chart of CP titanium thermal conductivity for three heats, read by eye as roughly 17-23 W/(m K).

sources.name: Rolled Alloys 304/304L stainless data sheet
sources.note: Bulletin 1029, 2012: typical 304 yield 35/23/19 ksi at 70/400/800 F (21, 204, 427 C); density; modulus; melting 2550-2590 F; expansion 9.2e-6 per F.

sources.name: Sandmeyer Steel alloy 17-4PH data
sources.note: Advises against 17-4PH service above about 300 C. SSA Corp (ssa-corp) gives a higher limit; the two producers disagree.

sources.name: SSA Corp, 17-4 Stainless Steel (AMS 5643, AISI 630) data sheet
sources.note: Metals distributor data sheet: properties maintained in service up to the 600 to 800 F range, which conflicts with Sandmeyer's 300 C limit.

sources.name: AK Steel Type 201 stainless data sheet
sources.note: 201 density, modulus, conductivity.

sources.name: ATI technical data sheets (stainless and specialty alloys)
sources.note: ATI 430 TDS (version 1, 2012-07-13: ferritic, 16-18% Cr, annealing produces no phase transformation) and the ATI 410/420/425 Mod/440A/440C TDS (version 1, 2014-02-18: hardenable martensitic, oil quench from 1,800 to 1,950 F, cutlery).

sources.name: Copper Development Association alloy data
sources.note: C12200, C26000 (annealed elongation about 54-65%), C28000 (about 45-50%) and C36000 (free-machining brass, lead 2.5-3.7 percent) properties, read 2026-09-24. The alloy pages refuse plain automated fetches; a browser user agent gets through.

sources.name: Materion safety data sheet, Copper Beryllium Wrought Alloy
sources.note: Version 09, 2025: the hazard arises when cutting, grinding, heat treating or welding.

sources.name: TW Metals Safety Data Sheet: Magnesium (AZ31B)
sources.note: MSDS 700, revised 2022-02-08: magnesium alloys ignite near their melting point; smother with approved magnesium-fire powder; no water, foam, halogenated agents or CO2, and water on burning magnesium makes hydrogen and may cause an explosion. A named replacement for placeholder-manufacturer-sds on magnesium.

sources.name: DOW CORNING C6-540 Liquid Silicone Rubber safety data sheet
sources.publisher: Dow (DuPont Silicones at time of issue)
sources.note: Issued 2018-10-18: formaldehyde vapour above 150 C in air. A named product SDS, not a generic one.

sources.name: Henkel LOCTITE technical data sheets
sources.note: Threadlocker Blue 242 TDS (revised 2024-10-05): service -54 to 149 C, release by heating to about 250 C, not for plastic parts. LB 771 Nickel Anti-Seize TDS (Jan 2015): nickel based, prevents galling especially of stainless, rated to 1,315 C.

sources.name: Cardinal Industrial Finishes technical data sheet C241-BK109
sources.note: Polyester powder coat, cure 10 minutes at 350 F (177 C) metal temperature. The site serves a self-signed certificate.

sources.name: Guide to the Safe Handling of Fluoropolymer Resins
sources.note: 5th ed.: PTFE hazardous fumes above about 330 C; ultra-fine particles at 420 C; COF2/HF around 450 C; PFIB above 475 C; polymer fume fever from contaminated tobacco.

sources.name: American Galvanizers Association technical pages
sources.note: Industry trade association, not a federal source; labelled as such in the text. In Extreme Temperatures (last updated Oct 2019, read 2026-09-24): 200 C (392 F) long-term continuous maximum for hot-dip galvanised steel, not recommended above 250 C (480 F), about 350 C for under 2 h at a time or a single excursion under 24 h; the outer zinc layer peels above the continuous figure. These are coating limits, not fume thresholds; the page says nothing about fume. Zinc melting point from its welding page. NASA RP-1228's 250 F is an aerospace plated-fastener limit, not a hot-dip figure.

sources.name: TWI Job Knowledge: Welding of titanium and its alloys, part 1 (Gene Mathers)
sources.note: UK industrial research body, not a government. Oxygen and nitrogen diffuse into titanium above about 400 C and embrittle it; weld colours from acceptable straw to unacceptable light blue, grey and white.

sources.name: Parker O-Ring Handbook ORD 5700, Section VII compatibility tables
sources.note: Fuel ratings (gasoline, kerosene, Stoddard solvent, hexane, mineral oils, paraffins) and service temperature ranges for silicone, fluorosilicone, FKM, nitrile, PU, neoprene, EPDM and butyl. Long-soak seal ratings. The URL is a third-party copy of the Parker section.

sources.name: Shin-Etsu Characteristic properties of Silicone Rubber Compounds
sources.note: April 2025 edition. Silicone swells, softens and loses strength in gasoline and other non-polar solvents, does not decompose or dissolve, and returns to its former state when the solvent is removed; continues burning once ignited. Its numeric tables extract badly, so only its prose is cited.

sources.name: Permatex technical data sheets
sources.note: Self-fusing Silicone Tape 82112, rev 02/2019: silicone gum, 200 C continuous and 260 C intermittent, full cure 24 h, clean off oil first, fuel-exposure statement, listed as non-flammable.

sources.name: Rogers Corporation ARLON self-fusing silicone tapes
sources.note: Bonds only to itself, permanently within 24 h; 180 C continuous; flame-retardant grade (FAR 25.853). Accessed 2026-09-24.

sources.name: 3M product data sheets
sources.note: Scotch Rubber Splicing Tape 23 data sheet, July 2021: self-fusing EPR backing, 90 C operating, 130 C emergency overload. The example of a non-silicone self-fusing tape.

sources.name: Permabond Engineering Adhesives technical resources
sources.note: Silicone is difficult to bond; only silicone adhesives, or a cyanoacrylate over a primer, hold well. Accessed 2026-09-24.

sources.name: Nord-Lock Group bolting technical articles
sources.note: Basic thread engagement rule: about 1 bolt diameter in steel, 2 in aluminium.

sources.name: DragonPlate carbon fibre FAQ
sources.note: Standard epoxy products rated -75 to 140 F; the example of a resin working limit. Accessed 2026-09-24.

sources.name: Panasonic (Sanyo) lithium-ion cell safety data sheet
sources.note: SDS-IBT-00026, Aug 1 2013: keep away from heat and fire; above 100 C causes heat generation and ignition. Hosted by a retailer, but the document is the manufacturer's.

sources.name: Covestro, Makrolon: The chemical resistance
sources.note: Edition 2016-12: polycarbonate not resistant to standard petrol and diesel; aromatics crack stressed parts. Its table columns extract misaligned, so only the prose is cited.

sources.name: Viton fluoroelastomer safety data sheet
sources.note: MSDS v2.0, Sept 25 2008: HF and carbonyl fluoride decomposition products; above 315 C the surface may carry HF condensate.

sources.name: Davlyn Group Silco Sleeve Firesleeve
sources.note: Maker's own rating for silicone-coated E-glass sleeve: 260 C continuous, up to 1,200 C brief direct flame or molten splash. Vendor temperature claims only. Accessed 2026-09-24.

sources.name: Coleman Camp Fuel Safety Data Sheet
sources.note: Version 5.1, revised 2022-04-07. Composition (light hydrotreated distillate 60-100%, pentane/isopentane/cyclohexene 5-10% each, hexane 1-5%), flash point below -18 C, vapour pressure 5.3 psi at 38 C, H225/H304/H336/H361, P243 static, P271 outdoors, do not induce vomiting, UN1268 class 3 PG II. P378 says media other than water, but Section 5 lists water fog. No NFPA rating appears on this revision.

sources.name: Material Safety Data Sheet, Coleman Kerosene
sources.note: A named product sheet dated 2007-12-13: remove fuel-soaked clothing and launder before reuse; launder or discard contaminated shoes and leather gloves; CO, aldehydes and ketones on decomposition.

sources.name: Klean-Strip safety data sheets (Denatured Alcohol, VM&P Naphtha, Kerosene)
sources.note: Denatured Alcohol rev 2023-08-10 (ethanol 30-90%, methanol 5-60%, flash 7 C / 45 F Setaflash, H301/H311/H331/H370, blindness, delayed symptoms 6-30 h, solid water streams spread fire). VM&P Naphtha rev 2015-12-30 (paint thinner use, flash 69 F TCC; https://www1.mscdirect.com/MSDS/MSDS00052/70250410-20160522.PDF). Kerosene rev 2015-06-01, whose main ingredient is Stoddard solvent with up to 5% trimethylbenzene (H304, H315, H340, H361, H373; https://www.cochise.edu/_resources/pdfs/sds-library/construction/Construction-SDS-73-Klean-Strip-Kerosene-GKP85-Apr2022.pdf).

sources.name: Hess safety data sheets (Kerosene K1 and K2 No. 0290; Gasoline, All Grades)
sources.note: Both rev 2012-08-30. Gasoline: flash -45 F, benzene 0.1-4.9%, Carc/Muta 1B, use only as a motor fuel. Kerosene (https://monroetn.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Kerosene.pdf): CAS 8008-20-6, flash above 38 C, carcinogenicity Category 2, naphthalene 0.04%, autoignition 210 C (410 F), vapour travel, do not induce vomiting.
