sources.name: Building Science Education, Energy Basics
sources.note: Short, undated pages on building equipment written for trainers and homeowners, including water heaters (gas tankless, heat pump, solar). One of the live replacements for the retired Energy Saver pages (see doe-energy-saver); prefer ENERGY STAR where it states the same thing with a number.

sources.name: New Jersey Department of Health
sources.note: A state agency, so restate, never quote into the bundle. Its Legionella programme publishes Guidance for Draining and Flushing Your Water Heater (September 2025): a setting of at least 120 F, mixing valves, and who should stay clear of the job.

sources.name: Portland Water Bureau
sources.note: A city utility. Its water heater maintenance page covers a leaking relief valve (a new valve or an expansion tank) and anti-scald devices at high settings. It also gives a 115 to 140 F setting range, lower at the bottom than CDC's 120 F floor for Legionella; cite CDC for the floor.

sources.name: Building Safety Journal
sources.note: Explanatory articles on the model codes. Clifton, C.L., Water heater safety in the International Codes, 13 May 2019: what each relief valve discharge requirement of IRC P2804.6.1 and IPC 504.6 is for. The code text itself is icc-irc and is sold, so cite the requirement, not its wording.

sources.name: Washington State University Extension
sources.note: The land-grant extension service for the Silverdale locale. The Pacific Northwest Gardener's Handbook (chapter 8, home orchards; chapter 9, berries and small fruits), the Fruit Handbook for Western Washington (EB0937, 2008) and county Master Gardener sheets such as Black Walnut Toxicity (C032). A state university, so restate the fact, never the wording.

sources.name: Mississippi State University Extension
sources.note: Stafne, Chilling Hour Requirements of Fruit Crops, Publication 3067: which winter temperatures count as chill and typical needs by crop. Its table is for crops grown in Mississippi, so scope-check it for other places. Not to be confused with msu-extension, which is Michigan State.

sources.name: Virginia Cooperative Extension
sources.publisher: Virginia Tech and Virginia State University
sources.note: Tree Fruit in the Home Garden, 426-841 (first published February 2015, last reviewed November 2025), Table 1: spacing, yield, bearing age and life expectancy of tree fruits. Written for Virginia, so scope-check it. A state university, so restate the fact, never the wording. Monitoring Livestock Vital Signs, APSC-169NP, by Gregg, Clarke and Greiner, publication date 29 May 2025 (https://www.pubs.ext.vt.edu/APSC/APSC-169/APSC-169.html, read 2026-10-04): a string-tied veterinary thermometer for 2 to 3 minutes; normal adult rectal temperatures (cattle 100.4 to 103.1 F, sheep and goats 102.2 to 104.9, swine 100.4 to 104, horses 99.5 to 101.3), pulse (40 to 70, 60 to 90, 60 to 100, 28 to 40) and resting breaths (beef 10 to 30, dairy 18 to 28, sheep and goats 12 to 20, swine 8 to 18, horses 8 to 16), values it credits to LeViness, University of Arizona, BCH-3000; fever as one degree outside the normal range; activity and heat; pulse sites, not with the thumb; the skin pinch test (1 to 2 seconds), moist gums, medium pink gum colour and 1 to 3 second capillary refill, shock or internal bleeding.

sources.name: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory technical reports
sources.publisher: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, for the US Department of Energy
sources.note: Viswanathan, Mongird, Franks, Li, Sprenkle and Baxter, 2022 Grid Energy Storage Technology Cost and Performance Assessment, PNNL-33283, August 2022: round-trip efficiencies (Tables 4.4 and 4.6), cycle life by depth of discharge (Table 4.3, Table 4.5), calendar lives, lead-acid sulfation and the 80 percent cap. Like lbnl, a contractor-operated laboratory report is not automatically a 17 USC 105 federal work, so licence stays unknown and use facts until its status is checked.

sources.name: National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly the National Renewable Energy Laboratory)
sources.publisher: Operated for the US Department of Energy
sources.note: The laboratory formerly called NREL; its sites moved to nlr.gov (atb.nlr.gov, developer.nlr.gov, docs.nlr.gov) by 2026, and older documents still carry the NREL name. Annual Technology Baseline 2025, Residential Battery Storage (5 kW and 12.5 kWh, LFP cells, 15 year life, 85 percent round trip); the PVWatts calculator (version 8.5.0; inverter efficiency default 96 percent); NREL/CP-5700-90527 on charge controllers (copyright IEEE). A contractor-operated laboratory, so licence unknown and use facts, as for lbnl and pnnl.

sources.name: UL Solutions
sources.note: Public summary of UL 9540 (energy storage systems and equipment, drawing on UL 1973 for batteries and UL 1741 for inverters) and UL 9540A (the thermal runaway fire propagation test cited by NFPA 855). The standards themselves are copyrighted and were not read; cite only what the summary page says.

sources.name: Tesla Powerwall 2 datasheet
sources.note: Powerwall 2 AC, North America backup version, footer dated 2017-03-21: 14 kWh total, 13.5 kWh usable, 5 kW continuous, 7 kW for 10 seconds, 100 percent depth of discharge, more than 90 percent round trip at the beginning of life (25 C, 3.3 kW), minus 20 to 50 C operating, UL 9540 listed. An illustrative manufacturer specification only. Hosted by a retailer because tesla.com refused the download; data/machines/home.ron quotes a regional version giving 90 percent.

sources.name: SimpliPhi Power PHI battery installation manual
sources.publisher: SimpliPhi Power (now Briggs and Stratton Energy Solutions)
sources.note: PHI 3.8, 2.9, 1.4 and 730 lithium iron phosphate batteries, manual revision 073019: the 51.2 V, 75 Ah, 3.8 kWh rating; continuous and 10 minute currents; charging 0 to 49 C, operating minus 20 to 60 C; no charging below freezing (C/20 at most if unavoidable); the maker's claim of 10,000 cycles at 80 percent depth of discharge. An illustrative manufacturer specification. Its claim that the batteries cannot go into thermal runaway is marketing and is contradicted for LFP generally by DOE's 2024 energy storage safety plan; do not repeat it.

sources.name: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive planetary fact sheets
sources.note: Earth Fact Sheet (last updated 15 November 2024): obliquity 23.44 degrees, perihelion 147.095 and aphelion 152.100 million km, solar irradiance 1361.0 W/m2. Mars Fact Sheet (last updated 19 May 2025): obliquity 25.19 degrees. Maintained by NASA staff at Goddard. Moon Fact Sheet (last updated 11 January 2024, read 2026-10-03): surface gravity 1.62 m/s2, 0.165 of the Earth's. The Earth Fact Sheet also gives the standard acceleration of gravity as 9.80665 m/s2, exact (CODATA 2018).

sources.name: NASA Space Place
sources.publisher: NASA, managed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory
sources.note: What Causes the Seasons? (article last updated 29 July 2025). NASA-branded, but its pages carry NASA/JPL-Caltech credits and JPL is run by Caltech, so its licence is not assumed to be public domain: restate, do not quote, until checked. For numbers prefer nasa-nssdca.

sources.name: NASA Online Directives Information System
sources.note: NASA's own procedural requirements, written by NASA staff. NPR 8621.1D, Mishap and Close Call Reporting, Investigating, and Recordkeeping (effective 6 July 2020, updated with Change 4, read 2026-10-03), Appendix A defines proximate cause, intermediate cause, root cause and contributing factor, and says root cause analysis continues until organizational factors are found or the data are exhausted.

sources.name: Internal Revenue Service
sources.note: How long should I keep records? (last reviewed or updated 30 June 2026, read 2026-10-03): records supporting a return are kept until the period of limitations runs out, generally 3 years, with 4, 6 and 7 year cases and indefinitely if no return was filed. US federal tax law only; other countries differ. Topic no. 420, Bartering income (last reviewed or updated 24 September 2026, read 2026-10-03): bartering defined; the fair market value of goods or services received is included in gross income; barter exchanges file Form 1099-B, and the term excludes informal noncommercial swaps of similar services.

sources.name: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service
sources.note: Runs the National Organic Program. Its recordkeeping rule, 7 CFR 205.103 (read in the eCFR 2026-10-03), asks that records be adapted to the particular business, disclose all activities and transactions in enough detail to be readily understood and audited, and be kept not less than 5 years. Cite the regulation text through ecfr as well. Market News (https://www.ams.usda.gov/market-news, read 2026-10-03): free, unbiased price and sales information, thousands of reports a year, including local and regional foods. Grades and Standards: large buyers use the quality grades as a common language. Issuing agency of 7 CFR 56.76 (shell egg grading and packing plants, wash water rules) and of the National Organic Program rule 7 CFR 205.203 (manure and compost), both read in the eCFR 2026-10-04 for Chickens and Eggs; cite the text through ecfr as well. Hemp Production (https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp, undated, marked website updates in progress, read 2026-10-04): to produce hemp you first need to be licensed or authorized under a state, tribal or USDA hemp program.

sources.name: NASA Reliability-Centered Maintenance Guide for Facilities and Collateral Equipment
sources.note: September 2008, read 2026-10-03 from the PDF on nasa.gov. Defines reactive (run-to-failure), preventive, predictive testing and inspection, and proactive maintenance; run-to-failure as a conscious decision; the six failure patterns and three studies (United Airlines 1968, Sweden 1973, US Navy 1982) with random failures at 77 to 92 percent and age-related at 8 to 23; scheduled overhaul raising failure rates through infant mortality. NASA-created, but some sections (the bearing-failure percentages, credited to a 2003 trade article; acknowledged General Motors material) reproduce outside work: restate those, do not quote them.

sources.name: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
sources.note: Call Before You Dig! (https://primis.phmsa.dot.gov/stakeholder-comms/cbyd/, undated, read 2026-10-03): call 811 before every digging project, even planting trees or shrubs; all states require a call 48 to 72 hours before digging; operators mark lines with flags or paint; free. The www.phmsa.dot.gov pages refuse scripted downloads; the primis pages do not. Its four steps: call, "wait the required time for facilities to be located and marked, respect the marks and dig with care"; state laws set how long operators have to mark. Re-read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You: the same Call Before You Dig page, quoted for the four steps. Re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check, for Life in Soil (811 before the earthworm count) and The Ground Under You: "your call to 811 allows affected facility operators to locate and mark their underground facilities"; the one-call centre contacts "the companies that may operate underground facilities" in the area. That lines a household owns are therefore left unmarked is the guides' reading, labelled as such. Re-read 2026-10-04 for Foundations and Ground: "Every digging project requires that you call the one-call center before digging", even small projects like planting trees or shrubs; dial 811; no cost; operators must by law mark their lines with flags or paint; state laws set the notice; "Call 811 before you dig, every time."

sources.name: Bureau of Labor Statistics
sources.note: Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (https://www.bls.gov/oes/, read 2026-10-03; latest release shown 15 May 2026, for May 2025 data): wage estimates for about 830 occupations, for the nation as a whole, individual states, and metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas. bls.gov refuses our scripted downloads (an Access Denied page), so the guide read it through a page summary; an independent fact check the same day loaded it in a browser and confirmed the wording. Restated in the guide, which is safe either way.

sources.name: National Archives and Records Administration
sources.note: Holds the founding documents; its transcriptions of the Constitution, the Bill of Rights and amendments 11 to 27 are the source of the Library's Constitution page (docs/reference/us-constitution.md). Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to fix the Standard of Weights and Measures.

sources.name: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.note: DOI 10.18434/M32189; created 1 June 2003, significant update April 2012, last updated 27 April 2022 (read 2026-10-03). Chapter 1, Exploratory Data Analysis, edited by James J. Filliben of NIST, is the part cited: what EDA is, the underlying assumptions and response = deterministic component + random component, the run-sequence plot, measures of location and scale, and detecting outliers. Some other chapters were edited by SEMATECH and Advanced Micro Devices staff rather than federal employees: restate those, do not quote them.

sources.name: United States Census Bureau
sources.note: Understanding and Using American Community Survey Data: What All Data Users Need to Know (issued September 2020, read 2026-10-03): sampling error; margins of error at 90 percent and confidence intervals; standard error as the margin divided by 1.645; the significance test and the warning not to rely on overlapping intervals; inflation adjustment of dollar figures. It was drafted by the Population Reference Bureau, a private nonprofit, in partnership with the Census Bureau: restate it, do not quote it. Data Visualization Standards (beta, undated, https://xdgov.github.io/data-design-standards/, feedback to a census.gov address, read 2026-10-03): bar charts should always start at zero; consistent axes for charts meant to be compared; no 3D graphics. 2020 Census Gazetteer place file for Washington (https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/gazetteer/2020_Gazetteer/2020_gaz_place_53.txt, read 2026-10-04): Silverdale is listed as a census-designated place (LSAD 57, functional status S, a statistical entity), unlike the incorporated cities of Bremerton, Port Orchard, Poulsbo and Bainbridge Island.

sources.name: US Securities and Exchange Commission
sources.publisher: Office of Investor Education and Advocacy (Investor.gov)
sources.note: Ponzi Scheme page (https://www.investor.gov/protect-your-investments/fraud/types-fraud/ponzi-scheme, undated, read 2026-10-03): red flags including high returns with little or no risk, guaranteed opportunities, overly consistent returns regardless of overall market conditions, and unregistered investments and unlicensed sellers. Cite for warning signs only; neither it nor the Library is investment advice.

sources.name: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.note: Nail Gun Safety: A Guide for Construction Contractors, with OSHA, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2011-202, OSHA Publication 3459-8-11, September 2011, which states it is in the public domain (read 2026-10-03 from https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/209984/cdc_209984_DS1.pdf; catalogue record https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/6013): about 37,000 emergency room visits a year; full sequential triggers safest and contact triggers twice the injury risk; hands at least 12 inches from the nailing point; disconnect the air to clear jams; never bypass safety features; ANSI Z87.1 eye protection and hearing protection; seek medical care at once. cdc.gov and stacks.cdc.gov refuse scripted downloads; the PDF was fetched through the web reader. The niosh-pocket-guide entry covers only the chemical hazards pocket guide. Also used from the nail gun guide (re-read 2026-10-03): always shoot away from your body and co-workers; never use the nailer with the non-dominant hand; disconnect the compressed air when leaving the gun, on ladders and stairs, passing it, clearing jams and in maintenance; scaffolds rather than ladders, sequential triggers on ladders, three points of contact; safety shoes. The guide covers air nailers only and says nothing about cordless ones. Noise (read 2026-10-03): Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Noise Exposure, Revised Criteria 1998, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 98-126, June 1998 (catalogue https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/6376, PDF fetched through the web reader): REL 85 dBA as an 8-hour TWA with a 3-dB exchange rate; Table 1-1 (85 dBA 8 h, 88 4 h, 91 2 h, 94 1 h, 97 30 min, 100 15 min, 110 about 1.5 min); ceiling 140 dBA; the EPA-required NRR derated by 25, 50 and 70 percent for earmuffs, formable earplugs and other earplugs, minus 7 dB more for A-weighted levels; double protection above 100 dBA. Understand Noise Exposure (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/prevent/understand.html, dated 31 January 2024): "For each 3 dBA increase in noise level, NIOSH recommends reducing the exposure duration by half." Occupational Hearing Loss (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/index.html, dated 13 April 2026): decibels are logarithmic, a sound 10 dB louder is ten times more intense; both read through a page summary. Noise and Hearing Protection toolbox talk, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2026-118, September 2026, produced with CPWR (the raised-voice test at 3 feet; wash hands before inserting earplugs; a baseline hearing test, rechecked regularly): restate, do not quote, because of the private co-producer. Read 2026-10-04 for Moving Water Without Power: Request for Assistance in Preventing Occupational Fatalities in Confined Spaces, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 86-110, January 1986, page last reviewed 6 June 2014 (https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/niosh/docs/86-110/default.html): deaths often from air that is oxygen deficient or toxic; "More than 60% of confined space fatalities occur among would-be rescuers". Applications Manual for the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 94-110, January 1994 (catalogue https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/5434, which also records a September 2021 revision; the PDF read, fetched through the web reader, is the January 1994 scan with poor OCR, so restate rather than quote at length): the load constant of 23 kg or 51 lb, the maximum recommended load under ideal conditions; the standard lifting location (75 cm high, 25 cm out, less than 25 cm of vertical travel); the 1991 committee estimate that such a lift is acceptable to 75 percent of female and about 90 percent of male workers. Re-read 2026-10-04 for Framing a Building, from https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2011-202/pdfs/2011-202.pdf (the stacks.cdc.gov copy refused that day): "About two-thirds of these injuries occur in framing and sheathing work."; framing nailers "considered to be the most dangerous to use"; "The full sequential trigger is always the safest trigger mechanism for the job."; full sequential triggers at a minimum for placement work such as building walls, nailing blocking, fastening studs to plates and installing trusses. The month, September 2011, is not in the extracted text; Framing a Building gives the year only. Nail Gun Safety re-read 2026-10-04 for its protective equipment list: hard hats; "High Impact eye protection" as "safety glasses or goggles marked ANSI Z87.1"; hearing protection, "either earplugs or earmuffs". Preventing Deaths of Farm Workers in Manure Pits, NIOSH Alert, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 90-103, May 1990, marked public domain (catalogue https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/111477, read 2026-10-04 through the web reader; the record's summary, not the full PDF, which the site refused): methane, hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide and ammonia; oxygen deficient, toxic and/or explosive atmospheres from fermenting waste; a 31-year-old dairy farmer and his 33-year-old brother, who entered the pit to rescue him, both died; five farm workers died after consecutively entering a pit; pits to be treated as confined spaces. Keeping Animals pairs it with the 86-110 line on would-be rescuers, re-read 2026-10-04. Read 2026-10-04 for Wells and Groundwater: Request for Assistance in Preventing Occupational Fatalities in Confined Spaces, DHHS (NIOSH) 86-110, January 1986 (summary page at archive.cdc.gov, last reviewed 6 June 2014): oxygen-deficient or toxic air; test before entry; "More than 60% of confined space fatalities occur among would-be rescuers". Pettit and Linn, A Guide to Safety in Confined Spaces, DHHS (NIOSH) 87-113, July 1987 (https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/5830): what a confined space is; oxygen used up by rusting and bacterial action or displaced by carbon dioxide; never trust your senses; an unplanned rescue can easily become a double fatality. Read 2026-10-04 for Electricity and How It Flows, Where Your Own Electrical Work Stops and Power Tools: Fowler and Miles, Electrical Safety: Safety and Health for Electrical Trades, Student Manual, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 2009-113 (supersedes 2002-123), April 2009, updated by Michael McCann (CPWR) and Carol Stephenson (NIOSH), which states it is in the public domain (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2009-113/pdfs/2009-113.pdf, fetched through a page reader because cdc.gov refuses scripted downloads, and a copy at safety.duke.edu read alongside; the quoted wording is in both). Used: household wire colours and the 240 volt cable; contact with grounded plumbing; wet clothing, humidity and perspiration; the shock table (its endnotes credit Lee 1973 and Kouwenhoven 1968, so it is restated) with 15 amps as the lowest overcurrent at which a typical fuse or breaker opens; 100 mA for 3 seconds against 900 mA for 0.03 seconds; a small power drill using 30 times the current that kills; dry skin 100,000 ohms or more, wet skin 1,000; contact force and area; currents through the heart or nervous system; arc blasts (35,000 F, the pressure wave, molten metal 10 feet away, often from equipment failure); fire extinguishers; first aid; the case reports (the 277 volt lamp with a live white wire, the furnace switch live when off and the county inspector, the restaurant receptacle, the two lamps, the cross-wired fixture, the pool mixing motor, the drill on a metal ladder, the carpenter shocked all morning by his saw, the powder-actuated nails); the safety model questions; the lockout checklist ("Simply turning a switch off is NOT enough."); label breakers; work with a buddy; overloads a major cause of fires; breakers matched to wire size; extension cord gauge, motor starting current up to 200 percent and voltage drop; flexible cords not a substitute for fixed wiring; GFCIs at 4 to 6 mA, a shock still felt, the line-to-line limit; overcurrent devices do not protect people, 20 mA through the chest; removing panels and dead fronts as work near live circuits; jewellery; hair; Z87 glasses; tennis shoes; the job hazard analysis for changing a wall GFCI. Section 2's paragraph of thresholds (a tenth of an ampere for 2 seconds, 30 mA, 75 mA, 4 A, 5 A) rests on its endnote 2, McCann 2007, unpublished data, and was not used. Also used after the 2026-10-04 fact check (Publication 2009-113): the lockout checklist's "Test equipment and circuitry to make sure they are de-energized. This must be done by a qualified person.", with its footnote giving OSHA's definition of a qualified person; the common tasks that put a worker near live circuits, including opening and closing disconnects and circuit breakers and opening electric equipment doors for inspection; the left-hand rule for disconnects ("stand to the right side of equipment with a disconnect on the right, and operate the disconnect with your left hand").

sources.name: NASA Science
sources.note: Eclipse Safety (https://science.nasa.gov/eclipses/safety/, page last updated 20 March 2026, read 2026-10-03): not safe to look directly at the Sun without specialized eye protection for solar viewing, except in the brief total phase of a total eclipse; through a camera lens, binoculars or a telescope without a solar filter it will instantly cause severe eye injury; regular sunglasses are not safe however dark; safe solar viewers ought to comply with ISO 12312-2; looking through optics while wearing them, the concentrated rays will burn through the filter; the pinhole and cardboard box projectors, with the Sun at your back. The page text is NASA's; some photographs on it are credited to others (the National Park Service, named photographers), so use the text, not the images. Distinct from nasa-space-place, which is JPL-run and restate-only. Also: "Always inspect your eclipse glasses or handheld viewer before use; if torn, scratched, or otherwise damaged, discard the device." and "Always supervise children using solar viewers."

sources.name: Federal Geographic Data Committee
sources.note: Publishes the US National Grid standard, FGDC-STD-011-2001. How to Read a United States National Grid (USNG) Spatial Address (https://www.fgdc.gov/usng/how-to-read-usng/index_html, undated, read 2026-10-03): an alpha-numeric reference system that overlays the UTM coordinate system; grid zone designation, 100,000 metre square identification and grid coordinates; always read right, then up; an even number of digits; 4, 6, 8 and 10 digits for 1,000, 100, 10 and 1 metre; the Washington Monument at 18S UJ 23480647 (NAD 83). The USNG page (https://www.fgdc.gov/usng) records the Florida statewide emergency response plan adopting USNG and a 28 May 2009 FEMA memorandum on standardising FEMA operational maps on it.

sources.name: GPS.gov
sources.publisher: National Coordination Office for Space-Based Positioning, Navigation, and Timing
sources.note: GPS Accuracy (https://www.gps.gov/gps-accuracy, undated, read 2026-10-03): GPS-enabled smartphones are typically accurate to within a 4.9 m (16 ft.) radius under open sky, worse near buildings, bridges and trees; common causes of error are signal blockage, indoor or underground use and signals reflected off buildings. The page credits its smartphone figure to a paper published through the Institute of Navigation (ION.org); quote GPS.gov's own sentence, not the paper. The old address /systems/gps/performance/accuracy/ now returns 404; archive.gps.gov keeps the old page.

sources.name: National Eye Institute
sources.note: Presbyopia (https://www.nei.nih.gov/learn-about-eye-health/eye-conditions-and-diseases/presbyopia, last updated 4 December 2024, read 2026-10-03): the lens of the eye hardens with age and stops focusing light correctly on the retina; everyone gets presbyopia as they get older, usually after age 45; early on, hold reading material farther away, use larger print and brighter reading lights; later, over-the-counter reading glasses or prescribed lenses; checked in a comprehensive eye exam.

sources.name: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders
sources.note: Read 2026-10-03. Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/noise-induced-hearing-loss, NIH Publication No. 14-4233, text updated March 2014, page last updated 16 April 2025): sounds at or below 70 dBA unlikely to cause hearing loss, long or repeated exposure at or above 85 dBA can; the table of familiar sounds (conversation 60-70, movie theater 74-104, motorcycles 80-110, headphones at maximum volume and concerts 94-110, sirens 110-129, fireworks 140-160 dBA); human hair cells do not grow back; impulse noise can be immediate and permanent; tinnitus; temporary loss that disappears 16 to 48 hours later, possibly with lasting damage; prevention steps, including protecting the ears of children too young to protect their own and having your hearing tested. Hearing Protectors fact sheet (NIH Pub. No. 20-DC-8122, November 2020, PDF): avoid, move away or turn down first; a gunshot at close range can cause immediate and permanent damage; lawnmowers 80 to 100 dBA; the NIOSH Sound Level Meter app for iOS; the steps for formable foam earplugs, clean hands, not cutting the foam, twisting to remove; earmuffs easier for young children; gaps from glasses, hairstyles, hats and facial hair; consult a hearing health professional. Sudden Deafness (https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/sudden-deafness, last updated 14 September 2018): consider sudden deafness symptoms a medical emergency and visit a doctor immediately. nidcd.nih.gov allows scripted downloads. The fact sheet also lists where protectors are recommended: auto races, sporting events, fireworks and concerts; motorcycles, dirt bikes, snowmobiles, ATVs and tractors; band or orchestra; loud workplaces; and shooting sports.

sources.name: Health Resources and Services Administration
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services
sources.note: Funds the national Poison Help line (it does not run the poison centers). Poison Help (https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/, undated, read 2026-10-04 with full browser headers): "The Poison Help line is a toll-free line (1-800-222-1222) that connects you to your local poison center. You can call this number anytime and anywhere in the United States and many territories." (the page description). Read 2026-10-04 for Soap, Lye and Cleaning, with full browser headers (the /what-can-you-do/ and index.html forms of the URL return page not found): Prevention Tips (https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/what-you-can-do/prevention-tips, undated): more than 90 percent of poisonings happen in people's homes; products in their original containers; no food containers for household cleaners and chemicals; locked cabinets or out of the reach of children; "Bleach is especially toxic and should not be mixed with anything other than water."; "Never mix household or chemical products together. Doing so can create a dangerous gas."; no commercial cleaning products on food or food packaging, no bleach on food, no cleaners on hands or skin improperly. First Steps in a Poisoning Emergency (https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/faq/first-steps-poisoning-emergency, undated): fresh air; clothing off and skin rinsed with running water 15 to 20 minutes; eyes rinsed 15 to 20 minutes; call Poison Help. Household and Chemical Products FAQ (https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/faq/household-chemical-products, undated): why drink containers are dangerous for chemicals. Poison Help home page and Prevention Tips re-read 2026-10-04 for How Your Body Works, Invasive Species and Rats, Flies, Mosquitoes and Ticks: the line description; "Bleach is especially toxic and should not be mixed with anything other than water."; original containers, never food containers; locked cabinets or out of reach of children. Added after the fact check (read 2026-10-04): About Us (https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/about-us, undated): HRSA "funds the Poison Help line (1-800-222-1222), which connects you to your local poison center"; the Poison Control Program funds the network of accredited poison centers. The three guides now say HRSA funds the line, not that it runs it.

sources.name: North Dakota State University Extension
sources.note: A state university, so restate the fact. Its news pages offer reuse under a Creative Commons licence whose terms were not checked; treat as facts only. Take precautions when using heat lamps for newborn livestock, news release, 2 March 2023 (https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/news/newsreleases/2023/march/take-precautions-when-using-heat-lamps-for-newborn-livestock, read 2026-10-04): heat lamps hung from a non-flammable hanger, a chain with a locking connector, never twine or rope, secured as if permanent; heavy-duty lamps and thick glass bulbs; dust, cobwebs and insects cleaned off and wiring inspected before use; plugged directly into an outlet, not an extension cord, protected by both GFCI and AFCI, without overloading the circuit; a 10-pound ABC extinguisher at each entrance; lamps checked several times a day. Don't Risk Hay Fires, news release, 25 July 2011 (https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/news/newsreleases/2011/july-25-2011/don2019t-risk-hay-fires, read 2026-10-04): excessive moisture the most common cause; stacked small bales at 20 percent moisture or more and big bales above 16 percent; fires usually within six weeks of baling; caramel or musty smell; a pipe probe and thermometer, 10 minutes per site; planks and a safety line on top of a stack, never walking on the hay mass; above 175 F a fire is imminent; call the fire department and do not move the hay; spread suspect bales away from feed and buildings. Added after the 2026-10-04 fact check (Don't Risk Hay Fires re-read 2026-10-04): heating in all hay above 15 percent moisture generally peaks at 125 to 130 F in three to seven days with minimal risk, then falls to safe levels in 15 to 60 days; above 130 F (55 C) a chemical reaction begins to produce flammable gas; keep monitoring a heating stack's temperature; hay treated with preservatives containing ethoxyquin and butylated hydroxytoluene produces hydrogen cyanide, a deadly gas, at about 240 F (115 C); consider not piling the whole harvest in one area.

sources.name: Clark County, Washington
sources.note: A county government, not federal, so restate the fact. Safety tips to prevent a chicken coop fire, news release published 6 May 2021, quoting Fire Marshal Dan Young (https://clark.wa.gov/community-development/safety-tips-prevent-chicken-coop-fire, read 2026-10-04): multiple fires in the county caused by heat lamps keeping livestock or pets warm on cold spring nights; tips it credits to the National Fire Protection Association: secure heat lamps, a spring clamp alone is not adequate; heaters on sturdy surfaces; lamps and heaters away from anything that can burn; cobwebs and dust brushed off fixtures and outlets; covered bulbs; agricultural or commercial grade electrical equipment; no extension cords in coops.

sources.name: Cornell Waste Management Institute
sources.note: Healthy Soils, Healthy Communities project with GreenThumb, Cornell University Cooperative Extension-NYC and the New York State Department of Health. Understanding Your Test Results: Lead in Soil and Chicken Eggs (October 2012, https://cwmi.css.cornell.edu/UnderstandingTestResultsLeadSoilsEggs.pdf, read 2026-10-04): no US health-based standard for lead in chicken eggs; soil guidance values of 200 and 400 ppm used by the project; for run soil above 400 ppm, supervise and wash children, keep soil out of the house, add clean cover; where lead is high or not well characterized, feed, grit and calcium in feeders rather than scattered on bare ground. For gardens whose highest egg lead was between 0.10 and 0.30 ppm (the highest band on the sheet), it adds: keep chickens away from structures painted with lead-based paint and out of higher-lead soil; no unwashed garden scraps from such soil; remove dust and soil from eggshells before preparing eggs; lead may collect more in yolks than whites, so consider serving fewer yolks, especially to young children (used in Chickens and Eggs after the fact check).

sources.name: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook
sources.note: Web edition on nasa.gov. Appendix C, How to Write a Good Requirement (page last updated 26 July 2023, read 2026-10-04): Shall = requirement, Will = facts or declaration of purpose, Should = goal; a requirement on people in the form "responsible party shall perform such and such" (active voice); one thought per requirement; stated positively rather than as "shall not"; consistent terminology; ambiguous terms to avoid ("as appropriate," "etc.," "and/or," "but not limited to"); unverifiable terms to avoid (flexible, easy, sufficient, safe, adequate, when required, if required, appropriate, fast, small, large, quickly, easily, other "ly" words, among others); verification by test, demonstration, inspection or analysis; TBD values minimised in favour of a best estimate marked TBR with who resolves it and by when; a rationale including any assumptions; "What is the worst that could happen if the requirement was not included?" and "What is the worst thing that could happen if the tolerance was doubled or tripled?". The page does not say which print revision of the handbook it reproduces. Used in Making an Agreement That Holds for writing terms that cannot be read two ways.

sources.name: Digital.gov plain language guide
sources.note: The federal plain language guidance (the old plainlanguage.gov guidelines PDF now redirects here). Principles and Writing: Style pages, undated, read 2026-10-04: "Use the active voice."; say "must" instead of "be responsible for"; "Good examples can substitute for long explanations."; positive language, with the example "You have to arrive by 5:00 if you want me to pick you up"; avoid double negatives and exceptions to exceptions. The pages' header images are credited to others; use the text only.

sources.name: USAGov
sources.note: Find a lawyer and affordable legal aid (https://www.usa.gov/legal-aid, last updated 17 November 2025, read 2026-10-04): programmes that give free legal advice and may help you find a free or low-cost attorney; "Some limit their services to people with low incomes."; the Legal Services Corporation, for legal aid for people with low incomes. No usa.gov page on small claims courts was found on 2026-10-04 (https://www.usa.gov/small-claims-court returned 404), so Making an Agreement That Holds labels small claims courts as general practice. Corrected 2026-10-04 after the fact check: the page lists the Legal Services Corporation as "Find legal aid in your community for people with low incomes." and does not say it funds legal aid, so the guide says you can find legal aid through it.

sources.name: United States Code
sources.publisher: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, US House of Representatives
sources.note: Federal statute text, quotable. 15 U.S.C. 45(a)(2), Federal Trade Commission Act (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section45&num=0&edition=prelim): the Commission's power over unfair or deceptive acts excepts banks, savings and loan institutions described in 15 U.S.C. 57a(f)(3), Federal credit unions described in 57a(f)(4), common carriers and air carriers, among others. uscode.house.gov returned a maintenance page on 2026-10-04, so the text was read that day in the Legal Information Institute's copy (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/45); the LII site is not itself a government work, so Making an Agreement That Holds restates the statute rather than quoting it. Re-check against the official site when it is up. 16 U.S.C. 817, Federal Power Act section 23(b), 2023 edition at govinfo.gov (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title16/html/USCODE-2023-title16-chap12-subchapI-sec817.htm, read 2026-10-04): a licence for power works on navigable waters, public lands and reservations, or using surplus water from a government dam; a declaration of intention to the Commission before building on other streams within the commerce power, and a licence if the Commission finds interstate or foreign commerce affected.

sources.name: USDA Rural Development
sources.note: Site Standards: Well and Septic, Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Program, lender training slides, undated (https://www.rd.usda.gov/files/RD-SFH-SiteRequirements1.pdf, read 2026-10-04): shared wells limited to four households; a recorded agreement or easement required to allow for maintenance and access; a shut-off valve for each home; citing 7 CFR 3555.201(b)(4) and HB-1-3555 12.6 A 2. The handbook chapter was not found at its old address, and 7 CFR 3555.201(b)(4), read in the eCFR the same day, requires adequate utilities and water systems but does not itself mention shared wells. A loan programme's rule, not a general law.

sources.name: Training Within Industry Service
sources.publisher: US War Manpower Commission, Bureau of Training (earlier the Office of Production Management, Labor Division); digitised by the US Government Publishing Office on GovInfo
sources.note: The US government's wartime programme for training supervisors, established August 1940. Read 2026-10-04 on GovInfo. How to Train Production Operators, Bulletin No. 2-C, November 1940 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-PR32_4000-82bd222304cdb7d39d9b4ff67645adbe/html/GOVPUB-PR32_4000-82bd222304cdb7d39d9b4ff67645adbe.htm): the four aims of breaking in a new worker, including avoiding accidents that injure them; key points as "knacks, special motions, particular timing, or particular ideas"; seven steps from showing at full speed to putting the worker on their own; "you must interfere before harm is done"; not taking over too soon or too often. Management and Skilled Supervision, June 1944, US Government Printing Office (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-PR32_5200-762c0ca1c57da3ab3eb402f71f0684fa/html/GOVPUB-PR32_5200-762c0ca1c57da3ab3eb402f71f0684fa.htm): over twenty million workers on jobs relatively new to them; Job Instruction's get-ready points and four steps ("Continue until YOU know HE knows."); "If the worker hasn't learned, the instructor hasn't taught" (the OCR ends it with an asterisk); Job Methods; the Job Relations foundations ("People Must Be Treated As Individuals.") and its four steps for a problem (get the facts, weigh and decide, take action, check results); Program Development ("Train those who do the training."). Both are OCR text: quote with care and check against the page. The originals say "he" and "man" throughout; quote them as written. Notes from the 2026-10-04 fact check. The 1944 booklet says the programme "was established in August 1940 by the National Defense Advisory Commission and was continued under the Office of Production Management and then the War Production Board"; the 1940 bulletin on GovInfo is headed Office of Production Management, Labor Division, which did not exist until January 1941, so the digitised copy is probably a later printing of the November 1940 bulletin, and GovInfo titles it More Production Through Training: How to Train Production Operators. "Train those who do the training." is a step under GET PLAN INTO ACTION in Program Development, about preparing trainers, not learners teaching back. "Pre-position materials, tools and equipment at the best places in the proper work area." is a Job Methods SIMPLIFY step about workplace layout; the get-ready point for having things ready before instruction is "Have everything ready" (followed in the OCR by an em dash and "the right equipment, materials, and supplies."), so restate it rather than quote the dash. Job Instruction step 1 reads "Place in correct position."

sources.name: Institute of Education Sciences
sources.note: Pashler, H., et al., Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning, IES Practice Guide NCER 2007-2004, National Center for Education Research, September 2007 (https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/PracticeGuide/20072004.pdf, read 2026-10-04), which states "This report is in the public domain." Prepared under contract; the opinions are the authors'. Seven recommendations with evidence levels: 1 space learning over time (Moderate); 2 interleave worked examples with problems (Moderate); 3 combine graphics with verbal descriptions (Moderate); 4 connect abstract and concrete (Moderate); 5a pre-questions (Low); 5b quizzes to re-expose key content (Strong); 6a delayed judgments of learning (Low); 6b tests and quizzes to find what needs study (Low); 7 deep explanatory questions (Strong). Written mainly for grades 3 to 12: label any use for adults or practical skills as an extension.

sources.name: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services
sources.note: A federal agency, but treated as facts only until its terms are read directly: its copyright page refused our download (403) on 2026-10-04, and a search summary of AHRQ's publishing guidance reported that its products may be reprinted without permission in the United States for non-commercial purposes while users outside the US must ask permission. Use the Teach-Back Method: Tool 5, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit (https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/tool5.html, content last reviewed April 2024, read 2026-10-04): ask people to state in their own words what they need to know or do; yes-or-no questions such as asking whether they understand are not teach-back, since people tend to say yes either way; it checks the explanation, not the person; re-explain differently and ask again; chunk and check through the visit; the show-me method for demonstrating a task. Restated in Teaching What You Know.

sources.name: Wage and Hour Division
sources.note: Fact Sheet #40, Overview of Youth Employment (Child Labor) Provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for Agricultural Occupations, revised December 2016 (https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/40-child-labor-farms, read 2026-10-04): minimum ages; the hazardous occupations; youths of any age may work in any job on a farm owned or operated by their parents; exemptions for 14 and 15 year old student learners in vocational agriculture and for holders of 4-H or vocational agriculture training certificates; where state and federal law both apply, the more stringent standard must be observed. The fact sheet prints 'buckling' where the regulation says 'bucking' timber: quote the list from 29 CFR 570.71 (see ecfr).

sources.name: National Wildfire Coordinating Group
sources.note: After Action Reviews, Wildland Fire Leadership Development Program toolbox (https://www.nwcg.gov/wfldp/toolbox/aars, undated, read 2026-10-04): the standard four questions (what was planned, what actually happened, why it happened, what we will do next time), with about a quarter of the time on the first two, a quarter on the third and half on the fourth; a quick round-the-circle version for tired crews; reviews held as soon as possible by the people involved, with everyone taking part. Its facilitation tips are credited to two private consultants (December 2003) and NWCG is an interagency body, so restate rather than quote. The page links the US Army's Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews (December 2013), cited under dod-technical-manuals.

sources.name: National Invasive Species Information Center
sources.note: Species profiles for invasive plants and animals, with links to federal and state resources. Asian Jumping Worm (https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/terrestrial/invertebrates/asian-jumping-worm, undated, read 2026-10-04): Amynthas spp., native to east-central Asia; present in the US since the late 1800s and recently invading natural habitats in the Northeast and Midwest; possibly introduced through the horticultural trade or bait. The Forest Service dates the arrival to the early 1900s, so Life in Soil says only "more than a century" and gives both. What are Invasive Species? (https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/what-are-invasive-species, undated, read 2026-10-04 for Invasive Species): non-native and invasive not interchangeable (tomatoes, hot peppers, lettuce, domestic cows); spread primarily by human activities, often unintended (ballast water, firewood, accidental release, wood packaging, escaped ornamentals, released pets); extinction, biodiversity, habitats. The page quotes the Executive Order 13112 definition as it stood before the 2016 amendment.

sources.name: Mine Safety and Health Administration
sources.note: Read 2026-10-04 for The Ground Under You: Stay Out - Stay Alive (https://www.msha.gov/sosa, undated): the public campaign and its hazards at active and abandoned mines (hidden vertical shafts hundreds of feet deep, gases that displace oxygen with no visible sign, decaying roofs, unstable old explosives, tunnels, and water-filled quarries "deceptively deep and dangerously cold" with steep, slippery walls). Safety Alert: Stay Out of Abandoned Mines (undated; the PDF properties give 8 September 2026, https://www.msha.gov/sites/default/files/Alerts%20and%20Hazards/Safety%20Alert%20-%20Abandoned%20Mines.pdf): do not enter any opening, treat every one as deadly; never swim or dive in quarries or pit lakes; no exploring, drones or rope descents; report hazards; entering posted structures is trespassing. The two documents give different counts of abandoned mines (about 500,000 on the page; 17,000 underground and 56,000 surface in the alert), so no count is quoted.

sources.name: Residential Rehabilitation Inspection Guide
sources.publisher: US Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research; prepared by the National Institute of Building Sciences
sources.note: February 2000. Prepared for HUD by the National Institute of Building Sciences under Contract C-OPC-21204, and it says its statements and conclusions are the Institute's, so its wording is treated as not public domain: cite it as the authority and restate in our own words. Read 2026-10-04 for Roofs and Keeping Water Out and Repairing a Building: binoculars for roofs that cannot be reached or walked on; least slopes (asphalt shingles 3 in 12, 4 in 12 and up normal; wood shingles 3 in 12, shakes 4 in 12; slate, tile and asbestos cement 4 in 12; metal from 1/2 inch per foot); service lives (asphalt about 20 years, a second layer about 15, replace when granules go and shingles curl, no more than two layers; wood 25 to 30 years; metal 50 or more if painted; slate, tile and asbestos cement possibly the life of the building; built-up and single-ply about 20); brittle coverings not walked on; low-slope leaks hard to trace; skylights commonly leak; gutters (uniform slope, hangers 3 feet apart or 18 inches where snow lasts, a downspout per 40 feet, 7 square inch downspouts) and downspout discharge; ice dams where January averages 30 F or less, de-icing cables as possible evidence of ice dams; plumbing stacks and exhaust ducts not ending in the attic; load path checks by a structural engineer in high-wind regions; lead paint by age of house; wet basements common and mostly drainage, sometimes a clogged gutter; wall and ceiling cracks (settlement, deflection, warping, seasonal movement; flexible sealant for seasonal cracks; settlement cracks repairable once movement stops; clean versus dirty cracks; tapering cracks, sloping floors, sticking doors; cyclical masonry cracks not filled with mortar; hand measurement less precise; structural or soils engineer for severe settlement). Its code-related numbers are from 2000 and may have changed.

sources.name: Oklahoma State University Extension
sources.note: A state university, so restate the fact, never the wording. Huhnke, R. L., Harp, S. L. and Hubert, D. J., Cattle Handling Safety in Working Facilities, BAE-1738, published February 2017 (https://extension.okstate.edu/fact-sheets/cattle-handling-safety-in-working-facilities.html, read 2026-10-04): a 1997 study of 150 cattle handling injuries on 100 Oklahoma cow-calf operations found more than half due to human error, most often when people were tired, hurried, upset, preoccupied or careless; cattle see in all directions except directly behind, judge depth poorly (they stop and lower the head, so shadows and unfamiliar objects cause balking), hear very sensitively and move towards light; the flight zone, 5 to over 25 feet for feedlot cattle and up to 300 feet for range cattle, worked at its edge 45 to 60 degrees behind the shoulder; the herd instinct and the agitated lone animal; groups of up to ten; not entering a crowding area with bunched animals; not standing on fences or reaching between or over them; releasing an animal not properly caught in the chute.

sources.name: USDA Agricultural Research Service
sources.note: The USDA's research agency; runs the Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory in Logan, Utah. Protecting Our Livestock From Poisonous Plants, an Under the Microscope interview with Daniel Cook, the laboratory's research leader (https://ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/protecting-our-livestock-from-poisonous-plants, page last modified 10 January 2025, read 2026-10-04): livestock choose plants that taste good; some poisonous plants are palatable, and a hungry enough animal may eat unpalatable ones; larkspur highly toxic to cattle but generally not to sheep; death camas reported toxic to all livestock and to humans; poisonous plants very common on US rangelands; some landscaping ornamentals toxic to livestock; very few antidotes. The interview quotes Paracelsus; that quotation is not ARS wording and is not reused. Gross, Wang and Saltveit, eds., The Commercial Storage of Fruits, Vegetables, and Florist and Nursery Stocks, Agriculture Handbook 66, revised February 2016 (https://www.ars.usda.gov/arsuserfiles/oc/np/commercialstorage/commercialstorage.pdf, read 2026-10-04): commodity summaries for carrots (0 to 1 C, 98 to 100 percent RH, 7 to 9 months; bitterness from ethylene), beets (1 to 2 C, 98 percent; 4 to 6 months ventilated), potatoes (table stock 7 to 10 C after curing, to limit sugar; sprouting accelerates above 4 C (40 F), so seed tubers are stored at 4 to 5 C; darkness essential; greening is chlorophyll, formed with bitter, toxic glycoalkaloids that also form on bruising, wounding and sprouting and are heat stable; the sprouting and chlorophyll points added after the 2026-10-04 fact check), dry onions (0 C, 65 to 75 percent), pumpkins and winter squash (10 to 13 C, 50 to 70 percent; chilling injury below 10 C) and apples (-1 to 4 C, 90 to 95 percent; ethylene). Its chapters have authors outside the federal government, so restate its facts rather than quote it.

sources.name: Federal Register
sources.publisher: Office of the Federal Register (National Archives and Records Administration) and the US Government Publishing Office
sources.note: The daily journal of the US government: rules, proposed rules, notices and presidential documents, quotable. Executive Order 13751 of 5 December 2016, Safeguarding the Nation From the Impacts of Invasive Species, 81 FR 88609, 8 December 2016 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2016/12/08/2016-29519/safeguarding-the-nation-from-the-impacts-of-invasive-species, text read 2026-10-04 from the full-text file): amends Section 1 of Executive Order 13112; invasive species "means, with regard to a particular ecosystem, a non-native organism whose introduction causes or is likely to cause economic or environmental harm, or harm to human, animal, or plant health"; non-native includes "its seeds, eggs, spores, or other biological material capable of propagating that species"; introduction as a result of human activity. Whether the order has since been revoked was not checked beyond a search on 2026-10-04 that found no revocation; cite it with its date. Safety Standard Addressing Blade-Contact Injuries on Table Saws, Consumer Product Safety Commission, supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking, 88 FR 74909 to 74939, 1 November 2023 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-23898/safety-standard-addressing-blade-contact-injuries-on-table-saws, full text read 2026-10-04): blade contact without kickback, including a glove caught by the blade and debris brushed while the blade still spins after shutoff; staff's assessment that most blade-contact injuries are not related to kickback. A proposal: cite its findings, never as a rule in force. WITHDRAWN: Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions, Consumer Product Safety Commission, 90 FR 46541 to 46542, 29 September 2025 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/29/2025-18810/withdrawal-of-proposed-regulatory-actions, full text read 2026-10-04): the table saw rulemaking (the 2011 advance notice, the 2017 proposal at 82 FR 22190 and the 2023 supplemental notice above) is withdrawn with three unrelated proposals; "The Commission does not intend to issue final rules with respect to these proposals." Cite the 2023 notice only with the withdrawal stated. Its finding that most blade-contact injuries are not related to kickback is "CPSC staff assesses", based on the 2017 Special Study, the Power Tool Institute's figures and SawStop's activation data.

sources.name: Armed Forces Pest Management Board
sources.publisher: US Department of Defense, Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Energy, Installations and Environment
sources.note: Technical Guides on military pest management, each cleared for open publication; a guide marks any copyrighted material at its point of use, and only the Board's own text is quotable. Technical Guide No. 30, Filth Flies: Significance and Control in Contingency Operations, February 2025, cleared 20 February 2025, superseding the October 2011 edition (https://www.acq.osd.mil/eie/afpmb/docs/techguides/tg30.pdf, read 2026-10-04 for Rats, Flies, Mosquitoes and Ticks): flies as mechanical vectors, especially of diarrhoeal disease; the house fly lays 4 to 6 batches of 100 to 150 eggs in manure, carrion, decaying fruit and vegetables, kitchen refuse and cesspool material; moisture critical and fully degraded material unsuitable; eggs hatch in 18 to 24 hours at about 25 C, adults emerge from pupae in 4 to 5 days at best; recaptures up to 5 miles in 24 hours and dispersal up to 20 miles documented; garbage in fly-proof containers, serviced often enough to prevent breeding; sanitation the key, pesticides a backup; light traps with glue boards changed monthly and bulbs twice a year; electrocutor grids not recommended near food; fly swatters. Written for deployments: apply to a household with care.

sources.name: Microhydropower Handbook, Volume 1 (IDO-10107)
sources.publisher: EG&G Idaho, Inc., for the US Department of Energy, Idaho Operations Office
sources.note: McKinney, Warnick, Bradley, Dodds, McLaughlin, Miller, Sommers and Rinehart, published January 1983 (DE83006697), prepared under DOE contract DE-AC07-76ID01570; part 2 at https://www1.eere.energy.gov/water/pdfs/doewater-10107-vol.1-pt2.pdf. Read 2026-10-04 for Water and Wind Power: the power equation P = Q x h x e / 11.81 (kW, cfs, feet); microhydropower efficiencies of 40 to 75 percent and 60 percent for a first estimate; penstock head loss of 5 to 10 percent as a design starting point; Category 1 developers (supplying their own needs) designing for "the minimum stream flow of the year", the minimum available flow of late summer, with the 95% exceedance site flow usable as the minimum on a flow duration curve; the 60 percent efficiency used with the pool-to-pool head because it contains a typical site's head losses; overspeed of an unloaded generator to two to three times normal speed, worst at high head, and never opening the inlet valve fully at start-up with the generator unloaded or the turbine reaches runaway speed (the last three added after the 2026-10-04 fact check); the container, weir and float methods (float corrections 0.8 for a smooth bed, 0.6 for large rocks; a straight reach at least 30 feet long; calm days), at least four days of measurements and correlation with a stream gauge; the hose-and-pressure-gauge head survey (0.433 psi per foot; a 0 to 10 psi gauge for drops up to 20 feet; the hose end not pointed into the flow); surge pressure and the butterfly valve; powerhouse safety (guards on belts and shafts, rails at intakes, fences, locked valves and headgate, an emergency shutdown switch, an electrical fire extinguisher); the National Electrical Code, an electrical permit and inspection, an electrician qualified for generators, and leaving connections to the utility's lines to the utility; state dam safety permits. A contractor's report printed for DOE, so its licence is not confirmed: restate, do not quote. Its legal and cost chapters date from 1983.

sources.name: Western Regional Climate Center
sources.note: Average Wind Speeds - MPH (https://wrcc-archive.dri.edu/Climate/comp_table_show.php?stype=wind_speed_avg, read 2026-10-04): averages from hourly data for 1996 to 2006 at automated airport stations; BREMERTON AIRPORT AWOS (KPWT) annual 5.3 mph, monthly from 4.6 (August) to 6.3 (March). Hosted by a state research institute, so its licence is not confirmed: restate the numbers.

sources.name: MIT D-Lab
sources.note: Verploegen, Sanogo and Chagomoka, Executive Summary: Evaluation of Evaporative Cooling Technologies for Improved Vegetable Storage in Mali, MIT D-Lab, CITE and the World Vegetable Center (release announced by MIT News on 20 June 2018), read 2026-10-04: clay pot coolers and evaporative cooling chambers; the pot-in-pot design averaging a 6.7 C drop and 80 to 100 percent interior humidity; measured with outside humidity below 40 percent and 29 to 37 C; the devices need low humidity, high temperature, water and a shady, well-ventilated place. Licence not stated in the summary: restate, do not quote.

sources.name: United States Coast Guard
sources.note: Boating Safety Division material, read 2026-10-04 for Floating and Boats, Navigating Without Instruments and What to Do When You Are Lost. A Boater's Guide to the Federal Requirements for Recreational Boats, revised November 2023 (https://www.uscgboating.org/assets/1/AssetManager/Boaters-Guide-to-Federal-Requirements-for-Receational-Boats-20231108.pdf): drowning the number one cause of boating fatalities and in many cases preventable; "You should never leave the dock without first checking the local weather forecast."; a float plan left with a responsible person; a means of sending distress alerts, most commonly a VHF radio, channel 16 the primary calling and distress channel, and a mobile phone not a substitute though an added measure of safety; a GPS or similar to give rescuers an accurate location; carbon monoxide near the rear deck and swim platform; safe loading (33 CFR 183 subpart C): even, low, seated, secured, too many people or too much gear making a boat unstable; the rule of thumb for boats without a plate, persons = length x width / 15, based on a 150 pound person, not accounting for displacement, never exceeding a plate, and asking the maker, a sister vessel or a naval architect; "Do not anchor from the stern as this could swamp the boat."; semi-V, flat-bottom jon boats, canoes, kayaks and stand-up paddleboards less stable; "Standing in a boat raises the center of gravity and risks capsizing the boat."; climbing back in and practising it; staying afloat (calm, no removing clothes, heavy clothing and waders do not make you sink, air trapped in clothing, PFD kept on, knees bent, float on the back); cold water survival in three phases (cold shock passing in about a minute, incapacitation in the next 10 minutes, unconsciousness in as little as an hour); a capsized vessel floating on or just below the surface, smaller outboard vessels built after 1978 supporting you when full of water or capsized, getting in or on the boat; severe weather (head into the waves at 45 degrees, passengers on the bottom near the centre line, bilges free of water). Its cold water list also repeats that about 50 percent of body heat is lost from the head; the Library does not use that figure. Life Jacket Wear / Wearing your Life Jacket (https://www.uscgboating.org/recreational-boaters/life-jacket-wear-wearing-your-life-jacket.php, undated; its footer's "Last Modified" shows the current month, so it is not a date): most boating drownings on nice days; a wearable PFD saves your life only when worn; a foam jacket worn correctly fitting snugly and not riding up above the chin or ears; 7 to 12 pounds (31 to 53 N) of buoyancy for most adults; 70 N equals 15.74 pounds; user weight and chest size on the label, adult sizes not working for children, trying a jacket on in the water; the weight categories (adult over 88 pounds, youth over 55 and up to 88, child over 33 and up to 55, infant up to 33); inflatables listed in adult sizes only and not for weak or non-swimmers; the federal child wear rule. 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics, COMDTPUB P16754.38, foreword dated 24 June 2025 (https://uscgboating.org/library/accident-statistics/Recreational-Boating-Statistics-2024.pdf): 556 deaths; 76 percent drowned where the cause was known; 87 percent of those who drowned not wearing a PFD where wear was known (the executive summary gives the 87 percent right after the drowning figure; Table 35, fatal victims by PFD wear and cause of death, counts drowning 48 wearing, 310 not, 7 unknown, and all causes 104 wearing, 426 not, 26 unknown, so 80 percent of all deaths where wear was known: the 87 percent is the drowning figure, re-counted 2026-10-04 after the fact check); alcohol the leading known contributing factor, 20 percent of deaths; 69 percent of deaths where the operator had no boating safety instruction; swamping 262 incidents and 57 deaths, a person falling overboard 239 and 138, as primary incident types; glossary definitions of capsizing, swamping, flooding and sinking. news.uscg.mil refused scripted requests (403) on 2026-10-04. Also from the Boater's Guide, read 2026-10-04 after the fact check of Floating and Boats: "Some items that are not required but are a good idea to have with your wearable PFD are a whistle and an emergency light."; 406 MHz EPIRBs and PLBs designed to alert rescue personnel, indicate an accurate distress position and guide rescue units to the scene, "even when all other communications fail", and to be registered with NOAA; anchor line measured to where the anchor attaches to the bow.

sources.name: The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), Pub. No. 9
sources.note: Volume I, 2024 edition; its title page says no domestic copyright is claimed under Title 17 U.S.C. and that certain sections are subject to third party protection, so quote only NGA's own text. Downloaded 2026-10-04 through NGA's publications API as Bowditch_Vol_1_LoRes.pdf (listed as uploaded 17 May 2024; the direct view link returned 403). Chapter 10, Dead Reckoning, read for Navigating Without Instruments: the definition ("Dead reckoning (DR) is a method for determining the estimated position of a vessel by advancing from a known fix of position along the vessel's ordered course and speed."); "This is an approximate position"; its most important use in projecting the position ahead and avoiding hazards; comparing the DR with a fix to find wind and current; the four rules (at least every hour, after every change of course or speed, after every fix, after a single line of position); fix expansion, an error circle growing with time (0.5 nm at the fix, 2 nm per hour, 2.5 and 4.5 nm), errors assumed additive in the worst case; set (direction) and drift (speed) of current, leeway, the estimated position; set as the direction from the DR to the fix and drift as the distance over the hours since the last reset.

sources.name: NOAA Search and Rescue Satellite Aided Tracking (SARSAT)
sources.note: FAQs (https://www.sarsat.noaa.gov/faqs/) and Register Your Beacon (https://www.sarsat.noaa.gov/register-your-beacon/), both undated, read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost: a personal locator beacon designed to be carried by an individual, "They can only be activated manually.", used by people in remote areas; GPS-equipped 406 MHz beacons sending their position in the alert; registration required by federal regulations (47 CFR parts 80, 87 and 95), free, verified every two years; a used beacon re-registered by its new owner; the US Air Force responsible for inland and the Coast Guard (lead federal agency for US SARSAT) for maritime search and rescue.

sources.name: National 911 Program
sources.publisher: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, US Department of Transportation
sources.note: The 911.gov site says it is maintained by the National 911 Program, housed within NHTSA's Office of Emergency Medical Services. FAQ About Calling 911 (https://www.911.gov/calling-911/frequently-asked-questions/, last updated 8 March 2023), read 2026-10-04 with full browser request headers (plain scripted requests got 403) for What to Do When You Are Lost: the call taker's questions; "Do not hang up until the call-taker instructs you to do so."; call if you can and text if you cannot, a voice call still the best way, and a bounce-back message where text-to-911 is not available; "All wireless phones, even those that are not subscribed to or supported by a specific carrier, can call 911.", but phones without active service send no location and cannot be called back; more than half of PSAPs text-enabled in 2021. The FCC's own 911 consumer guides refused scripted requests on the same day (403, then a page-not-found redirect) and are not cited.

sources.name: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission
sources.note: The commission administers Washington's recreational boating law, chapter 79A.60 RCW, and its boating safety education programme. Statutes read 2026-10-04 from app.leg.wa.gov for Floating and Boats: RCW 79A.60.160 (a serviceable, appropriately sized, readily accessible life jacket aboard for each person; a child twelve years old and under wearing one on a vessel under nineteen feet while under way on an open deck or cockpit, except below deck or in an enclosed cabin, on a Coast Guard inspected passenger vessel, or where no one would reasonably expect a danger of drowning); RCW 79A.60.630 (the boating safety education programme, phased in to all boaters by 1 January 2016, a ten dollar card); RCW 79A.60.640 (a boater education card to operate motor-driven boats of fifteen horsepower or more, at least twelve years old, and its exemptions, among them people born before 1 January 1955). Washington does not place state works in the public domain: restate, do not quote. The commission's own boating web pages were not read.

sources.name: Washington State Military Department
sources.note: Home of the state Emergency Management Division and the State 911 Coordination Office; the department named in the state's emergency management law, chapter 38.52 RCW. Read 2026-10-04 for What to Do When You Are Lost: RCW 38.52.400 (https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=38.52.400: the chief law enforcement officer of each political subdivision responsible for local search and rescue, under state and local plans using the incident command system; the local emergency management director notifying the department of every mission; access to a search area restricted to authorised people; no unauthorised person to interfere with a search), read alongside RCW 36.28.010 (https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=36.28.010: the sheriff as the chief executive officer and conservator of the peace of the county). Texting911 (https://mil.wa.gov/texting911, undated): text-to-911 available statewide, every 911 centre able to receive texts; call if you can, text if you cannot; the dispatcher not necessarily knowing your location from a text; no texting while roaming; English only; no photos. Washington does not place state works in the public domain: restate, do not quote. Texting911 re-read 2026-10-04 after the fact check: as with all text messages, a text to or from 911 may be delayed, arrive out of order or not be received at all (restated in the guide, never quoted), so the guide adds, as its own reading, to keep trying to call when a text gets no reply.
